Amazon Prime offers password protection to prevent family members or other unwanted individuals from charging content to your credit card through a six digit pin. However the only way to input that pin (other than downloading an app to your phone) is to use an awkward scroll wheel, and additionally oddly marked buttons to get through the numerous number menu options. It is a bit of a pain. The voice control feature is a waste of money, it only finds items that Amazon can charge you for. I attempted to look up Thomas the Train for my daughter which was not only available free for Prime Members but was also on Netflix and Hulu which I had and was free, instead all it would find was items that Amazon could charge for. This is a common problem with the voice command feature. This when coupled with the horrendous navigation menus and difficulty finding what you want make this a poor choice considering other options from Roku, Apple TV and others. A little more tweaking and this could be a great product.

Unboxing these was a bit fiddly, with layers of boxing woven though each other and stuck together with stickers. The earbud case is small and smooth, with a button to open. if it were magnetically closed it would be a lot harder to get a grip to open it. The earbuds within are easy to get in and out, which is refreshing. I like the magnetic holding on other brands, like Jabra, my personal favorite, but they can be hard to get out and come out suddenly, which just ends with you tossing them under the oven or something.

Bluetooth connecting was smooth. I like to try all the weird new earbud designs, and I was intrigued by the donut shape of these. They're relatively easy to put on and are labeled with L and R. They don't have a snug fit, but instead just rest in the ear in a way that seems secure. There are some rubber bandy things that adjust the fit to several different sizes.

With the hollow center and more casual fit, these don't have a really immersive and deep sound experience, and they lack more advanced features like noise cancellation. On the other hand, they don't leave you with sore sweaty ears, and it's hard to beat a hole through the center for effective hear-through.

Sound is good as expected, though less immersive. Controls are minimalist, with no buttons and a double tap as the "do something" default for near every function.

They're a good set of earbuds for someone who finds most earbuds too obtrusive.

I was looking for a MAC time machine backup drive and noticed the external drives labeled as MAC were $10 - $15 more. I then read the Q&A on this drive and someone gave the most perfect instructions:

"right out of the box it's not Mac ready, but the solution is real easy. You go to Utilities and open up Disk Utility. With the drive plugged in, select it and go to the Erase tab and there should be a drop down menu with Format. Select Mac OS and click erase and after that's done, the drive should be formatted for Mac and you can save to your heart's content."

I might only add where to find Disk Utility in case you didn't know ... in finder go to the applications folder and in that folder is utilities and in that folder is disk utility.

I did just as the person in Q&A said and the second it was done reformatting a box came up asking if I wanted to use this drive as a time machine backup drive. I said yes, and within 107 seconds I was done. Color me impressed!

We got the 1tb drive because we have a 1tb 21.5" iMac from Nov 2013.

I hope this helps someone. I will update this review later as to longevity of the drive.

UPDATE: May 6, 2018
7 months later and this little backup drive does what it should do. We have never needed to utilize the files it stores, but it is nice to know the files are there. I periodically check to make sure my Mac is recording on this drive and it functions perfectly as a time machine drive.

One of my test recordings is the Erich Kunzel/Cincinnati Symphony recording of Tchaikovsky's "1812 Overture" with cannons, and the low-end loss was noticeable. The Toshiba KiraBook is technically an UltraBook, an ultra-thin laptop built for an on-the-go lifestyle. It has features of a tablet, though, and it brings an awful lot to the table. This particular KiraBook is more powerful than many notebooks on the market and is well-suited for heavy business use, though there are a couple of negatives that require mention.

The KiraBook was designed for extreme efficiency and utility while making it as portable and lightweight as possible. This means that, as is true with most UltraBooks, there are certain features that have been eliminated from the feature set. Most notable is the absence of a CD/DVD drive. If you need to read/write CDs or DVDs, you will need an external USB-based drive to connect to this system. Also missing is a VGA or DVI connector (though there is an HDMI port). Though this may not seem like a big deal on the surface, it is an issue if for any reason this system will need to be connected to a projector or an external display, something that business users often need to do. The most startling omission, though, is an Ethernet port - this system can be used *only* with wireless networks unless a USB-based Ethernet connector is connected to it.

With a 3.1GHz Core i7 processor, 8GB of RAM and a 256GB solid-state drive (SSD), Toshiba built this system for extreme speed. I timed the boot-up from completely powered off to sitting at the desktop and ready to work - 8 seconds. It is even faster when coming out of standby. I realize this is mostly a function of the SSD, but the CPU and quantity of RAM contribute just the same. Working with applications it is easy to see that this is a top-drawer system that is ready to work at a moment's notice.

As is true with other UltraBooks I have seen, the KiraBook is not upgradeable and has no user-serviceable parts. That is, the user has no ability to replace the hard drive or add memory without sending the system off for service. This is a double-edged sword: on one hand, it means that it is a maintenance-free system and the user does not need to be concerned with fiddling with the hardware. On the other hand, though, it does mean that when there is a need to replace the hard drive or memory, there's no getting around a service call.

This system comes preloaded with Windows 8 Pro. Most home users will not need the extra features that come with Windows 8 Pro but business users will see some benefit when the system is connected to a network. In particular, the Pro edition of Windows 8 allows for connecting to a Windows domain, allows for remoting the desktop as a host and allows for setting group policies. There are other differences between Windows 8 Home and Windows 8 Pro, but these are (in my opinion) the three primary differences.

One thing that caught my attention about this system that bothers me just a little bit is the ventilation. Toshiba put a minimum of ventilation on the base which, to me, does not look like nearly enough if the computer is going to be used under heavy load. It would be very advisable to use this computer with a cooling base if it's going to used in the same location most of the time. Now, that said, I have not noticed the system getting too hot when in use, but mostly it is handling such things as email and web surfing - under a number-crunching load I would expect it to get very hot and the fans to kick in.

The touch-screen features of the KiraBook make this a fine system for people who wish to have the features of a Windows tablet without giving up the keyboard. The touch screen works well and it is very responsive without being too sensitive. It does require some getting used to, especially when one is used to a standard notebook touchpad. It is possible to use a stylus with the KiraBook which will cut down on some of the "fat finger" errors when touching the screen but that could prove to be an inconvenience.

Aside from the touch features, the KiraBook has by far the brightest and most crystal clear screen I have ever seen in any system. Images on the screen are sharp, bright and colorful. The default resolution (2560x1440) is a little small though, especially on a 13.3" screen, and it may give some users a little trouble. Windows 8 makes setting the resolution very easy and there are a number of available lower resolutions, so users should have no problem setting the screen up to their liking.

Though it is mostly a matter of personal preference, I really dislike the touch pad and I turned it off. It is very large compared to most other laptop systems I have used and as a result I have a bad tendency to tap it while typing. There's something a little more serious about the touchpad, though. Looking very closely at it I can see through the gap next to the edge of the touchpad - that means there is enough clearance that stuff can get down inside through that gap. It's a small gap, but it's enough for a strand of hair to get in, and enough hair and dust in the system will cause heat issues.

The cover is a brushed metal finish and is smooth and attractive. This is a very handsome machine and is resistant to showing scratches and dirt.

My first order of business with this machine was to build recovery media. No manufacturer includes recovery media with their systems anymore and it is up to the consumer to generate the DVDs. Fortunately, Toshiba's utility for doing this is intuitive and straightforward and in short order I was able to generate a set of DVDs without much thought or effort. As a plus, the utility can be run to generate more than one set of media, which is not true of all manufacturers.

In operation, I have found no real issues with this system. As the specs would suggest, it is very responsive and the Windows 8 OS makes it very user friendly. Almost all frustrations I have encountered have been with Windows 8 and the learning curve from earlier Windows editions, not the physical machine.

Battery life has been very good though not stellar. Using the system primarily for email and occasional visits to the web, we ("we" being my wife and I) usually close the lid and let the system go into standby. When we do this, it lasts about 24 hours before it dies. So, plugging in the KiraBook every other day seems to work well for our needs. If doing things like software development or calculating math-intensive functions one could expect the battery life to drop significantly.

The KiraBook comes with 2 years of Norton 360 protection and also includes Norton's anti-theft package, which allows one to track the computer if it is stolen. I have had no issues with Norton on this system and I think Norton's security offerings have come a long way in the last 5-6 years - it stays out of the way, it does not seem to bog the system down and it's easy to use. The 2 years of updates is great - most new systems I have used come with only 30-90 days of updates.

I have mentioned that I would classify this machine as a business machine, not a gamer's machine. Though it has enough power to run some of the more resource-dependent games, the screen is a little small for gaming and the graphics processor is not up to the task of more recent offerings.

Toshiba has put together a nice system aimed squarely at business users who need a lightweight, powerful and user-friendly system that can move with them. The KiraBook is not without its faults but it is a very good choice when considering the target audience. I would not recommend it for gaming users, but for the traveling professional it is a good choice that's worth consideration.

I am very familiar with GPS units, though most of my experience with them is with hand-held sport units. I gave my wife a Garmin Nuvi for Christmas and it has been a great navigator so I was excited to work with the TomTom and compare it to the Nuvi. So far, while I cannot say one is better than the other, they are both different in the features they provide and they both navigate well. I do prefer the TomTom though that is a matter of personal preference at this stage.

The TomTom Start is a very solid unit and feels very well made. I am very pleased with the construction of the TomTom. It is built to handle a little jostling and a few bumps though I would make very effort not to drop it regardless. One thing I do not like, though, is the mounting cup. Yes, it does hold the TomTom in place very well and it is unlikely that it will "let go", but it is a little awkward to attach to the glass and the swivel is very stiff. Also, while trying to adjust the angle the mounting cup popped right off the TomTom and I had to reattach it.

Though I am no fan of the mounting cup, it does remove easily and this particular TomTom is no too big to fit in a third-party window mount. I have such a mount so I can work with that and be happy.

On power-on the TomTom comes up very quickly and is ready to go, a lot faster than I expected as the Nuvi is a little slower at acquiring satellites before it's ready.

The menu system on the TomTom is very simple and easy to use. The large, colorful touch buttons on the screen make finding the desired function straightforward. The first screen offered (after the welcome screen) gives just two choices: Plan Route and Browse Map. I especially like the Browse Map feature - when in an unfamiliar area it quickly shows proximity to gas stations, restaurants and other point of interest (which is very configurable). However, the points of interest list is not necessarily complete - there are at least two chain restaurants within a mile of the house that do not show at all on the browse map.

When not actually navigating, most of the time a user will spend is with the Plan Route function. There are a lot of options here. There is a selection for navigating Home, regardless of where you are, and since entering your home location is part of the start-up process this feature is at the ready almost immediately. Entering an address is likely going to be the normal method of selecting an endpoint, though there are other choices such as navigating to points of interest, a point on the map or even a latitude/longitude location. There is even the functionality to save a location in a Favorites list.

There are six choices for voices, though only three speak the street names - and of those, only one is in English (one of the others is Canadian French and the other is Latin-American Spanish). If you don't care about street names and you speak English you have choices. If you do care but do not like the built-in voices then you can go online and get more though there are associated fees.

I ran into some difficulty when I attached my TomTom to my computer, a Windows 7-based laptop. After messing with it I finally connected it to a 32-bit Vista machine and had no issues at all. I am not sure why it fought me on the Windows 7 machine but I am relatively sure that it has to do with my configuration, not the TomTom itself. (UPDATE: It was definitely on the Windows 7 side as I have had similar issues with other devices.)

Getting updates is easy. Once connected, TomTom Home (the application that interfaces to the TomTom) goes out and finds the updates, then with a minimum of interaction takes care of making said updates. Updating the map takes a while, which should be a given.

So, all this is great, but how does it navigate?

Voice aside, the navigation is good. The TomTom does a fine job of getting you from point A to point B using the conditions you stipulate: fastest route, shortest route, no highways, etc. The screen is acceptable in size to allow clear viewing of the map and the voice augments the visuals. I have not yet used it in the car to go to work; I am eager to see if it selects a better route for me than the one I have been using for the last 2-3 years.

The Tom Tom Start is my first exposure to TomTom's line of navigators and so far I am pleased with it. It's a little different than my wife's Garmin Nuvi, in ways I like. It's perfectly fine for navigation and finding points of interest, and the map updates on this model make this a device I will use for a long, long time.

UPDATE 03/20/2013: I recently had a good reason to use my TomTom in North Carolina - a family gathering in a neighboring town that was 10-12 miles away from the starting point. I was not at all familiar with the area so this would be a good test. All had printed directions, but we chose to allow the TomTom to take us there instead. The result was that we arrived sooner than others that left before us; we were guided on a very straightforward path that seemed more logical than the printed route (which came with a map). Going home that night, we again configured the TomTom to take us on the fastest route and it did so without a hitch - we knew that route very well already and the directions we were given were spot on.

And, I did use it to track to work to see if I could improve my route. With the exception of the first couple of miles (my commute is roughly 65 miles one-way), the route lined up almost exactly with the route I have been taking for years.

My opinion of the TomTom remains unchanged. It's a good navigator at a good price point and it has served me very well. My experience with TomTom has been very positive and I would not hesitate to recommend one.

For background: I don't have any affiliation with Ubiquiti, and I'm not a network engineer with inbuilt preferences or dislikes of networking equipment. I do have a lot of experience with all kinds of computing and networking technology.

For my relatively large house I've needed multiple wireless routers set up as wireless access points (WAPs), but over the years have gotten more and more frustrated with the limitations of this kind of setup. I could solve the signal distribution problem by setting up many WAPs, but I still had the problem that my devices wouldn't roam seamlessly from WAP to WAP as I moved around the house.

So this year I decided to look into a better solution. One option is a "mesh" solution like Eero, Orbi, or Google Home. Another option was to go with
wired WAPs, like these Unifi devices. After quite a bit of research, I decided to put my nickels down and try these "Pro" units. Why? Because I wanted (1) very strong wireless signals; (2) commercial grade manageability; (3) products already proved in the market, and favored by many experts; (4) products priced competitively.

I'm happy to report that after much tinkering and experimenting I'm absolutely delighted with these devices. I have three of them spread around the house, with a "Cloud Key" controller device (highly recommended) giving me management access from computer, tablet, or phone. I'm getting excellent bandwidth (usually at the max my phone/tablet will support), and trouble-free roaming. I'm able to see all relevant information, including interference information (from the pesky neighbors!) in the "console". I'm able to easily configure the networks, and updating the software and firmware is painlessly easy.

This is good stuff. Not for everyone, since you do have to be comfortable with technical details that would daunt the less experienced. What occurred to me after wasting half an hour with this thing is that what is needed is an iPhone app to control your television and stereo, not a single freaking light bulb and a long, long list of codes printed in mouse type.

See photo. The remote looks good, shiny Darth Vader black. There are three manuals, one of which is about an ounce and a half. One is a long list of codes and the third unfolds to about 10x17 so that between the three differently-sized printed manuals you have a lap full of clutter which is difficult to manage while you're trying to press buttons in some order.

I couldn't get it to do much of anything, and by the time I realized that half an hour had gone by and I was getting hot under the collar, I thought: FAIL. Why waste any more of my time? Ah, but by THAT time I was and am good and frustrated at this RCA product. RCA. Who knew they were still in business? Who the heck would buy an RCA product? I'm sure they made great gramophones back in the day, but Sony came by and ate their lunch and even that was forty years ago.

If you were an RCA exec, wouldn't you want to make certain that anything your company made was functional? I've got a couple college degrees. I can tie my own shoes. I can do all kinds of things, but I couldn't figure out how to program this little (EXPLETIVE DELETED) thing. Which frustrates me.

The first thing I noticed (after I cut the I-dare-you-to-open-me hard plastic packaging) was that it hurt to open the battery compartment. There's some idiotic L-shaped trigger you have to depress, meaning that you're digging it under your fingernails, which I think most people would find painful. Just a dumb design move. No other word for it. Dumb.

The remote looks good and has some interesting ribs underneath it. The buttons are not what you might expect, the volume and channel buttons are flabby feeling and weak, not definite-feeling. The center "OK" button is kind of clicky, like cellophane. There's a whole array of buttons, but it's not worth my time to try and program each one. And I grew to dislike the hard plastic feeling of the remote. There are other plastic materials that feel better to the hand. LOOK AT SONY PRODUCTS, RCA, LOOK AT SONY PRODUCTS FOR A FREE CLUE.

I'm annoyed and frustrated. This seemed like such a neat idea. But sitting on my couch juggling three differently-sized manuals AND this remote and wondering why none of these instructions were doing anything was really frustrating, just not how I want to spend my free time. I'll happily continue to exist with my TV remote, my surround-sound remote, my AppleTV remote and the AT&T cable box remote, you know? BECAUSE THEY WORK and they work without frustrating me.

Here's my idea: RCA hires an app developer and somehow figures out how to have your devices tell the app what their codes area. Something like that. Because the notion of combing through a manual full of codes in tiny type is worse than doing your income taxes.

THE WORLD HAS MOVED ON, RCA and you are apparently living in the 1970s with burgundy leisure suits and avocado-colored kitchen appliances.

STAY AWAY FROM THIS REMOTE, IT WILL ONLY FRUSTRATE YOU and dig in the skin under your nails. Ouch. Did this thing really have to be so frustrating? Do you imagine this is the kind of experience consumers are after? Not just one more freaking remote control, but one that promises convenience and delivers frustration? Not a good product. Stay away from it.

I've been using an Altec Lansing iM227 (a model that is no longer produced by Altec Lansing, but comparable models are still offered) for a couple of years and have been very pleased with it. The Xboom, however, gives me much the same performance at half the size.

The sound quality of the Xboom is impressive for the size. It puts out nearly the same bass level as the iM227, which is surprising given how small it is. It does suffer a bit in the mid and upper ranges, which do not come through as clearly and sharply as the iM227. But the output is more than adequate for enjoyment.

I really like how the two halves of the speaker can be closed up and turned into a small ball that is only about 2 inches tall. Very compact so it easily fits into a bag or jacket pocket - this speaker is designed to be carried around easily. It comes with a decent cloth pouch plus a USB charge cable.

While it will work when it is in its compact mode, for best sound it needs to be unlatched so it expands to about 3 inches tall.

Unlike the iM227 it has an internal battery (the iM227 runs on 3 AAA batteries). That's both good and bad: good for ease of use and compact size; bad in case the internal battery fails, which renders the speaker useless. The Xboom has a stated run time of "up to 12 hours" according to the specs, which is pretty accurate - I got about 10 hours out of a fresh battery. Recharge time is about 2 hours.

Operation is very simple: plug in the attached cable to your device (I'm using it as a speaker for a small mp3 player), turn it on, and listen. The Xboom has a volume control, which the iM227 lacks, and an on/off switch. There's a power indicator light on the bottom of the speaker.

Unlike the iM227, the Xboom can be daisy-chained to other Xbooms for a bigger sound. I only have one, so I can't say how well that works, but it's a nice feature.

Complaints are virtually nil. If I had to come up with something, I'd say that it would be nice to have the power indicator light on the top rather than the bottom so it would be more easily visible as a reminder to power down and save battery life. Minor point, however.

While the sound quality of the Altec Lansing is better, the size and convenience of the Xboom makes it the one I'll take along with me and use more often. Very good value for the price, and I would highly recommend it.

Keep in mind that since this has a PVC jacket, and since PVC produces toxic smoke, this shouldn't be run from room to room (per code) despite its long length.

Also keep in mind that cat8 doesn't do anything above cat6 unless you have a 10 or 40Gb/s NIC/SFP at both ends of your link, and the total link length is shorter than it was with cat6.

So unless you need a strong backbone link in a data center, don't think you need this.

For streaming Amazon and Netflix videos, playing Steam games, and general web browsing, the screen is beautiful and the computer has been working flawlessly since I got it four month ago. I have no complaints on those fronts. However, there are some other things to talk about.

One of the minor flaws is that the mouse turns off after several minutes of inactivity. You have to click it to turn it back on again before you can use it. That may sound like a trivial thing but it can become an ongoing irritant, especially if you work on several different computers and have to remember to click this particular mouse before usage.

Another minor flaw, one that became a major irritant for me, was that the screen would turn off after 5 minutes without any keyboard or mouse usage. It would even turn off while I was watching movies. In the Windows 10 Power & Sleep settings I would change the screen turn off time from 15 minutes to Never. That would fix the problem temporarily. However, every time I rebooted the computer, the screen turn off time would reset itself to 15 minutes. So I would have to go back into the settings to change it again.

Fiddling with the Windows power plan and scouring the net for solutions turned up nothing. Yes, the power plan was set the way I wanted it. No, the problem had nothing to do with a screensaver. No, there was nothing in the Bios that would trigger the reset. After four months of constant irritation, I finally stumbled across the solution by accident. It seems that ASUS has it's own power plan that overrides the Windows one. The default setting on the ASUS power plan was to turn the screen off after 15 minutes. Changing the ASUS setting to Never finally solved the problem. Why ASUS felt the need to put it's own power plan on their machine when Windows 10 already had a perfectly good one, I have no idea. I especially don't know why ASUS set their plan to override Window's.

That problem touches on the potentially major flaw with ASUS. In trying to find a solution to a minor problem on another ASUS machine, I found that their customer service sucks. When, after much effort, I finally got to talk with a live person, their accent was so thick that I literally could not understand what they were saying. When I asked for someone who spoke clearer English, the service rep got all huffy and I never did get to talk with anyone else and my questions never got answered.

This happened after I had already bought the ASUS Zen Z240-C1, otherwise I wouldn't have gotten a second ASUS machine. Now I've got my fingers crossed that nothing major happens to this one lest I get tangled up in their customer service mess again. So, this machine itself deserves a 4 star review for good performance with only minor flaws. However, ASUS customer service would get no stars from me at all and that will keep me from buying anything else from them.

I have purchased this for a small office, I run mail and a file server so I need to have the network up at all times.
The device is nice and easy to setup, concept is good and the price is not bad. This is where the good ends. I received the unit pulled it out of the box and started playing with it everything works well, then I turn off the stereo and I hear a very faint buzz coming from the unit. Since I work with electronics almost daily (component level repairs) I knew that the power supply will die soon, (it was a sign of a cheap ps).
I decided at only $130 im not going to send it back I will fix it myself (i don't really care about warranty).
Under the cover there are 3 boards. 1 relay outlet board, 2 power supply, 3 controller. The controller board (the one with the display) was ok, it didn't look bad at all. The relay outlet board I have found 2 cold solder spots, that would cause malfunctions with an outlet down the line. After fixing it I pull out the power supply and OMG, that this looks like someone was first learning how to solder, the board had a ton of faults, remaining flux and cotton from swabs. I decided to throw the power supply out instead I installed 12v to 5v converter for the controlls and connected 12v for relays. Installed external plug for a 12v ps and it works great with no problems.

This unit is ok.
It should have a good power supply (a $5 ps from china is 100 times better than what it came with)
It should be using solid state relays (it would be silent, and it would last much longer, also you would only need 5v to supply it)

Good Luck

This notebook lock and security cable works with laptops that have a Kensington security slot (about 99% of them on the market do), so it will work for most notebooks except the MacBook Pro. Be sure to check to make sure your laptop has the security port which looks like a small slot usually found in the upper right outside corner.

To use this cable run the end of the cable around a fixed object that can't be moved without effort or drawing attention, such as the leg of a heavy table or a post, then loop the locking end through the loop and attach it to your laptop. The locking mechanism has a built in bar that fits into the Kensington slot, so just insert it into the port, then turn the key 90 degrees to lock it in place. You'll need the key to unlock it when you're ready to take the laptop so be sure to bring it along. When you want to remove your laptop just rotate the key in the opposite direction to unlock it. This set comes with a spare key as well in case you misplace one.

Very nice high quality item, but you're sort of left in the wind to figure things out yourself. Here are some things to note, so you don't encounter the same issues as I did.

-The app to download is called PRINT MASTER. You'll naturally want to download Phomemo app, but you'll soon realize it won't connect with your printer. Then you'll notice there is a specific Phomemo 110 app, so you download that as well. But after installing this app, a pop up says "we are discontinuing this app, please download PRINT MASTER." There, I saved you from the run-around I encountered. LOL!

-You are given a starter roll of labels, but to use the templates in the Print Master app, you'll need to choose the proper dimension. It would be nice if this info was given in the manual, but the manual doesn't even mention the free roll. Everything is in mm, but I happened to have a mm ruler and measured the labels to be 40x30mm.

-Lastly, the most important advice you need to know is you need to turn on AUTOMATIC. You might ask AUTOMATIC what? My reply is.. EXACTLY. LOL! You see, once you go to print your label. There is a setting called AUTOMATIC. There is no explanation as to what this means. The default is WHITE, which is OFF. What it means is where it will stop after it prints your label. If it's OFF, it will NOT stop. It will continue spitting out blank labels. I saw a YT reviewer who had this issue, and I didn't think anything of it, until it happened to me. LOL! You need to turn this to GRAY, which is ON. It will then automatically stop after it prints your label. Why in the world is the default set to continuously print blanks? We all tend to use default settings because we trust the manufacture knows what's best for us. I mean why would you turn something on if you don't know what it does? So I can see why many make this mistake. But now you know. Turn it on! Even if you need multiple copies, for example 5 copies. You still need to turn it on, so that it will stop after 5 labels. I would love for someone experience with these things, or the seller, to comment below what that setting is for, and why is the default off?

I am usually not a big fan of on-ear headphones. I have learned through experience that Philips makes good headphones, though, and based on the brand name I selected this set of headphones to try out. So far I am pleased with them.

After wearing these for a while I need to take them off for a short time before I can put them back on and keep going. This is true with most on-ear phones I have tried. For on-ear phones, though, these aren't bad and the ear fatigue is less than many I have used.

This particular set boasts an on-demand bass boost, and for me that's a huge plus. Most headphones have the bass boost baked right in and there's no way to turn it off. I don't care for heavy-handed bass (gives me headaches), so for me it is a feature I will leave turned off most of the time. However, there are times when the bass needs some help, and these deliver. When activated, there is a very noticeable increase in bass response that will certainly make some people happy.

So, about the sound profile... A set of headphones isn't worth any amount of money if they sound bad. These are fairly balanced phones when the bass booster is turned off. The highs are bright and clear, the midrange is warm and the bass is present but not overwhelming. The bass becomes front and center when the boost is turned on.

These connect via Bluetooth and they pair and establish connection quickly. I have no complaints.

These are good on-ear phones that work well. They're reasonably comfortable, and they connect well. The most interesting feature, to me, is the on-demand bass booster which is better than having a continuous bass boost that's built in. For me, that's a major positive point and is the reason I will continue using these. These sound good.

Philips Magnavox PR1903C is a simple television set designed for the technologically apathetic. It has very few features and very few of the mechanical and technological updates one would expect in a modern television.

This television set offers the usual minimum features a consumer expects to find in any television- like adjustments for color, brightness, etc.- along with a few extras, like a language control that allows the consumer to switch from English to Spanish to French, sleep timer, and close captioning. Most all features have to be accessed from the remote control- the front of the television offers no such options- not even to access the menu. Also, there is only one input jack on the back of the television, placing severe limits on accessory compatibility.

If there is one redeeming factor for this television set, it is the quality of the picture.

This surprised me at first, because the overall quality of most everything else is below average, leading me to believe that the picture quality would follow suit. But the picture is actually quite good on Philips Magnavox PR1903C. The sharpness is very good and I cannot detect any small lines or other problems with the viewing. In this regard, the television set deserves commendation. I can't really find anything wrong with the picture quality for this type of set.

Going back to the negative points, I have noticed that this television set is prone to wear out a little faster than others. One sign of wear that is easily noticeable is the button on the front of the screen, to access the power. This button is a large, round button that is plastic in construction and is enclosed inside a round space. When pressing the button in, it is supposed to snap solidly in place but instead it rattles back and forth a little, making me worry that it is going to pop off. Of course, the way it is situated inside the round space, it cannot come out (as far as I know). But the looseness is obvious and it is a little surprising. With the limited amount of times the power button on the front of the television set is used (it is usually powered on/off with the remote control), I wouldn't expect it to wear out so quickly.

Overall, Philips Magnavox PR1903C is an unacceptable television set for the many reasons listed above. I like the sleep timer and the picture quality is certainly very good, but the strikes against this television are numerous. There are too many bad points to make it worthy of a recommendation.

Overall, this is a decent full-size USB keyboard. The keys are nicely sized and have a medium length throw. There’s little tactile feedback, making the keys feel rather mushy. But, on the plus side, it’s 100% silent in use – no clicky sound of any type.

The layout is a standard QWERTY with a separate number key pad and F1 to F12 at the top. There’s also a separate pad for cursor up/down/right/left.

The back light is very nice and has the unique feature in that you can change the color. There are several to pick from including a “mixed” mode that has several colors making for a rainbow look. Color selection is easy via a dedicated key at the top of the keyboard. Just press it to cycle through the colors. The back light can also be set to off.

The build quality is decent. It’s all plastic and pretty lightweight, but durable enough for normal use. There’s a kick stand on the back that folds out to prop up the keyboard at a comfortable angle, and non-skid feet to hold it in place. I had no problems with this staying put even when banging away at full typing speed. There is some flex in the frame when typing with force, but nothing horrible.

There’s a small area for resting your palm, but it’s rather short to provide much (if any) ergonomic support.

It does not have any indicator lights such as for caps lock, num lock, etc.

Installation is simple on a Win machine -- just a plug-and-play with no drivers needed.

While the overall design is nice and I love the back light feature (plus the ability to change colors), the lack of tactile feel and the lack of status indicator lights drops my rating to 4 stars. Still well worth considering as a replacement full-size USB keyboard, especially if you’re looking for a 100% silent keyboard.

Let me preface this review by explaining that I work in the IT industry and support a variety of businesses with enough thorough experience in networking to say with certainty - the router I received is absolute garbage.

Now, normally I'd say for this price that you should set you expectations quite low - being in the field I'm in, I understand that almost all consumer routers are not great options, and the ones that are somewhat viable are on the $300+ range. Not everybody has the money or cares enough to invest this much - I get that.

So, that leaves me and my old roommate pretty much one option; the TRENDnet Wireless AC1750. He doesn't need much and especially doesn't want to spend much, it was tough getting him to go high enough in price to even this router- the old router he had came with his cable subscription 3 years ago. It worked fine but was sometimes slow with downloading over WiFi, not surprising. From the research and reviews, and most importantly the price - we decided to try this Trendnet AC1750 router.

WOW what garbage - he no longer gets WiFi in his bathroom corner of the house - it is a VERY small 2 bedroom apartment. How in the world can this router not handle a signal from 20 feet away, with only 2 walls in between? A router of this caliber (even at this price) should EASILY be able to handle covering a 2 bedroom small apartment. Period.

UPDATE (11/1/2014): I'm getting complaints from my partner about how deaf I am and how loud I crank up the TV, so I figured I'd better get some headphones to use with my Samsung Smart TV (which is not Bluetooth-capable, so I'll have to get a transmitter). I gave up trying to use Bluetooth such a long time ago that I didn't realize these headphones were Bluetooth! I was hunting all over the place for a pair of wireless headphones with the look and feel of these, and in the process, I rediscovered these are Bluetooth! (Heck, it's been three years since I first got these, so forgive this little old lady for not remembering.) Anyway, I realized there were (were) two problems with me using these as anything other than wired. First is that the signals (the blue or white lights, which flash or breathe depending on what you're doing) can't be seen if they are under your fingertip. So you have to make sure you don't completely cover up the light. Second, it really does depend on what kind of Bluetooth-capable device you use. To test these, I paired them with my new MacBook Pro Retina. My old Mac didn't do very well, kept dropping the sound, couldn't stay paired, etc. I got a new MacBook Pro, now running Yosemite, and I'm sitting here listening to Pandora coming all the way through about 15 feet and a thick wall and it's great! And this is the "discontinued" set that I've had all this time. They charged up in very little time, too. So if you can get 'em, get 'em.

Because of very small ears and ear canals, I cannot successfully wear the in-ear headphones, but most over-ear headphones with decent sound that I've tried have been too unwieldy and uncomfortable to wear. Not these. The ear cups feel like memory foam covered with soft, breathable leather, and they conform to your ears, making for a pleasurable listening experience. They fit snuggly without pinching, and they have little brail-like raised nubs on the left side of the headband so you can tell in the dark how to put them on. (The wired cord fits into the right-side headphone cup, which is where the rest of the controls are.)

The wired sound is fantastic. I can hear all the nuances of the music even when it is turned down quite low, which is the way I prefer to listen to music; otherwise, my ears start hurting even at moderate volume. The wireless sound is also good, unless you walk too far away from your computer. I walked from my bedroom past the bathroom and into the kitchen, and only when I got into the kitchen did the sound start breaking up.

I had a terrible time getting the bluetooth pairing to work, though. (The instructions are terrible, and one should not have to go hunting all over Philips' website for the proper PDF to download just to get the headphones up and running the first time. I gave up looking and asked on the Amazon Vine forum to see if anyone else reviewing these headphones had found the requisite information; fortunately, somebody had.) I first tried pairing them to my MacBook Pro while visiting my sister in Atlanta, in a condo sandwiched between other condos, and could not get them to work at all. I had resigned myself to using them wired, but when I got home to my rural house, I was able to get them to connect and work by first deleting the original pairing and starting over. I don't know if I was experiencing interference or not. I have always found Bluetooth to be quirky, so I don't blame the headphones for what's clearly a Bluetooth issue, but Philips would do well to explain this most maddening aspect of their product a little better in a printed product insert.

Another thing that is badly explained is the setup for both input and output. I have not had the opportunity to test the internal headset/microphone and I'm not even going to try because I'm afraid I'll screw up the output from the headphones. I'm just using my computer's internal mic for any conversations I might have.

If you're looking for an inexpensive but very good radio \Bluetooth speaker, this is it. The sound quality isn't perfect but it's very good. If you're looking for speakers for dubstep or heavy bass, you'll need to spend more but it does have good bass for everything else. Additionally, the bass level is adjustable with the tone knob. It's loud, not house rocking loud, but loud enough to hear well outdoors from my living room.
I was surprised to see that this is not rechargeable but connects to the wall, so, not portable. This, however, was exactly what I wanted because every BT speaker I've had breaks down at the charger port. I bought and returned the SEVIZ "40 watt" (actually 4 ten watt speakers) in less than a month for exactly that reason.
I'm not surprised by all the complaints about the radio adjustment given that we live in a time that people have gotten used to everything being automatic, but if you're old enough to know how to use a radio like one from the 80s on back, it's not a problem. It is, after all, a "vintage", non digital, speaker. If you want more precise radio adjustment, buy one with digital tuning.
I get so many stations it's ridiculous and I live at 6000 feet, rural, at least a half hour away from all but two stations, so, if you're not getting stations you must really be in the boonies. I get stations from Mexico and I'm 45 minutes away. The stations also come in very clearly with no interference at all.
I have had a slight issue with the BT competing for a connection with my other speaker and then having a connection with no media or no phone and having to manually reset the connection, but this only happens if both speakers are on.
It's also very solidly built, although, it is manufactured in China. It's MDF, not wood, but it looks great. It's also not one of those vintage speakers you get and end up surprised at how dinky it is and how much it looks like a kid's toy. It's big for a BT speaker.
For the price, this is a great speaker. For the price, you're not getting a Kenwood, an automatic tuner, or tons of bells and whistles. If you want a good speaker for YouTube, TV, or other generalized use, this is it. I definitely recommend it. I'll update if anything untoward happens down the road.

This is a very solid speaker. It is heavy duty and it has metal housing. The sides are not as fragile as others I have used which sound this good. It comes in a beautiful gift box which has cushioning and the typical Santana design to it. The speaker itself is pretty heavy so it is not something you toss in your backpack and run off with. It needs a bit more care than that.

CHARGING
This has a USB charger that will take about 4 hours to charge it up with. There is also a connection where you can get a FAST charger from the company, but you have to contact them for it. The charging cable comes with it just need a USB outlet. The directions warn to only use the original cable that comes with this to charge or there might be damage to the speaker. The voltage must be 5V with current rated at 115A.

CAN THIS RUN WHILE CHARGING?
I do not see in the instructions warnings against this, and it does work while plugged in.

PLAY TIME
This speaker runs out of juice pretty quickly. If you want it to last the entire time of 10 hours, I highly suggest you not put the volume up past 30%. Any higher and the battery time runs down pretty quickly. At 60% you are at the edge of running this down pretty quickly- as in 4 or 5 hours play time only.

PAIRING
I have had no issues pairing this with tablets or phones using Android. Just like when you turn the power on, it says PAIRING in a very loud voice so you will know when it is in pairing mode.

VOLUME
The volume button on this is tricky. If you are not thinking and just quickly press the volume once, instead of it getting slightly louder, you will skip a track. You have to press the volume down and not let up if you want the sound to go up or down depending on the button you press meaning +/-.

CARD SLOT
This speaker can also work off of a TF card (also known as a microSD card). You just have to change from bluetooth mode to card mode using the MODE button.

IS THERE AUX CAPABILITY?
I have an old MP3 player that has higher quality recordings than anything new I have. That only uses AUX and it works great with this.

PAUSE / PLAY
You can pause or play music with this using the MFB button

HOW DOES THIS PERFORM?
Let me tell you, this thing ROCKS. I mean it. This speaker is fabulous. Not only does it work great out of the box (after being fully charged) but it sounds better and better as you break it in. It fills the house with music that is great quality and does not have interference or any lag issues either.

WHAT ABOUT BASS, MIDS AND HIGHS?
I have to say that this speaker is one of the few that I have used which does a beautiful job of intense bass, balanced clear highs but the mids are not muffled at all. It is impressive and what I thought a speaker always should be.

CAN YOU USE TWO TOGETHER?
This allows you to add one other speaker to the system so you can have them in two places. I do not have another Europa speaker at the moment I can test that with.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Although this blows any other wireless speaker I have had out of the water, it does blow through power rather quickly unless the volume is pretty low. It is not only amazing out of the box (After charging) but it gets better with more use. This baby ROCKS.

MY RATING
Finding a speaker which does not overwhelm you with out of whack bass, piercing highs, or muffled middles is not always easy. This speaker seems to divide it all out very well. It is one of the nicest speakers I have used (wireless) to date. FIVE STARS!

Not only do I love this, but would definitely consider a second one along with the fast charger in the future to round out the whole system.

ANOTHER THING
This product has a notification on it that some of the proceeds from this product will go to help underprivileged children through the MILAGRO foundation (miracle) that Carlos Santana and his family started in 1998.

I bought into the hype and some early favorable 'professional' reviews on this product (and am now convinced the website that posted it was probably paid by Whistler to hype up the release) and purchased it back in late June. I could have easily gotten a similar quality product for much less...or better yet, spent more and got a better, more reliable unit. Convinced that it wasn't working as advertised, I purchased a V1, the 'King' of radar detectors, and compared them in my car side by side. First off, the 78SE gives TONS of false alarms. Often it would go off when the v1 wasn't making a peep. Sometimes, it would go crazy when I was out in the middle of a road surrounded by corn fields! Is this because it is more sensitive? I think not. I had tested them on some speed signs set up in my area, and the V1 would go off a 1/4 mile or more before the Whistler made a detection. A 1/4 mile in the world of radar is an eternity--the difference between getting a ticket and not. By the time the 78SE starting making weak little burps warning you to start being on the lookout, the V1 was already going off at full blast. The v1 would also detect the speed radar when it was up and over a hill--presumably from the minute signature bouncing off different objects alongside the road. Again, not a peep was heard from the 78SE.

I am not saying I expect the 78SE to be as good as a $400 V1. I do, however, expect the performance to be enough to serve its purpose, which is warning you of radar before the cop has your speed. This detector simply won't do that, which makes owning it more or less pointless IMO. The numerous false alerts make you on guard when you don't need to be, and eventually you will simply ignore all the warnings--even the legitimate ones. When the real threats arise, it is doubtful you will know before the cop has your speed--MAYBE it will provide a small benefit in the most optimal conditions (a flat road going perfectly straight)...but how often is that the case? Save your hard earned $$ for a detector that will work...or if your dead set on spending less than $200, do more research and see if you can find something better or at least cheaper!

This is a very inexpensive, relatively low quality TV antenna. You get what you pay for. They advertise this for both indoor and outdoor use, but the mostly plastic construction will not last long outdoors in areas that get a lot of wind, ice, or bright sunlight. The attached 3 foot cable really tells you what their intended use case is. If your TV is near a window, hang the antenna in the window, plug it in, and you're done.

The advertised 50 mile range is for ideal conditions, mounting the antenna outdoors in an area where there are absolutely no obstructions between your home and the TV broadcast tower (no trees, no buildings, etc). Expect much worse range for an indoor mounting and if there are any obstructions. If you live in an area with trees etc, you should get a more sturdy antenna that can be mounted on a pole on top of your roof so it can receive a signal over the trees.

This antenna is advertised for UHF frequencies only. Most TV stations use UHF these days, but in my area there are a couple that use VHF and this antenna is not usable for those channels. If you really want VHF, I suggest getting a different antenna from this one.

I am very happy with the Totu 12 in 1 USB C Hub. I am very impressed with almost every aspect of this device. The port placement is perfect for my needs and preferences. It has every port you could really need for the next 6 months to a year, at least considering how fast tech changes. I love the Display port on it as it's the first USB hub I have owned with a DP on it. I go through a lot of USB hubs but this one I am going to try to hang onto. The only thing I don't understand is why they bothered to put USB 2.0 ports on there when they are all backwards compatible, at least as far as I know. I'm guessing it has something to do with interference but I am not sure on that.

I think the size is perfect because of all the features, but it is a little larger the some but still extremely portable. The USB ports on this do not charge devices very well but that is normal and to be expected. I really don't use the HUB for video very often so I really didn't use graphics ports more then to test out the display port to add a fourth monitor to my system. It had no problems working with my Alienware M17xR4 with AGA, The AGA has an ASUS Rog Strix 1080 Ti in it with 2 27" Monitors and a 55" TV attached to it. I was able to add a fourth monitor using the DP on the USB hub, but the 4th monitor also worked through the video card as well. It took a little load off the graphics card but seemed to slow down the system a bit. It's kind of like using the internal monitor on the laptop when docked. I am guessing it was attempting to use the internal GTX 1080 or Intel graphics adapter but didn't confirm my theory on that. The fact that it worked at all actually kind of surprised me. My laptop usually stays docked and attached to the Alienware Graphics Amplifier. When I do take it with me this hub is a true life saver.

Data transfer rates were higher then expected even when using multiple ports at once. This is also the first USB C hub that I have found that allowed a second USB C hub to be installed on a different USB C port. Not sure if it's designed that way or just luck though. Usually both are not detected only one, but for some reason I am able to connect both and that's how it should be considering that was the goal of USB in the first place.

Overall this is one of the best hubs I have owned to date. It adds a lot of functionality for a good price. The Micro-SD and SD card readers are easy to access and use. It's very user friendly and required no real setup even in my advanced environment. That kind of shocked me to be honest. It even works with virtual machines when configured. This is an excellent product that pretty much stays connected to my system now. In my opinion it's definitely worth the price and you won't regret this purchase.

This is a surprisingly good radio, especially since it is also a shortwave receiver. It is a hefty size and weight so I would not advise taking this in your backpack on a long hike, but it would be great for camping and to have as an emergency radio at all times. I thought about putting this on my shoulder next to my head and walking down my neighborhood reminiscing the 70's, but luckily my husband talked me out of it.

The local stations come in loud and clear and adjustments in sound quality can easily be made with the adjustment knobs. Setting the clock was difficult for me and it took several tries before I finally got it set. You will definitely need the instruction booklet on how to set everything that you want set. The antennae is super long and just keeps extending almost to the ceiling. I had to turn off the beeps that you hear every time a button is pushed, it was really getting on my nerves and it eats up battery power. D-cells are required if you don't choose to use the included power supply. Makes for a little extra weight, but it's a good weight, much like the radios back in the day when they lasted forever.

It's simply loaded with features that will take some time to figure out how to use and set and I will only be using a few of them. I don't particularly need any alarms but if you do they're there. Using the shortwave aspect is not as easy because you will have to spend some time trying out the various SW settings and slowly searching for reasonably clear stations. I still want to hit on a station from China but so far have only found about 3 stations that I can actually understand what they are saying. I'm not disappointed in this because I have 3 other shortwave receivers and I get the same thing from them. It takes time and practice to find what you are looking for.

Overall, I think this is an absolutely excellent radio and highly recommend it to anyone who is looking for a larger, heavier quality shortwave receiver radio. I could easily take this to the pool or use outside while working to listen to my favorite AM or FM stations since it has such a robust sound.

Short story of the review is that these are just as they say they are--a pair of relatively inexpensive "basic" earphones. As such, they seem to be a decent value and have some good points, but if you're looking for sound quality over price, you'll want to go elsewhere.

Pros:
Packaging: small and minimalist as it should be

Provided with: multiple size earbuds caps and ear inserts (more on these later), a very short charging cable, and a decent zip-around traveling pouch

Pairing: No problem with any of my Apple devices. Instantly recognized and paired with an iPhone (8 and 6), iPad (Pro and Air 2), and MacBook Pro. Couldn't be quicker or easier each and every time

Comfort: This was an issue for me, though obviously this is a pretty subjective category. I had to step down immediately to the small caps/rings, which is no surprise--I do that with I think all of my earbuds. But even with the smalls I just couldn't get a a good seal or a comfortable, though oddly enough much worse with my right. The left was not "great" but was certainly good; right was a bad seal and wholly uncomfortable no matter what I tried. Weird.

Sound quality: Again, it's a matter of pricing here. I don't own many basics and it's been years since I've had a set of lower-tier earbuds, so it's hard for me to compare at an equal level. The sound is what I'd call adequate, especially for exercise or listening to an audiobook. But there's no comparison to my PowerBeats3 or Jaybird X2s, and not even to my Jabra Elites, which I"d call my mid-range ones. The first two are in a whole other class in terms of range, sharpness, richness, and comfort, while the Jabras are a good step up in both sound and comfort. Sound here is more than a little thin at both ends, and just not very rich or full. Less noticeable with an audiobook, but definitely not the buds I'd choose if I'm focusing on listening to music, as opposed to having background sound while I"m doing something else. Phone quality is pretty similar--adequate, at times a bit muddy.

Controls: easy, intuitive, and responsive

Overall, if you want a basic set where quality of sound isn't a deal breaker, or a pair of cheaper ones for places you might have to worry about forgetting them, these will suit the bill, assuming you don't have the same comfort issue I did. But for someone looking for rich, full sound, particularly for music, I'd strongly advise moving up the ladder

So I picked one at random and decided to record it just to write the review and then I can add this to the pile of gadgets that I don't use anymore.

That wasn't easy either. You have to start it recording, let it go for the amount of time that you want (this isn't mp3 downloading where you can get a few hours in a few minutes), and make sure your computer doesn't go to sleep. Also, the station dropped out after about 20 minutes and when I came back 4 hours later I discovered that the software doesn't reconnect you automatically, so you really have to use this to listen to music at your computer and then replay the same music in the same order in your car.

The device is also missing features that I just assumed it would have like identifying when songs start and stop to separate tracks, identifying the music and labeling the tracks so I know what I am listening to, or the ability to mark a song at the unit while I am playing it back and later be reminded to go buy that song.

The device was very easy to set up, despite the fact that my 64 bit version of Windows doesn't support their 64 bit client and I had to run the 32 bit version (not a big deal just not sure why they bothered to include the 64 bit version if it doesn't work). I updated to the latest software quite easily as well.

This is a buyer beware situation. The device works as advertised, but has no bells and whistles that aren't mentioned in the product description (like auto-reconnect, which I would consider a standard part of this device's operation). And it is easy to use (if you don't mind baby sitting it). But you can access 100 times that many radio channels online and record them using free software that will do these other things and then download them to your mp3 player in minutes (assuming that you have one, if not check out the Samsung ones and remember to get one with speakers if you will ever want that capability, don't waste your money on a Zune or an IPod unless you have a good reason to).

For me, the product was a free test product, so I didn't waste anything. but I would be returning this if I had paid for it.

We have an old DVD player in our basement that tries to up convert but it is not always that great. It has some nice features that were great when we got it, but we wanted another one to replace it that did not take up so much room.

WHAT THIS WAS USED TO REPLACE
The DVD machine this replaced was a really old Philips. It played all regions. No fancy settings, except a sleep timer setting that shut it off after so long. The menu was ancient and very clumsy to navigate.

DID THIS PLAY AS WELL AS THE OLDER ONE?
This DVD player played DVDs as well as the older one. So far we have not had any issues with it. It was only hooked up to the HDMI and the used a mini USB to USB cord the plugged into the outlet. We made sure that it was powerful enough to run the player.

PICTURE
The picture was comparable to the old DVD player- perhaps a bit nicer in some cases. I am actually surprised that it has performed as well as it has.

TRAVEL
I have to say that traveling to a cabin we go to occasionally was nice. We are able to bring this DVD player with us to plug into any TV and watch some DVDs if we want to. It is without TV service so DVD is the only way to really have entertainment if we want it.

DOES IT PLAY BLURAY?
This is not designed to play BluRay.

ANY ISSUES?
This is not a top of the line DVD player with super high definition. If you are looking for that, this isn't it. Is it good DVD quality? Yes. I think so. If you have the right set up, it is a great way to take up little room and still be able to play DVDs. I am not sure I would have this as my permanent player in my bedroom or anything. But it is great to use once in a while at home or travel.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Although this is not fancy or super high quality, it plays DVDs as well or better than our old player so we are happy with it. The footprint is small and it is portable.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is a decent player and so far has been good in a pinch to use for playing DVDs. I like the small footprint and portability especially when we have to go somewhere for a while. It is nice to be able to tuck it into our luggage/bags to take with us. The remote is a bonus.

- The "dynamic" picture mode looks good on a few shows but on others will seriously distort colors. - It doesn't support the normal phone "cast" features that pretty much every other TV and phone supports. It supposedly supports a screen mirroring feature via their own SmartThings mobile app but the configuration is so awful and inconsistent that I have yet to get any casting to work (I'm a techie so these things are not often difficult). Maybe in the future, Samsung will get their act together but right now it's a very bad buy for most people.

I have several of the Logitech M510, and think this is the best general purpose mouse you can buy. Do make sure you install the Logitech SetPoint software (you can download from their website) to properly configure the devices. You'll need that to make good use of the unifying receiver, among other things.

So if you're looking for a good mouse keyboard combo, I can happily recommend this set. Let's address the elephant in the room first: some reviewers reported that the offline model does not come back on after a complete power down, while other reviewers say it does. I assume that this was an old problem that has since been addressed. It seems that this line-interactive model (which I am reviewing) is new, and I feel 96% confident that this unit will come back up after a complete power down. However, I am not going to test it because even when we install industrial UPS units as part of telecommunications systems for my work as a Systems Engineer, we never drain the batteries 100% on purpose because it is known to shorten the life, same as car batteries. (My research into home models does not address this as a feature of line-interactive versus standby models, but line-interactive are supposed to be more active, as you can imagine).

That said, if I ever have a power outage long enough to find out for sure, I will update and let you know (I do actually update some of my reviews, especially when it's something I use every day like this).

Anyway, I wanted this most for my (2) 4-bay QNAP NAS boxes. They are both relatively low power devices, and I have pretty good power at my home, but it is so very aggravating when a split-second outage takes them both down (for quite a while because they are slow to reboot) and then they both yell at me that I need to scan all the disks and the file system is not clean, etc., etc.

I noticed this model didn't have some of the features I deem unnecessary, like the front LCD display stating some basic information, and the coax and RJ-45 line protectors (I have all my cabling systems grounded extremely well), but the one thing I was concerned about is that I wouldn't be able to use the power software since I wouldn't be leaving this plugged into my Windows server (co-located with the two NASs, but with its own battery, so very clunky to try to use as the master on a setup like this).

The great part is that, the QNAP operating system immediately recognized this unit, allowed me to do a master/slave setup with the two NAS units, AND I can even see the battery status and estimated runtime directly on the NAS without the need of the downloadable software on the Windows Machine. I can even see it on the slave device. Setup was incredibly easy, and it appears you can have at least 6 slaves, although I'm not sure if it allows for more if you fill in the first six devices. This is awesome.

And you can configure the two NAS devices to power down after x minutes once power is lost OR to go into safe mode after x number of minutes and then come back to life when power is restored. Perfect. And that pretty much negates any need to configure with the software on windows.

The only thing the software for Windows really shows you that the NAS doesn't is your power draw, but you can plug it back into there to see that if you want to add a device to backup power, and then put it back on the NAS. Once the systems are stable, your backup time should stay about the same, and then of course you can assume that your load is the same as well.

After adding just 1 NAS, I had a 45w load and an estimated run time of 155 minutes!
After adding the second NAS, I had a 72w load and an estimated run time 113 minutes!

I have a custom, very cool, but unfortunately always-too-small telecom closet that I have to do a lot of screwing around with before I can add the additional loads, but my intent is to add:

device 3) router/primary switch connecting DVR to network
device 4) cable modem
device 5) DVR for security cameras
device 6) Power supply for cameras

The idea is it will allow for graceful shutdown of my servers, but keep the security stuff going for as long as possible.

My readings at the panel for this entire load was anywhere from ~110-206 watts, with an estimated average of 176 watts. I'll let you know what my runtimes are once I schedule an ASI (authorized scheduled interruption) here at the house and get everything else up and running (for those of you who like numbers).

Also, this is smaller than I thought for this load rating. Very happy about that, because one of the reasons I've waited this long to get a UPS is because my telecom closet is so cramped. This works out so nicely that I can't believe I didn't do this years ago. Would have saved me a lot of headaches. And for all the systems I have in my house, it's sort of insane I didn't have a decent UPS before.

Anyway, I'm quite happy with this one, and especially its easy integration with my 2 NAS systems.

It was easy to set up and works really well. Much faster than my Linksys 54G. I can't believe I waited this long and put up with dropped internet as long as I did. I have 10 devices running through this and it handles them with ease. Satisfied.

I have been a fan of Seagate drives and have a few that I got years ago that are still working great. This model, however, lasted less than a day before quitting. While drive failures happens regardless of the brand, this is the second Seagate that has died on me shortly after using it, making me wary of the brand.

The overall look of the drive is somewhat unique, with a metal casing that looks like an old style drive. It comes nicely packaged and includes a USB 3.0 cable. Granted, you’re paying a lot for the look – a 750mb brand name drive can be purchased for a lot less than this price point. Given the price point, I was surprised that it did not include a padded case to protect the drive when it's carried in a laptop bag.

Startup was simple – just plug and play. The drive self installed and, after just a minute or so, I had access to the files that come loaded on the drive. In addition to registration and warranty info, it includes the Seagate drive utility software. I’ve used prior versions of that and was not impressed with the functionality, so I didn’t install the utility.

Initially it worked fine, and I was able to copy files back and forth without incident. It had decent speed and it worked well from both a USB port right on the PC as well as one on a USB hub. It does not need an external power source, so there’s just one cable needed for use.

After copying a bunch of files I took a break, but left the drive plugged in. When I returned a few hours later and tried to copy more files, all I got was drive not available errors. Unplugged and replugged the drive and it was recognized as a drive, but said I had to format it before use. Tried to format it, and the format failed. Did the unplug/replug dance a few more times and, although it was receiving power and I could feel the drive spinning, the blue indicator light would not come on any more.

Given how quick this failed, I can’t give it more than one star (and zero stars would be more accurate). Since these types of drives are most often used for backups, reliability is key. It seems Seagate drives are no longer as reliable as they were in the past.

Note: at the time of this review this cable set is described as '3.5mm Male To 3 RCA Cable' when it's really a 3-RCA male to 3-RCA male for composite signals. My HDTV has legacy composite jacks to connect older DVD players and I am using the review sample that I received for that purpose.

I replaced it with a premium grade cable by Monster, which cost me significantly more than this one is priced at, and there is no discernible difference in video and audio quality.

The outer shield is slightly different in appearance form the standard 6 cut ones that most RCA connectors employ, but the fit of this set is as precise as others that I have used, and the integrated strain reliefs are some of the beefiest I have ever seen on any brand of RCA composite cable.

Among the reasons why I awarded this five stars is value (relatively low price with high quality construction). This set sports construction features that are not usually found in sub ten dollar cable sets (the price range at the time of this review). For example, the connectors are gold plated, and the copper wire is oxygen free. The overall cable is both flexible, but heavy duty and is not likely to fail if properly used.

My advice is if you are shopping for composite cable, consider this one before investing a lot more in a 'premium; brand that does not really outperform this one.

We bought this as a gift for our son, to keep him occupied on long car trips, and while traveling. It is compact and light enough to tote around without breaking your shoulder, and comes with accessories for playing in the car, an AC cable, and also has a rechargeable battery for wireless viewing anywhere. It even comes with a remote (but not a pretty one)

For adults this is a great little gadget - it never gets into a snit over bumpy roads or potholes, and with your headphones on, it can give you hours of viewing when you’d rather be alone. The screen even swivels around for the best possible picture in cramped situations.

For kids however, there are some things you should note:

1. The silver finish gets scratched and dirty quickly

2. The power is controlled by a slider button which doesn’t feel as sturdy as it should – ditto the button to open the section where the DVD goes

3. The button to open the player is right in front where little hands can accidentally press it while in use.

4. On the right hand side, there’s a button to choose the DVD format. This often slides to the other side when taking it out of the case, and fools you into thinking that the player isn’t working.

5. Our video display stopped working on Day 2, until we reset it by unplugging the player without turning it off and then plugging it in again.

6. The control buttons on the player itself are not very user friendly, and I still have no idea what some of them do, but I haven’t needed to use them so far anyway.

7. You can’t play old or scratched discs, as these will damage the player. (I don’t know about you, but most of my kid’s DVDs are scratched and battered)

Picture quality and sound are good, as is portability. Overall, this is a very convenient DVD player for traveling or commuting, but one that requires care and attention to work properly.

P.S. (Update to earlier review from March 2013 - added April 17th, 2013)
We found that the records only get as clean as you are willing to put forth the time and effort for. Since we wrote our review, we've seen and used one of the fancy automatic ones and believe me, this one does the job, better, if you're willing to put in the effort, without the over the top price tag. It uses the same cleaning fluid as the expensive motorized ones and does an even better job because you can pay attention to details and especially dirty spots, are cleaned easier with this system.
We also use the glue method when a recording is exceptionally dirty. Amazing! Wonder who thought this up? But, it does pull the dirt right out of the grooves! Between this system and the glue method (we use plain old white Elmer's School Glue) you can't get your recordings any cleaner. As SOON as we have a clean record, we play them into our computer, run them through our program to eliminate pops, clicks, and etc... and then download them as MP3 and/or put them on a CD. Then we put the records in a NEW sleeve to keep them clean and put the cover, old sleeve (if it's collectable) and the clean record in a new paper or static free plastic sleeve to store them until they are sold or needed again. If you're going to invest the time and money into old Vinyl, make it worth your while.
We also like the fact that you can re-use your fluid more than once and you can keep an eye on it and know when you have to change it. We have a recipe for the fluid but, it's also easily found on YouTube. This is the most economical way to clean vinyl you'll find and it probably does the best job, as well.
It seems now that Vinyl is seeing a resurgence now that these youngsters have found that MP3's are not the sound sensation they were led to believe they were! Some vinyl, no matter how popular, due to copyright laws and problems, will never see a new vinyl groove or cd pressed of them so we need preserve as much original vinyl as possible. This is the best way to do it at present!
One note, be careful NOT to wet the record labels. We do quarter turns and wait for excess to run off before turning again, but, you experiment and see what you come up with. If you find better ways, we'd love to hear about them!
