My first question was "What is 802.11ac?" - In December 2011 "802.11ac" was the next evolution of WiFi & enabled wireless speeds over a gigabit per second.

"b" was the first there was (802.11b) which provided up to 11 mbps data rates per radio in the 2.4 GHz spectrum.
"a" was the next evolution (802.11a) which provided up to 54 mbps data rates per radio in the 5 GHz spectrum.
"g"came out shortly after enabling 54 mbps per radio in the 2.4 GHz spectrum.
"n" was ratified in 2009 (802.11n) allows for data rates up to 600 mbps per radio.
"ac" builds on 802.11n.

setup took 2 minutes; I plugged the TP Extender into a wall plug outside the room the router was in. Wait until the `power' and `wi-fi' LEDs light up; then press the WPS button on the router (this is the reason it isn't going to work at a motel/hotel). Then I pressed the Range Extender button on the TP Extender the lowest on the front of the device (must do it within 2 minutes). The LED on the TP Extender should go from flashing to solid, showing that WPS connection has succeeded. Done.

tips:

there are 6 lights on the TP Extender the top two should be green, if they are RED your extender is too far from the router. If it is no color it means you need to reconnect the router and the extender by repeating the steps above.

> to minimize wireless interference keep the Range Extender away from cordless phones, Bluetooth devices and Microwave Ovens.

> If possible place the TP Extender in open corridors or spacious locations rather than a crowded room.

Frankly I have not noticed any difference in our wi-fi but we have a smaller home (1700 sq feet) the router we have is 2 years old and is in one room in the house while I use my 3 year old laptop (Sony Viao series E) in the livingroom 2 rooms away and 2 walls away. I do plan on bringing it with us on vacation where I am hoping that where we do get poor reception (where we have access to a router), we will get a noticeable improvement.

The device has a reset option (if the TP Extender doesn't seem to be working): While the Range Extender is plugged into a power outlet, press the RESET button (located next to the ethernet port underneath the TP Extender) with a pen for 1 second. Wait 2 seconds until all the LEDs flash once.

*Bonus - The Range Extender's ETHERNET port allows it to function as a wireless adapter for a wired devices (Blu-ray players, game consoles, DVRs and smart TVs) allowing the device to share the wireless network.

I've only had the August EP650 for a couple days now, and there are a number of quality, comprehensive reviews -- so I thought I would write something specifically from the perspective of someone who hasn't owned a stereo Bluetooth headset since they first came out.

The tech has come a long way, and I'm really quite pleased by how good these are for the price. If you're like me and have a bad recollection of the early days -- with the flaky connectivity and the terrible, tinny sound -- you'll be pleasantly surprised.

Build quality feels pretty decent for the price; comfortable; buttons are easy to find with the headset on, and I've been putting them on while taking public transit, without playing anything, just so I can concentrate on reading, and not the prattle.

So, thumbs up. If you've not been happy with Bluetooth cans in the past and don't want to spend too much to check them out again, the August EP650 is a very good option.

They did a quality job on these. Luxury without excess. Packaging is acceptable. The case feels great, the zipper is awesome. The headphones fit in very easily, and there is a mesh pouch inside for accessories.

The headphones have a giant L and R printed on the interior foam, which is convenient to figure out which way to put them on, but isn't visible once they are. The buttons are easy to access, labeled, and simple enough to remember.

Bluetooth was easy to connect and had audio cues.

I'm usually not a fan of gesture controls, but they work really smoothly and intuitively here.

The product itself feels high quality, and they're very comfortable and secure. Noise cancellation is fine, and a nice addition, but I don't find it notable. What was more impressive to me was just how little I noticed the usual irritations of wearing headphones. They don't have a background noise at all, they don't feel like they're going to fall off if I bend over or make a sudden move, they don't press uncomfortably, and they don't make noise when I turn my head.

I've tried a few modern wireless noise cancelling headphones, and I'd say some of the others win in one feature or another, but these are an excellent complete package.

To be fair - the card never gave me problems with Portal 2, Order of War, Medal of Honor and a few other games needing solid 3D rendering - it appears to be issue with World of Tanks game in particular.
Not sure whose fault it is: 1) may be game developers, with whom nVidia claims to have business partnership), but, equally valid, 2) it may also be nVidia drivers that crash the program (the issue seems to be reported more often with newer nVidia drivers by multiple players).
Anyway - if you're into World of Tanks a lot - I recommend picking up some decent Radeon card - the one I have on the other PC (HD 6870) never gave me any issues with my favorite game.

For the most part I have had good fortune with Logitech peripherals. As I write this I am using an MX Ergo trackball which is the best mouse/trackball I have ever used. I looked to the MK470 mouse/keyboard combination with the idea of using it with a laptop running Linux. I had high expectations for the keyboard but lower expectations for the mouse due to the size and shape. Both failed me, but in completely different ways.

I will start with this: this combo does not use a unifying receiver so if you want to use another peripheral with this combo you’ll need either another USB port or connect via Bluetooth. That’s all right as long as you recognize that up front. It’s a mild disappointment, but it was clear up front so this was not a surprise.

The mouse and the keyboard both have the batteries installed already. The keyboard takes 2 AAA batteries and the mouse takes one AA battery. I question the logic behind using different battery sizes.

I plugged the receiver into my laptop running Linux with the latest kernel, and both peripherals were immediately usable. That’s a plus.

The first problem I have is with the mouse. The mouse works just fine but is such a low-profile device that it is uncomfortable for me to use. I have a travel mouse that actually fits my hand a little better and that says a lot. For someone with very small hands this one will serve acceptably as a basic two-button travel mouse. To be fair, I knew this ahead of time so I cannot complain too much. It does work correctly and in a pinch I can work with it.

The keyboard is a completely different matter entirely. It works just fine – except for the “P” key. For that specific key, I have to bear down very hard to get it to register at all. I tried leaning the keyboard on its side and tapping it gently in case something was caught in the switch and I have tried my best to clean it without disassembly. No matter what I have tried, the “P” key continues to be insensitive to the point of rendering the keyboard unusable.

I really wanted to like this keyboard, and I knew the mouse would be small. Unfortunately, because the keyboard I received doesn’t work properly I can’t use it and can’t rate it favorably. It’s a shame – I imagine I got a bad unit (it happens), but I cannot recommend a product based on an assumption.

UPDATE 10/31/2019:

I popped off the "P" key and looked at the mechanism underneath, since the keyboard was not otherwise useful. It does not appear to be broken, damaged or obstructed in any way. For this particular key, the plastic key cover needs a small bead in the center underneath to push down the silicone membrane to make contact. Using a very small piece of tape and a tiny ball (about the size of a pin head) I was able to add such to the key cover to get it working without damaging any parts, without changing the feel while typing, and without spending any money. However, this should not have been necessary as this should have been tested properly before pack-and-ship; my review and rating stand.

I bought this TV to replace a wonderful but very old Panasonic 32" CRT that finally gave up the ghost just before Christmas. It is a totally satisfactory replacement and I recommend it strongly.

I had admired the new LED screens, but as I began investigating refresh rates and looking at the displays in stores, I came to the conclusion I would prefer a plasma screen, but my space would not accommodate anything larger than a 42". Which made this model absolutely perfect. Sears had the best price, but they were sold out by the time I placed an order. However, Walmart had the next best price at $398, so I ordered one for pickup at a local store. As it turned out, they were out of stock locally, but were able to get one within 10 days. It was well worth the wait.

In comparison to similarly sized LED TV's, this model is slightly heavier ( just under 40 pounds out of the box). Of course, in comparison to the old CRT, it was much much lighter. The stand assembled easily and seems quite sturdy. 8 screws total and a ratchet and it was ready for cables to be attached.

This is an HDTV. I may eventually bite the bullet and get HD service from Comcast, but even with the normal, non-HD cable box, the image is wonderful and light years beyond my old CRT. And the sound is GREAT! Unlike many of the LED models I considered, the sound on this model is better than on my old CRT and no need to get a sound bar. Right now I have it hooked up to an older Panasonic VCR/DVD recorder/player (non Blu-ray), an Apple TV (for streaming Netflix and which uses one of the two HDMI connections) and my Comcast cable box. It was easy to set up and I am very satisfied with the image quality. Speaking of which, I used the settings provided by R. White in his review, although I changed the tint to a -3 rather than the 0 he uses, and strongly recommend you try them as a point of departure. I am now assessing universal remotes to replace the four I currently need to operate the various components and will probably settle on a Logitech Harmony model.

If you are looking for a good and serviceable TV and don't need a larger size than 42"' or more than two HDMI connections, or the other bells and whistles, this is a fantastic choice. I don't understand the relatively low marks it gets in its review by CNET; In my opinion, it is much better than the review indicates. The advantage with the plasma is you don't need to worry about the refresh rate and the picture is great no matter what angle you watch from. (Note that if the room in which you are will place this unit has a lot of natural light, you may prefer the LED.) Also, as other reviewers have said, for this size of TV, I really don't think the eye can distinguish between 720p and 1080, and the image quality is really quite satisfactory. With the addition of an Apple TV or Blue-ray player with WiFi, you have the equivalent of a smart TV without paying the premium for one. Even at $500, this TV is a very good buy and better than you will find most of the LED's of similar size. If you can find one for under $400, grab it! But you should move fast, because these are going quickly.

Screen quality is good and the cables are pretty rigid so no worries there. They actually connect by recessing into a slot rather than on the edge of the device.

Lastly is customer service. I really enjoyed GAOMON's customer service which I wish more companies would do.

There are a few caveats though. To get the pen the most accurate no matter where you point on the screen you need to understand where you touch the dot when calibrating. Next you need to hold the pen in the exact same orientation and way when you draw. That means holding the pen the exact same way with little deviation of that angle to get things to line up as well as say an iPad Pro. If you don't the distance when you calibrate really well is under say... 0.5mm or less. I am really stingy about this, but for someone who isn't this isn't a big thing to worry about.

Next are the hotkeys which act more like a macbook's butterfly keyboard in terms of presses. They press well and have very little travel almost like the old iphone home buttons. This may bother some, but didn't for me. I did need to place some tape with texture to understand where my buttons were without looking.

The screen protector I didn't install and I found it really annoying to even attempt to install. Then again I've written with fountain pens for 5 years now so am very used to buttery smooth pen work.

At this pricepoint, this is a great value for this configuration. The laptop was extremely easy to set up (power on and a few simple screens to set up account; Windows of course has to make things slightly annoying, so it requires you to sign in to an account or create a new one; on one occasion it allows you to bypass account integration, but for anything with apps, you will need to create an account). Unlike other reviewers who seemed to have issues, I had zero issues with any bloatware or preloaded programs.

The touch-screen works great; part of the reason for choosing this model was the added touch-screen to a good configuration laptop; 2-in-1 laptop/tablet is far more expensive and if you already own a tablet, this is a reasonable compromise to obtain some tablet-like convenience and retain the "workhorse" capabilities of a laptop. The onscreen keyboard will take time to get used to, especially given that the keyboard will occupy only the central one-third or so of the screen.

Audio/video performance is OK, nothing to get super excited about. The optical drive, 2 USB 2 ports, 1 USB 3 port, 1 HDMI port, Ethernet-enabled configuration and the 750 GB drive is an excellent value. Wifi performance has been good so far. The laptop is much lighter than the lenovos I am used to; the power adapter itself is much lighter. The replaceable battery is light and much thinner than most models.

Overall, impressive start with this laptop; time will tell how robust this machine is. Will update review after 6 months and a year.

Necklace-style earbuds seem to be going out of style these days. They are bulkier and heavier and generally less comfortable than the more compact earbuds, but they do have important advantages. The necklace lets them hold a much bigger battery than compact Bluetooth earbuds, especially compared to the "true wireless" style and thus the battery life is tremendously better (up to 15 hours with the noise cancelling turned off). Sound quality of these earbuds is good: generally loud and clear with a good frequency range. Noise cancelling seems weak to me, though I've never been a fan of noise cancellation on earbuds, since the earbuds block so much external noise already. My main complaint is that these earbuds are much more expensive than LG or Motorola necklace-style earbuds that I have found to have about the same sound quality.

I can see why the needs permissions for most of that, but it is still a lot of access if anyone were in a position to abuse it.

Opened the app, gave it an email address and password to create an account.

Clicked Add Device, then Wireless Device.

Clicked the check mark twice, and then entered WiFi password.

Waited while things blinked for about a minute. Ring changed from green flashy, to blue flashy, to blue solid. Camera has another look around and does some clicking.

Named the device and gave it a password.

Clicked on the still image that looked like it came from the camera and was into the live feed, displayed on my Android smart phone (Galaxy S6). Clicking on the arrows on either side of the screen turns the camera. apparently, it can see in any direction, but once it gets to a certain point, it needs to turn around and go the other way, it can't just keep spinning.

Thus far, everything seems to be working except the motion tracking, which was kind of the main selling point. I have it turned on in phone settings. Looking at their support pages, it seems that it won't motion track once you gave been in the room a while. They recommended I leave the room for 10 minutes and come back so that the microwave array will find me interesting again. Also, apparently you can view your feed on a computer by logging in on their website.

After leaving for ten minutes and then returning to the room and sitting near it, it took about a minute for it to notice something was amiss, at which point it did a slow scan of the whole room and snapped a picture of me when it saw me move. It then stopped, still looking in the wrong direction.

My end verdict is that it's actually quite a bit nicer than previous wifi cameras I've tested, but falls far short of what I would like to see in a motion tracking camera. The motion tracking is slow and dense, when it works at all. There are enough additional features, like using as a speaker, communicating with someone through it, temperature and humidity data, etc, to give it a more versatile set of uses, but without the motion detection/control being solid, it all feels thrown together and tacked on.

These will send an alert through the app when they detect vibration and the alarm will go off for around 20 seconds. It’s loud and will scare off the majority of intruders.

The sensitivity can not be controlled via the app but only on the sensor itself and the alarm can not be stopped within the app - this makes them less than smart other than their ability to send an alert to your phone. Receiving an alert is important especially when away from home. I use these in conjunction with my security cameras so if one was to go off I can quickly pull up the camera for that area and check activity.

If the app was improved allowing for setting sensitivity and alarm cancellation this would definitely be a 5 star product - even as it is, this is a reasonable product at a decent price.

As someone who works with cameras for a living, I tend to occasionally misplace/lose my lens caps. Having a one-size-fits-all backup like this claims to be, is therefore intriguing to me.
What I found however, is that this fits alright for smaller sized primes (such as those with a front element of 52mm), but a lot of my zooms or larger primes with bigger front elements are difficult or impossible to fit over. Rear cap was also somewhat of a hit-or-miss; I own E-mount, EOS, Nikon F, Minolta A-mount and Micro4/3 lenses, and none of them are too large in their rear element, but some lenses get wide right after the mount and won't allow a cover like this to squeeze over easily. Some of the smaller primes, especially pancake lenses like the Canon 40mm STM, really can't fit both a front and rear "cap" like this since the entire lens would be engulfed in one end or the other.
On top of all that, even if it DOES fit over your lens, I'm cynical as to how how useful it really is. The purpose of a lens cap is to protect the glass from two things: getting dirty and getting damaged. For starters, the material is soft and won't prevent a hard object collision. I'm not exactly willing to test that theory but considering I can press in and feel the glass through the cover, I'm guessing a hard object in your camera bag could still hit it and crack/shatter/damage it. Perhaps the rubber would soften the blow, but a real lens cap would prevent any blow from happening in the first place!
For dust and debris protection, perhaps it is a little useful, however this sort of material tends to attract a lot of static cling. Just leaving it in my gear bag for a bit, I'm finding dust and hair clinging to it like a balloon. Now, it is possible that means the dust/debris will stick to the cap and not your lens, which is useful, however it doesn't give me a lot of confidence to see stuff stuck to the thing I'm about to use to protect my lens from more of that stuff.

I suppose it's good as a backup in my gearbag in case I lose another lens cap and want something to keep dust off it until I get a replacement, but otherwise I'd strongly recommend getting a proper front and end cap for your lenses.

I own the Bose QuietComfort headset, which is fantastic for use at home or on planes, but it's just too cumbersome to lug around New York City. I've been contemplating the MDR-NC10 for use on subways and general wanderings around the city for some time now, but held off in part due to some of the negative reviews on this website. When I saw the updated MDR-NC11 for sale at Brookstone, I thought, with their 60 day satisfaction guarantee, I could try them out and always return them if I didn't like them. (I do not work for and am not in any way affiliated with Brookstone; just like the fact that they have a realistic product return policy.)
In a word, this set is great! I don't have this uncanny ability to tune out noise, an ability which most New Yorkers seem to possess intrinsically; I need a little technical help, and this set does it. Anyone who has ever ridden the NYC subway knows that it creates some of the worst noise pollution of any public transit system, but with these earphones, even when just seated snugly in my ears, much of that noise is kept out of my head.
I have used it to listen to music that I previously could not expect to enjoy outside of my own four walls. Minimalist acoustics in tracks like Famous Blue Raincoat (Leonard Cohen), Drop (Red House Painters) and Colorblind (Counting Crows) are just some examples of music that I can now clearly hear while riding a rush hour train! Even the subtle string arrangement in the latter half of Famous Blue Raincoat is clearly audible. Amazing!
To be honest, I'm not entirely sure how the NC10 and NC11 differ technologically, but comparing the actual device to pictures of the NC10, Sony seems to have made it a little bigger/bulkier, which I don't understand. Given the size of the new control handle, you could have fit your standard play, stop, next track, previous track, etc. buttons of a portable device remote control on there. The relative weight with the required AAA battery means that you have to find a really good place to attach the clip or risk having it come undone due to gravity. Definitely an aspect that Sony could improve. The other thing I would have liked to see is a control for what appears to be a built-in bass boost. It helps with some recordings, but sometimes you just want to turn it off.
By default, the earphones have M size buds fitted. S and L sizes are included in the package. I found that I needed M for one ear and S for the other in order to have both phones sit comfortably but snugly in my ears. It's worth spending some time to figure out the right combination to maximise the satisfaction you'll derive from this set.
Overall, I'm incredibly happy with these earphones and think I should, with their help, be able to endure New York for a few more years yet! :)

The feet are well designed with hard steel spikes with nice rubber feet for indoor uses. Both options allow for good stable footings.

Also there are some great other details like leveling bubbles on the top of the tripod and ball head. Where I wish they had put more into this tripod is the ball head. It doesn't seem to live up to the tripod body. There is a second leveling bubble on the head itself which is fantastic. But probably the biggest drawback is the quick release plate. It is not quick at all, it requires quite a bit of screwing with thumbscrew to attach. Also there is not set screw on the "quick" release plate.

Pros
+ Height
+ padded legs for comfort in cold weather
+ Light Weight
+ Great feet, both the grippy robber shoes and the steel spikes
+ built in leveling bubbles
+ Functional and strong leg locks
+ built in hook on bottom of center post
+ Second leveling bubble on the head

Cons
- No built in strap
- Carrying case is ok (this is more a neutral than a con)
- the head is not great
- limited leg angles
- Head could be better
- Somewhat awkward and slow quick release plates
- Lacks a panning arm.

In General, this is an awesome tripod, but for the money I would have expected a little more, especially a strap and a better head unit. But I have to admit I love this tripod. Anymore, an emergency radio has been largely replaced by smart phones for getting emergency updates and it is not a common item that people frequently buy or have around. That said, having a radio like this is useful when traveling and either cell service is bad or using a phone is impractical. In such cases a radio like this is a really good resource. For us, while not a necessity this radio sees daily use as a weather radio.

One of the things that has been around our house for many, many years is a weather radio. We are in range of two weather stations and we have a dedicated emergency weather radio that provides us emergency notifications as well as current conditions and forecasts around the region. The difficulty we have had with it is that reception is not the greatest and we often have static over the broadcast. We have a secondary weather radio that has even worse reception that our main one.

I did not have high expectations of this radio at all. We tuned it to the closest station with the expectation of hearing a lot of static and interference. Much to our surprise, the broadcast is clear and uncluttered. We tuned to the other station and got the same – a clear broadcast. What was a real surprise for us is that we could suddenly pick up a third station. We had no idea we were close enough to any other station to hear their broadcasts. It’s not as clear as the others, but it is clear enough to be understood.

As a weather radio, this unit is excellent. We have no complaints.

Most of the other features we have tried though do not use regularly. It has a flashlight built in that is bright enough to navigate through the house during a power outage and it has a couple of different modes such as SOS flash that make it useful in different emergency situations. It has different charging modes so it is ready to go when needed, the most frequent of which we use is the solar charging but it can be plugged in and it also can be hand-cranked to generate enough power for emergency use. A particularly helpful emergency feature is the ability to charge your phone, and the battery is sufficient to give one full charge to a smaller smartphone with power to spare.

If I could change one thing I would make it more ruggedized. It is good in that regard and should be able to handle getting dropped or jostled and bumped, but there is definitely opportunity to go farther. This is by no means a show-stopper or even a complaint, but a data point – if you need something that can handle a lot of abuse, this isn’t it, though in the price range it would be difficult to find better.

This is a nice emergency radio and my family really likes it. Though designed and marketed as an emergency radio, it actually sees daily use solely on the basis of how well it performs as a weather radio.

- EXCELLENT graphics

CONS
- Crappy mousepad
- Battery life a little over an hour and a half

I had high hopes for the Magellan Switch Up. Since Magellan has been producing various GPS devices for many years, I figured that they must have a team of designers who could pull off a new fitness device with as many features as the pre-release hype described. Unfortunately, the features are there, but the all important GPS is not!

While the Switch Up has a marvelous display, and a feature set that is enough to make even the most seasoned endurance athlete's jaw go slack and agape, the one thing that drives all of those features is completely absent - an accurate GPS. Lacking the ability to very accurately determine distance renders all of the seemingly impressive features, save the clock function, completely useless.

To all of those who gave the Switch up a glowing review, I challenge you to take it out and compare the distance that the device is telling you with an actual, measured course. How it "feels" or "seems" is completely irrelevant. Test it against a hard measured distance, and I wager that you will be shocked at the devices inability to properly calculate distance. It really is THAT bad!

While many first generation devices have been "fixed" through firmware updates, the updates to the Switch Up have done nothing to fix the accuracy of the GPS of this device. Since the heart and soul of a fitness device is an accurate GPS, the Switch Up is a zombie amongst a throng of real fitness devices.

Will Magellan do better next time? Let's hope so, because the Switch Up is completely useless in its current state.

Ok I will be clear - I am NOT a super techie like some of the other folks who are reviewing this router, so I can't explain some of it's fancy gizmos and tricks. What I can do is tell my impressions of this unit from the point of view of your average person who knows a little bit about the techie things and can set up my own wireless network at home. The things that make this router different from the lower priced options out there seem pretty straight forward to me - it's fast and it's secure and you can use it for multiple wi-fi connections in your house. What more can your average family ask for? Well I'll tell you... SIMPLICITY of set up would be on the wish list. Here's what happened the day the new Netgear N750 router arrived.

Out of the box we noticed there was no instruction book. Just a single sheet with basic instructions. Ok, so it's a simple process, simple enough not to need a big book of directions. At first this was true, then things got complicated. It did hook up easily enough and had no drama talking to our cable provider's internet service and the Windows 7 desktop computer saw the router and they communicated very easily.

The Good.....As a test of the range, we used a Blackberry and walked throughout the house and the front & back porches searching for the wi-fi signal. This is a 4000sqft house with two stories on a normal size lot, so when the Blackberry saw the Netgear network and was able to connect to the internet even out in the yard we were delighted! Upstairs, downstairs, in the kitchen, at the opposite end of the house and in the garage we had a solid, strong signal from the router. We then tested the connection with a Roku box, a Wii game system, a netbook computer, a different smartphone scattered all over the house. Every piece of equipment found the network and connected to the internet like they were supposed to. And using the Wii, netbook and Blackberry all at once to load a photo heavy website was amazing - twice as fast as the old, cheap Cisco router and smooth as silk.

The Obnoxious...The next step of course, was to the name the network and do the security block so strangers can't piggyback on it. Especially since it was broadcasting out into the yard and off the porches. And that's where it got complicated and obnoxious. It took two hours to sort out the security settings. The first time we did everything as directed by the software. The end result was a loss of signal from the router everywhere except the room it was physically located in. Multiple subsequent adjustments rendered it useful in three rooms, but no longer were we able to pick it up or access the internet upstairs or on the back porch or even in the far bedroom where the Wii console is located. Not good. The end result was to wipe all the information, reboot the entire computer and router and start over using the lowest security settings. (Can you say frustration?) Once this was done we had a signal and were able to maintain the connection with the Roku, netbook, and smartphones throughout 80% of the house and a weak signal on the porch. The Wii however, cannot hold the signal at the far end of the house which means the router will have to be moved to a more central area of the house.

End result.... The weakened signal issue might not be a big deal or even worth taking a star away from my rating, but I keep coming back to this one thought. The el cheapo, 2 year old, VERY basic "off the shelf at a big box store" router we had been using put out a stronger signal for a third of the price of this Netgear N750. However, the Netgear router IS faster than the old one and there isn't a noticable reduction of speed even when multiple things are connected at the same time. If that's more important to you than overall range, then this is a darn good router for the average home.

To use this SANDISK EXTREME UHS-I SDXC memory card the way it's intended (for advanced photography), you need an SDXC device (camera or camcorder). You also need an SDXC device that's compatible with this new, latest SDXC format. I was disappointed to learn that my older Panasonic Lumix DMC-LX2 camera, which is compatible with many SDXC memory cards, is NOT able to recognize and use this memory card.

A word of warning: If your SDXC or other device is incompatible with this SDXC card, the device may suggest that you format the card. Do not do this! Formatting will ruin the card as an SDXC card. SDXC devices are backward compatible (and can accept SDXC, SD, or SDHC memory cards), but SDXC cards should be used only in SDXC devices. (To learn more about the do's and don'ts of SDXC memory cards, you can Google "SD Association Using SDXC memory cards".) If you have a Panasonic camera, you can find a list of cameras that are compatible with SDXC on the Panasonic web site. Presumably other camera manufacturers' web sites have similar lists.

Although this card doesn't work in my camera, it can be accessed with a USB reader or adapter that is SDXC-compatible; or through a WinXP, WinVista, or Win7 PC card reader slot, if the PC has the exFAT file system update (KB955704) that can be downloaded from the Microsoft Download Center. My fairly recent Win7 PC (ASUS Essentio Series) is not compatible with the above file system update, but already had a driver that enabled it to access the SDXC card without formatting.

Unlike the Roku boxes where all of your channels are at the top level, on the Amazon box, they are buried. It also forced me to re-enter my password constantly for Netflix. This is so annoying. Overall, I wish I could recommend this box, but I really don't recommend it. I think the Roku is so much better, as it isn't focused on just Amazon content, but rather overall viewing content from many channel providers. I live in a hilly area of the San Francisco peninsula and I was a Dish Network customer. I got local channels, some movies, and lots of junk all for around $60 a month. I decided to cut the cord and put up an outside antenna. I selected this one.

It is very easy to assemble and can be done in about ten minutes or so. The antenna elements fold out so it's fairly compact and easy to take up to the roof. It comes with lots of cable and it is already connected to the antenna. You can have the unit up and working in around thirty minutes to an hour, depending on the length of the cable run, the stabilization of the mast, and tacking it flush to your outside wall, then through the wall. ALL the necessary hardware, and cable routing clamps are included.

The acid test was turning it on and having my wife operate the remote control box so while I was on the roof I could verify that it did rotate a full 360 each direction. It did.

I tried an indoor antenna that cost twice as much and only got a few channels. With this antenna I am getting upwards of thirty (even some stations that are over sixty miles away). Reception is crystal clear.

In addition to the antenna you may need some or all of the following:
--1 Antenna Mast (depending on your location you may need a couple to get some height, in which case you'll also need fifteen to thirty feet of guy wire, three guy wire mounts to put on the mast to stabilize the mast and antenna. You will also need mounts to attach the wire to the roof. These usually screw into the roof (opening the possibility of leaks. If you're screwing these guy wire mounts get some of the calk roofers and antenna installers use and apply liberally around the spot where the mount screws into the roof.
--Mounting hardware such as a Vent Mount or two depending on the height of your mast, a Chimney Mount or a Wall Mount. You don't need them all, just the one that fits your installation plan.
--Two couplers for joining lengths of cable. They're cheap and when you need one there is not a work-around.
--Two AAA batteries for the remote control.
--Additional 75 ohm coax and two male ends IF AND ONLY IF the 75 feet of cable that comes with the antenna is shorter than the run from the roof, down the outside walls and through the wall into the room where the television is located.
--A thing called a "Wall-Through" which is inserted into the hole you drill from the outside wall into the room where your HDTV or other set is located. It can be cut to the proper length so the fittings on each end that seal the hole are flush to the walls. You drill the hole through your wall, insert the Wall-Through, mark its proper length, and cut it to that length. Next put it back through the hole, and thread the cable through it into the inside room. Finally slip the cap for the inside end of the Wall-Through over the coax and secure it snugly to the inside end of the Wall-Through. You can put some calk around the cover of the outside fitting of the Wall-Through to prevent water leakage.

**********You will need some or all the items on the above list no matter what brand or type of outdoor antenna you purchase.

Note on the remote control box:
I've read reviews for this type of rotating antenna where people complain that it doesn't rotate a full 360. I noticed that unless you really aim the remote control at the remote control box, the box doesn't pick up the signal from the remote unit. This is NOT a reason to avoid this item.

Conclusion:
This antenna works really, really well, is a breeze to install, and comes with a complete set of necessary hardware necessary for assembling the antenna. The total cost of this project for me was approximately $165, as the mounts are not cheap and a good antenna mast costs about $35 per 5 foot section. With what I was paying for my Dish Network, I'll recover my cost in a few short months.

You can also buy a streaming video box like a ROKU for around $100 and get streaming NetFlix, Amazon movies on demand and lots of other entertaining programming. It's like having Dish or Cable without the high monthly fees and that's a good thing. For this addition as well as your DVD or Blue Ray you do need a TV, HD or otherwise, that has multiple inputs for video sources.

Because life has been so full of curves, my husband and I were trying to re-create our anniversary at home this year. One of our happiest times was at a little bed and breakfast that had a tiny CD player next to the bed. When I saw this, I could not believe it. I knew we had to have it.

HOW WE USE THIS
We did not opt to hang this on the wall. Since most of our CD players have long bit the dust, I wanted something I can move from room to room. We use this on the enclosed stand. It is perfect.

HOW WELL DOES IT PLAY CDs?
This plays CDs really well. It has played our CDs for music as well as books on tape. You can not save your place to go back to, however, so it is up to you to either endure the entire thing over again til you finish or try to listen to a whole CD at once. Some of the books I have are not marked on the CD in chapters so it won't forward to them.

SOUND QUALITY
The sound quality is rustic. It is not a really great speaker, but it is good for what we want. If you really want amazing sound, then I would suggest you just use MP3 or phone/tablet and a nice bluetooth speaker. For a good vintage sound with just enough to give you a nice song or book, this is actually refreshing.

DOES IT PLAY SD CARDS?
This does play the cards well too, but I prefer to use those with my phone or tablet and a nice bluethooth speaker.

REMOTE
The remote is really nice- it is white so it is easy to read. The only problem is that it does cross over to LED rope lights sometimes so in addition to changing a song, I change the color of my lights and have to get the light remote out again to set them back. The remote takes two AAA batteries.

CONTROLS
The controls are on the top of this unit, that is why having it on the wall seems to be counterproductive. You can turn it on or off using one of the buttons pressed for 3 seconds. The color coding on the lights to show you mode is helpful. I like the simplicity of this.

ALARM
I don't use the alarm or sleep mode on this.

CAN YOU USE THIS FOR BLUETOOTH SPEAKERS?
This can not be used with bluetooth speakers or headphones. It is an input only not output.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a nice little CD player for books on tape and also for vintage type CDs as they sound more like the past. It can not be used with a bluetooth speaker or headphones but still is nice to have handy to play in various rooms.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This is a nice player, is portable and has a cover on it. Controls are easy to use and the remote is nice. Honestly, my husband and I had so much fun re-creating our favorite get away anniversary at home and this CD player was an important part.

I debated with myself over getting this case for what would be my first PC build, knowing that it was a unique case and would require more time and patience than a typical PC case. I also knew I might end up hating the way it looked and didn't want to spend $170 on something I kept hidden out of sight. Having built my PC, though, and used it for almost a week, I can say that I certainly do not hate it. Building in the case is actually rather easy (though cable management can be tricky at times) and there is plenty of room for decent components.

Pros
-A unique design that I really enjoy looking at
-Fairly small footprint
-Top to bottom airflow means you can put the case in a corner without impeding cooling
-Can accommodate full-sized components without too much trouble
-Makes for a fun PC build

Cons
-Cable management can be tricky (I used [[ASIN:B001E1Y5O6 Velcro Reusable Self-Gripping Cable Ties, 0.5 Inches x 8 Inches Long, Black, 100 Ties per Pack (91140)]] and highly recommend them)
-Reset button is very easy to push when plugging in headphones or a usb peripheral.
-Side panels are perhaps too easy to remove and could make moving the case a challenge
-The case only allows a slimline slotloading dvd drive (I used [[ASIN:B004CJKVO0 Sony AD-7690H-01 8X SATA Internal Slim DVD+/-RW Drive (Black), Bulk w/o Software]]) though I do like the clean look it gives the case

For those worried about not being able to access the eject button on the dvd drive, I found that if you mount the drive as close to the front panel as possible, simply pressing on the panel in the general area of the button will work.

UPDATE: The reason a remote is essential; is due to who might be viewing this in the backseat.

While the vehicle is in motion, it is dangerous for an adult to lean forward to constantly adjust the volume or explore apps.

Some people, especially kids, do not sit that close to the backseat. It’s actually unsafe to do so as a collision can cause injury or death to both the backseat passenger and the front seat passenger as well.

In addition, sitting close to the unit during a collision might cause injury from the unit itself.

As many of these devices are targeted for kids, it is even more dangerous for them to lean forward to adjust it while a vehicle is in motion. Some are also restrained by a car seat or booster seat and cannot adjust it. While phone screen-mirroring is a feature, some single parents don’t have a second adult in the vehicle to assist with that.

Also, disabled people in the backseat might not be able to adjust/navigate the unit without a remote. Even using phone mirroring can be challenging as opposed to a remote much like a TV, DVD player, cable box, etc.

For at home use – I sit too far away to constantly jump up and down to adjust the volume and/or navigate apps. I might also have it on for background noise during chores, and don’t want to have to stop what I’m doing to turn down the volume so as not to disturb the neighbors.

I thought I’d update for those wondering why a remote might be a safe, if not essential accessory to have.

The design aesthetics are subtle for a gaming laptop. This laptop sits at a sweet spot for the price/performance ratio using an 8750H processor and a GTX 2060 graphics card. Laptop is very well ventilated for cooling with perforated holes on top and bottom and has vents on the sides and back of laptop. It’s covered in mostly all aluminum for a premium feel. There are complaints of this being a fingerprint magnet but I take that any day for that premium feel. The AC adapter is one of the smaller 180w power bricks as compared to the competitors. Amazing how the webcam and the power supply shows the progress of miniaturization.

Durability: This laptop has a solid tank like construction comparable to the way Alien laptops are constructed. However, the display has some flex but that is to be said for a lot thin and light gaming laptops. Quality control issues are a concern from some posts, but these sound like issues that would present themselves right away once you boot up and can be returned or replaced in the event that should happen.

Noise: For basic daily non-gaming use, the fans runs fairly quiet even with 40 chrome tabs running. By comparison, my 9370 laptop has the fans running pretty noticeable with 40 chrome tabs. Fans run loud when turbo is enabled but the noise is on par or below comparable gaming laptop noise but most gamers wear headphones when playing games on a laptop.

Display: The 1080 IPS 144Hz near borderless display matches well for this tier of gaming laptops and is pretty decent, Although it was mentioned in other posts about brightness levels, it is plenty bright for indoor use. There are some screen backlight bleeding but it to be expected and is not noticeable or impacts my daily use.

Keyboard: One of the better keyboards for a thin and light along with good 1.7mm of travel and solid feedback. I was disappointed that I could not change the volume up, volume down, and mute key on the right to page up and page down.

Battery: Battery life is pretty good considering it’s a gaming laptop. I get around 4-6 hours from browsing the web. It runs only on Nvidia Optimus only on the rtx2060 model but the rtx2080 model has a software switch in the predator sense software to switch between GPUs.

Gaming Temperatures: The idle temps I was getting is between mid 40s to high 50s. Fan kicks in around mid 40s but is barely audible. My max Unigine Heaven benchmark max temps are 89c CPU and 75c GPU. However, average temps are around 5-15 degrees during the benchmark.
Upgrading the ram or SSD will be a pain due to the inverted motherboard. I hope this design trend does not continue with future laptops.
However, despite the difficulties involved in upgrading, there may be no need as the ram and drive space size should be sufficient for most people. The dual channel ram of 16GB is enough for most games and use cases, while the 512GB of NVM SSD drive is a pretty decent storage space by recent standards.

Should I buy now? For those on the border for buy a gaming laptop now or wait. I would say right now is the best time to buy a laptop based on current vs predicted future performance. The 8750H processor and 2060 graphics are both mature products from Intel and NVidia meaning the percentage gains from generation to generation will not be as high as they are with the current gen products. The increases will likely be in the single digit gains such as going from the 8750H to the 9750H (6% improvement) and that increase would not affect gaming (1-2 frame rate gain) in any perceptible way. Acer’s Helios 300 and Triton 500 are the best price/performance ratio for gaming around right now.

I decided to buy a pair of noise canceling headphones after moving to a different location at work where I am in closer proximity to a rack of computers that runs constantly. After a short while the whirr of the fans in the computers and the rack in which they are mounted gets very tiring and annoys the ears. After doing some research, I finally decided on the Bose QuietComfort 15, and almost immediately I have seen that I made the right choice.

I was fortunate enough to get my hands on one of these before I committed my money so I could test the quality. I was very pleased when I put on the headphones, turned them on and all of the ambient noise around me simply vanished. The sound of the air conditioning, the murmuring of people chatting around me, even traffic outside was reduced to such a degree that I felt like I was in a bubble. I bought them on the spot.

I put these headphones through two major tests outside of work.

First, I plugged them into my iPod and turned them on. All I could hear when the music played was the music. Talking around me was overcome by the noise cancellation and the music, which was not set to a particularly high volume. As many have commented, the bass is very rich with these headphones but that's fine with me, as I really appreciate good bass response. Treble and mid-range are also good, though not quite as bright as the bass.

The really big surprise was when I plugged them into the mixing board where I was doing live recording. I was shocked at how effectively I could hear every sound coming through the microphones but practically nothing else. The sound was clear, crisp and not muddied in any way I could ascertain, which gave me a much better idea of what was recording onto the CD. I had used a lesser headset for this purpose, but no longer.

Some noises do get through, such as loud talking and even the typing on my keyboard, but those sounds are muffled quite a bit. The idea is to eliminate droning, obnoxious noise such as engine noise (there are several mentions in the documentation about wearing these on planes), while still allowing certain things to get through. These are certainly not perfect in that regard but they do come close.

In the past I have bought headphones only from either Sony or Sennheiser, with a very strong bias for the latter. This is my first set of Bose headphones and they are definitely the best pair I have ever used (let alone owned). I regard these as very much worth the price and gladly recommend them for anyone wanting to hear nothing but the music without blasting out the ears. These are high quality earphones and will please the enthusiast looking for good sound as well as the traveler looking for a quiet ride.

I've been using Chromebook laptops and Android phones and tablets for years, but until I saw this product, I didn't know that Chrome tablets were a thing. This Chrome tablet appears to be targeted at the classroom environment, where the teacher wants all the kids running the same Chrome web apps at the same time. That is different from the typical Android environment, where there is little built-in support for synchronizing multiple tablets.

If you are using these tablets in a classroom, they work great. The screen is is brighter and sharper than the Amazon Fire tablets (which are admittedly much cheaper). The pop-out stylus works well and does not need a battery. This is a smart Wacom stylus that is much more accurate than a cheap rubber-tipped stylus or using your finger. Unlike most Android phones these days, this tablet supports micro-SD cards for expandable memory and it has a headphone jack. The tablet has stereo speakers, but they are on the sides, so aren't as loud or clear as tablet with front-facing speakers. The tablet is a little thicker than an iPad, but it is also sturdier with a rubberized shell for easier gripping and drop resistance. The tablet is lightweight for the 10 inch screen size at barely 1 pound. The camera is mediocre, but I am always carrying my phone with its much better camera, so I just use that.

Speed is really good, especially startup speed, which only takes a few seconds (much better than Android tablets). The Chrome operating system gets regular system updates for security patches and new features, unlike the Android operating system on most tablets that often gets obsolete quickly.

If you're using this tablet stand-alone (not in a classroom), it is still pretty good. The Chrome operating system runs both Chrome apps and Android apps, so it is a little more confusing than a pure Android operating system. The application launcher shows both types of apps and figuring out which is which is a hassle. Also, sharing data between Chrome apps and Android apps is a lot more complicated than sharing data between 2 different Android apps. A casual user should think hard about buying an Amazon Fire 10 inch tablet instead of one of these, mostly because the Amazon tablet offers much of the same functionality of this tablet for 1/3 the price. The Amazon tablet is much slower and doesn't have as nice a screen and doesn't have the pop-out stylus and doesn't have access to the full Google Play Android app store, so you do get what you pay for.

First impression - not as impressed as some

Disclaimer: Everyone's ear is different, and tips make a big difference. Because of my ears, I have to use big tips and a shallow fit. Those who can get a deeper fit my hear something completely different. Also, I'm being really picky to help others decide if this is the right phones for them.

I wanted to try these on my computer because that is where all my music is stored that I've used for decades to audition audio gear. So this will be based on Pandora on my phone at 192kb. This is fine because this is how I will be listening to them.

I could not get a comfortable fit with the included tips. The largest tips were not large enough for my ears. So I dug through my collection and found a good fit. Pairing went fine.

They feel a little heavy to me but maybe that is the price of Bluetooth and the magnets? This is my first pair of Bluetooth in-ears. Build quality seem good for the price (I got them on sale) and I'd say the build quality is about average for their normal selling price. While they look like they have good strain relief it's actually very stiff plastic creating a 'hard point' where the wires come out. I like the little magnet for when I want to take them out but not take them off. It's one of the reasons I got these. If you run, I'd worry a little bit about the weight they add.

The sound. I like tight bass, well controlled, no extra bloom/extension But these are bass shy to my ears. For a workout, I like a fun sound and these ain't that. They are a bit bright and brassy at times I noticed the most on 70s classic rock. They lack a richness in the mids that I noticed most with male vocals. Turning them up did not improve they sound, as they got louder they became painful bright/brassy and bass did not improve. They went loud enough to distort the drivers so volume should not be an issue for anyone.

They do a pretty good job of revealing detail and room acoustics are rendered decently and there is some space around the instruments but not much of a soundstage.

While not sterile they lack some musicality that I'd prefer. Did I mention that male voice sound thin. They lack a fullness and resonance for the male voice. I notice this lack of 'something' on drums as well which are buried in the mix. It seems like the SQ is geared to making them sound impressive and accurate and while they succeed in that to some extent it's at the expense of other parts of the sound. I can see getting some fatigue after a while if you listen for more than an hour or so. Sibilance is not an issue. You hear the sibilance on some songs because it's there but it's not going to wear you out.

I can see why some people would like these especially if you are coming from lower quality mushy sounding earphones. If you are used to better earphones and looking for some less expensive earphones for working out you may like these if you like a 'clear' sound but the word that keeps coming to mind as I listen to them more and more is 'thin'. Not thin/thin but a lack of richness and resonance. If you want some bass especially some extension/bloom (again wearing/tips can make a difference) and a bit of 'drive' I'd consider a different set.

Yes, the UI and apps are very clearly Android. No, it isn't a mini tablet.
Players like this are an interesting market that is hard to pin the audience down for. There are music players that are cheap on the market for those that would rather have a dedicated player (ie, not their phone). However the user interface tends to be wonky and slow, and newer generation features like bluetooth 5+ and streaming are often a mixed bag, if even available.
The idea behind players like this one, is that it is based on a supported operating system (Android, in this case) so it can play almost any format you throw at it, has plenty of support for popular streaming apps and features, as well as a familiar user interface that is already so polished, it seems silly to reinvent the wheel like the super cheap older media players.
Is it a mini tablet or phone without service? Not exactly. This is not a Google certified device, it does not have the play store or any Google apps on it. Unlike some other Android based players, I couldn't even get sideloaded apk files to install (it kept throwing errors at me). It seems like this device was purposely locked down to keep it an mp3 player. That's good in some ways, my kids aren't allowed unlimited screen time and their schools don't want them bringing smartphones around, so this is a strictly music-player oriented device (especially once you remove things like the browser for them, which it allows you to do). But I also know there are more capable players out there, some of which have quad DAC audio chips. Also, what happens when an app gets updated and goes out-of-date? Sometimes streaming services make changes and updated clients are required for it to work, however you are largely stuck with the version that this came with unless they issue a firmware update or something.
This is still cheaper than the higher end mp3 players that support high end DAC and app updates, but not by much. It seems to be a sort of in-between product. If you have a use for something like this, it could be a pretty good option. But if you're expecting a handheld tablet or alternative concept to an ipod touch, it is not exactly that.

2. Voice command works, mostly, especially on simple commands like "Go Home." More complex commands, like an address, return a wide variety of responses, most of them wrong. 3. It's slimmer and lighter.
4. Easy to import my favorites from my old Nuvi into the 2595LMT. Using a PC, after plugging the old Nuvi into a computer using the USB port,

a. Navigate until you find the "current.GPX" file on the old Nuvi and
b. Copy it to your desktop (this is also a way to make a backup should you desire.)
c. Rename the file: replace "current" with any word you want, as long as it's not "current") so that it is names "anyword.gpx"
d. Attach the new Nuvi 2595LMT to the computer and navigate until you find the folder with its "current.gpx" file.
e. Copy the "anyword.gpx" file from the desktop into the same folder where the "Current.gpx" file resides.
f. Disconnect and restart. All the old favorites will be added to the current list in your new Nuvi.

5. It doesn't say "recalculating" when you disregard its directions

I'm reviewing the Vanguard Adapter 46 backpack. This is a complicated backpack with lots of different options to help customize it for you and your gear. You can configure the straps so you use only one strap (either one) or both at the same time. This bag holds a lot of gear, so I choose to use both straps in a standard backpack configuration. There are lots of movable dividers to you can set up this space in lots of different ways, depending on the size and amount of gear you are carrying. Slide the bag on to one shoulder and you can easily access your gear without putting the backpack on the ground. This bag has so many options that you really need to try it out for yourself to see if your gear will fit and if you can use it easily. Same goes for any camera backpack. I found it to be comfortable, easy to use (once I set it up), and sturdy.

These are around the same price as all the junky Chinese wireless earbud brands on Amazon but sound much better, are much more reliable, and are made by a company with good customer service that stands behind their products.

Ankers has several wireless earbuds with the cords that go behind the neck but only these, the spirit, the spirit pro, and the spirit x are worth considering for purchase. Their other earbuds are older models that cost just as much but have less features and weaker specs.

The bass on these is weak but I use these mostly for working out and for that it is fine.

I already have a pair of Apple EarPods but I wanted another wireless pair of headphones as well so I could switch back and forth while the other pair was charging.

These do not work with Apples w1 chip Bluetooth protocol, only apple and beats headphones work with that standard right now so those wireless headphones brands will sound better than anything other wireless headphones will with Apple products.

They also do not have aptx, which is the best sounding Bluetooth standard for anything other than Apple.

Ankers spirit pro headphones do support the aptx standard and supposedly have better bass than these so those are that models advantages.

However the spirit pro cost twice as much as these and only supports Bluetooth protocol 4.1 while these headphones support Bluetooth protocol 5.0.

Why is that important? Because the 5.0 protocol is the new “low energy” Bluetooth standard. Meaning that if you have both a device and headphones that support it you will get much more play time out of the same size battery.

Ankers other most recent model of earbuds, the spirit x headphones, have the same specs as these headphones in terms of the protocols they support but have a different form factor, obviously, and have 10mm drivers while these have 6mm. They also have a little more battery life.

I think I might buy the spirit x headphones as well in order to have a backup and to compare their sound.

As an Apple user the spirit pro headphones are just not worth the extra cost for me since I will never use the aptx protocol and they do not even support the Bluetooth 5.0 protocol.
If they were Bluetooth 5.0 compatible I might consider spending the extra 25 bucks in order to get that extra bass.

While these don’t sound spectacular they will get great battery life when I use them with devices that support 5.0 Bluetooth and they are very affordable.

Context: I have have an '05 Subaru Outback Limited, which has a 6-CD changer but no cassette deck or AUX-in. I have a decent amount of experience in audio, low-voltage electric, and soldering.

ASIN of other parts I purchased:

RCA-3.5mm cable: B00LM2Y2U4
3.5mm panel-mount jack: B00OGLCR3W
Antenna adapters for Subaru: B000K53QBA
3.5mm braided, right-angle cable: B01K3WYKW8

I installed this in my Outback after thinking about doing so for years. I've never used the sound system in my car and it felt like a bit of a waste, and I would like to listen to audiobooks and music on my commute or long trips. Previously I considered tying the audio into the wiring harness for the CD player in order to attain maximum quality, but it was sufficiently unapproachable that I put it off for years. I ended up going with the iSimple instead of a generic FM transmitter because I wanted to get the maximum possible quality at the maximum power, hopefully improving the battery life of my MP3 player (a Sandisk Sansa Clip+).

As for installation: I watched a video on Youtube by a guy named Dirtcheapdaily (How to add an auxiliary port to any car | Ep.81) which made the process very simple. It took me about three hours total from start to finish, and required that I remove the center console from the car and make some modifications on the workbench. However, I wanted my car to look stock, with everything hidden away - if you don't care about any of that, you could literally do this in 20m.

However, the steps I took were: remove some panels from center console and radio - pull antenna wires out from behind head unit- connect iSimple model to antenna wires via adapters to check length of wires - remove center console and bring to workbench - add velcro and attach iSimple to space inside center console where it won't interfere with anything - drill holes in wall of center console storage compartment - cut switch wires, feed through holes, resolder w/ heatshrink - feed audio wire through hole, solder to 3.5mm jack, seat in hole - trim, then solder power wires to back of cigarette lighter (only has power when ACC is on) - tie all wires down so they don't wander - return center console to car and temporarily reconnect to adjust gain and switch to best radio station, and make sure parking brake doesn't interfere with modules or wires - reassemble car and test one last time.

Regarding quality: after adjustment, I'd say the audio quality is pretty good. When the switch is on, there is no interference whatsoever from other stations. It is not as good as a true line in, but I don't see that as being very important as I frequently have the windows down, hear road noise, or have the car vents running, so for me fairly good is good enough. It is better than many external FM transmitters I've heard, and much more consistent.

I do wish the gain on the unit was a bit stronger, I have it maxed out an still have to crank my volume up to 50% if I have my MP3 player on ~50% volume, which isn't an issue it itself but at 20 the other radio stations are truly deafening. It is possible that the gain is limited by FCC regs, though. For now, I just set all my presets to the radio station I have selected on the unit to avoid accidentally shifting to a different one. This way I can run the MP3 on 50% and the battery will hold out longer than otherwise.

So, as for recommendations - I would say that if you want the best quality in the most unobtrusive form factor, this is a good investment so long as installing it into your car isn't -too- much of a hassle. I found the process educational myself but for some it might just be frustrating. If you just want audio and you aren't too attached to how you get it, I would order an external plug-in FM transmitter first and only upgrade if you feel it would be necessary.

The Salange 7500 LUX Mini Home Projector is a barebones projector that provides good brightness, good focus, full-sized HDMI input, but not much else. Connect a FireTV or AndroidTV device to this projector and you have all of the "smart" features that you'll need.

So the good of this projector is that it is somewhat compact, not as small as the pico projectors, but small enough... it's about the size of a bread box (as the saying goes). The focus ring is fairly tight, meaning that once you find your focus, it won't move. The USB outputs enough amps to power a FireTV and overall, it is very straightforward to use.

The bad is that there is no keystone adjustment, not even the analogue kind that tilts the lens. The resolution is only 720p and I found that projecting at a shorter range of around 9 feet, I'm able to see every pixel on the projected image. At a longer distance, the pixels may meld together better.

In summary, this is a low-priced projector that will project an image through an HDMI input. If that's all you're looking for, this will work, but if you're looking for something that you may set up more permanently, this isn't it.

Awesome little product! I have an expensive smoker but I still use one or two of these smoker tubes. I have the 12" for quick cooks - 2 hours or less and the 18" for 6 hours or less. I use both when I want real extreme smoking! The trick is to fill the smoker tube with pellets and use a little torch with map gas to light the pellets, wait at least 5 minutes and blow out the flame and set in the smoker or barbeque. Remember to set the tube on some aluminum foil because the ashes will fall through the grates and make a mess. Note: if you light both ends of the tube, you get double the smoke but half of the time before it goes out. I have bought several of these for gifts for friends with smokers and they all say great things about this product.

Update: I have a RecTec smoker and I use their wood pellets because the burn so clean as compared to my old Traeger with Traiger pellets. I tried using the RecTec pellets in my smoke tube this past weekend and I didn't get as large of volume of smoke but they burned a lot longer than the Traeger pellets. I switched back to the cheaper Traeger pellets for my smoke tube because I like the larger volume of smoke and because I set the smoke tube on some aluminum foil, I don't get all of the ash in my smoker.

This actually works pretty well. How well it works for you is highly dependent on your car, and your car's FM radio. It's important to have reasonable expectations for this -- if you want to hook up your MP3 player to your car stereo, the best way is through an Aux input jack. Now, if your car stereo doesn't have an Aux input jack, that's where this product comes in handy. (Another way to hook up your MP3 player is using a cassette adaptor, if your car stereo can play cassette tapes. These also work pretty well, if you can deal with a wire hanging out from the slot where you insert tape cassettes.)

This unit is smaller than I expected, and hangs out of your cigarette lighter with a cord that plugs into your MP3 player. The reception quality over your FM radio depends quite a bit on the position of the unit and the wire. I've found it works best to position the unit somewhere that works, like in the ashtray, or wedged between the seats, rather than let it dangle. If you let it dangle, then its position relative to your FM radio will keep changing as you drive, and that can make the reception quality change. Even small changes in the the position of the unit, an inch to the right or left, can make a big difference in the sound. Sound quality will also vary depending on where your car's radio antenna is located, either in the back of the car or in the front. You need to experiment with this to find the best location.

There's a "Pro" button that cycles through 4 sound quality settings. You'll want to try all four to see how they work. Sometimes the type of music you're playing will sound better with one of those four settings.

Set your MP3 player's sound output as high as you can to overcome static on the FM radio. You need to set the unit and the FM radio to the same frequency. The unit's ClearScan button makes it easy to find an unused FM frequency in your area -- you then tune the car's FM radio to that frequency and you're good to go. As you drive, if you find that you get increasing noise combined with your music, that's often an indication that you've moved into an area with another station, possibly a weak station, on that same frequency. At that point, you'll need to retune the unit (and the car's FM radio) to a different unused frequency.

The part of the unit that plugs into the cigarette lighter also has a USB jack where you can plug in your MP3 player's charging cord, so you can charge your player while you're in the car listening to tunes. Pretty handy.

Considering that my car's stereo doesn't have an Aux input, and that I don't want to replace or upgrade my car's stereo right now, this unit works great. I'm not expecting perfection with the sound quality, but it's pretty good. Better than most FM stations on the dial. Certainly good enough to make me happy to enjoy my own tunes.

Bose headphones are noise suppression first, sound fidelity second. If it’s sound fidelity you want, buy a comparably priced studio monitor headphone without noise suppression.

I’ve owned and worn out every iteration of the Bose noise-canceling headphones over the last 20 years for jet cabin noise suppression. Commercial airplane cabin noise is a proven travel fatigue-inducing component. A 2-17 hour flight with noise reduction headphones delivers noticeably less flight fatigue.

The QC-35’s are nearly worn out after another ‘million miles.’ They got 5 stars for the Bose attention to long-wear comfort. They’ve been beaten about, dinged, I’ve replaced the ear and head cushions twice. I suspect I have a wiring failure that’s about to reveal itself fully. I use the Bose most frequently without music for just the noise suppression. They work great as a sleep aid in hotels with and without music. Noise suppression is my #1 priority in this category. I have tested 2 of the latest Bose noise suppression headphone competitors. For several reasons, mostly head comfort and suppression extent, they still have a way to go to meet the Bose total experience.
The ambient noise suppression that these new 700 headphones provide is a significant improvement over the QC-35’s. The bass quality of Bose has always been a question mark easily revealed in a sales counter testing for comparison. Honestly, after an hour, the bass issue disappears in the Bose sound ambiance.

As to music reproduction, Bose does not represent the product as a monitor grade headphone. I happen to have a pair of Blue Ella monitor grade headphones. It is an error to compare the Bose work-horse noise suppression headphones that the 700 series represent with studio monitor grade fidelity. There is no question that studio monitor grade headphones deliver superior fidelity for the time they are worn.

Can I comfortably wear the Blue Ella’s on a trans-con flight? No (plus they are prone to a five-finger discount). They simply aren’t designed for hours of head comfort. The Blue Ella’s are fantastic for a couple of hours but are no way suitably head comfortable for a 17-hour flight to Australia.

The Bose 700’s are a clear step up for the QC-35 users. These are lighter on the head, and though they don’t have hingey elements of the QC-35, I’ve not experienced a flexibility problem from this lighter weight and flexible design. They are an improvement in the Bose reputation for the best designed, long-wear consideration.

I have had the opportunity to review more iPhone / iPad cables than I can possibly remember and over the years I have found there are certain characteristics that I look for in a cable that will increase its chances of being a high quality, long lasting cable.

I knew as soon as I saw these cables by Phantom they had those characteristics and after using it for the last 6 weeks I have been nothing but impressed.

I’ve found long, 6.6’ or 2m or longer, cables must have increased shielding in order to not lose speed in data transfer. In addition, they must employ some design element to resist kinking due to the stresses from being that length.

These cables suffer no noticeable loss in speed from their length during either charging or data transfer. The braided nylon covering is tight and resists kinking or becoming tangled. As with any braided nylon covered cable avoid them rubbing against sharp or rough surfaces for maximum life expectancy.

The primary failure point of any cable is where the cable meets the plugs. Due to the strains constantly put at those junctions this is where electrical shorts are most likely to occur and thus cause eventual failure. The ports on these cables taper and extend up towards the cable body protecting this critical juncture point greatly reducing chances of failure in these locations.

While some cables have ports that are so bulky they will not fit through case charging ports I have not found that to be the case with any I’ve tested with these cables.

This cable set is reliable, charging and data transfer speeds are great and they are designed to last. The price honestly can’t be beat for this level of quality.

I definitely recommend this set.

This AMFILM PREMIUM SCREEN PROTECTOR FILM CLEAR is an excellent choice for protecting your Google Nexus 7's touch screen. It's easy to install, absolutely invisible once installed, and doesn't interfere with the sensitivity of the touch screen. I was able to achieve a bubble-free installation on the very first try.

The installation instructions (printed on the retail packaging envelope) are easy to understand. The film itself--the middle layer, which is sandwiched between two masking sheets that are removed at the beginning and end of the installation--is stiff enough to lay down easily. Unlike some protective film, the adhesive doesn't aggressively grab dust motes from the air while you're installing the film. You get two sheets of film (giving you two chances at a perfect installation), a microfiber cleaning cloth, and a stiff cardboard square for smoothing out bubbles.

Because Google Nexus 7 protective film needs only one cutout (for the camera), it's especially easy to install. Just be careful that you center the film with the hole over the camera, and align it parallel to the tablet's top edge so that it lays down perfectly straight. When I got a tiny overlap at a top corner, there was a bubble at the edge that wouldn't smooth out. Rather than remove the otherwise bubble-free film, I raised the corner and trimmed the film with scissors--which fixed the problem.

This is probably one of the most useful surge protector power strips I’ve come across. It’s about the same size and shape as a small standard strip, measuring about 9 inches long and 2.25 inches wide. It has two power outlets that are unusually shaped – they appear to be designed so they can use both U.S.-standard 2 and 3 prong plus, plus a range of “overseas” plugs. They look weird, but they work fine with everything I plugged into it.

It also has 4 USB ports on the end so you can use the power strip to plug in a USB cable to charge a phone, tablet, etc. Two of the USB ports are rated at 2.4A; the other two are rated at 1A.

There’s an on/off switch at the top that powers down the full power strip. There is a separate power cord that attaches to the power strip to plug it into the wall outlet. That’s a very handy feature if you want to take this along on a trip, since it makes the power strip far easier to pack than if it had a permanently-connected power cord.

The case is plastic, but feels solid and durable. It has 4 non-skid pads on the base that grip the tabletop very well with no sliding when plugging things in and out.

While it would be nice if there were a third power outlet instead of just 2, this is a compact size that fits in well on my kitchen counter, and lets me plug in my phone and tablet for recharging, plus run a laptop off of AC power, with all outlets surge-protected.
