I paired and typed with this keyboard on the following four devices:

1. iPad3
2. iPhone5
3. BLU Life One 4G LTE Smartphone - GSM Unlocked
4. Nexus 7 3rd generation

It paired easily with the first two iOS (Apple) devices. However, the first-time pairing with the Android devices (items 3 and 4) took a lot of trial and error. I spent about 20 minutes trying to get each Android device to recognize the keyboard. I wound up charging the keyboard thinking it lacked power but it had a sufficient charge. When charging the keyboard did not help the situation, I turned the keyboard on and off, turned Bluetooth on and off, kept trying the pairing button with each attempt, etc., etc. Eventually, it finally worked but not without a lot of frustration. Also, with one of my devices, it paired using the MAC address of the keyboard and not the name.

In order to pair a Bluetooth device, one has to:
- Turn on the keyboard. Note that keyboard light will flash blue but only for a few seconds and it’s hard to see it. (Sometimes it did not flash for me, instead it was a steady blue).
- Enable Bluetooth on the device you are pairing it with. The device must be no more than 32 feet from keyboard.
- Press and hold “pair device” button on keyboard for about 5 seconds--LED light starts flashing on keyboard.
- When the “Bluetooth Wireless Keyboard” is found on your device, select it to complete the pairing process.
- To maximize keyboard functionality, once paired press FN + S for an iOS device and FN + A for an Android device. It’s at this point that the keyboard is ready to use.

There are multi-function hot keys like Shift + ~ to return to the Home Page or Shift + ! to begin a Search using the default browser on the paired device. However, the best use of the keyboard is for straight typing, in my opinion.

PROS

- I like the feel of the keyboard. It’s pliable, folds easily, and does not slip out of my hands.

- A micro-USB charging cable is supplied for charging the keyboard.

- Supposedly, this is waterproof. However, I did not dare submerge it in water. I will take their word for it.

CONS

- This keyboard is not designed for a touch typist like me. For instance, the QWERTY keyboard layout is a bit off because the B key is located on the right-hand side of the fold. I use my left hand to hit the B key but with this keyboard, I either have to over stretch my index finger to reach the B key or use my right hand.

- There are no risers for the keyboard; instead it lies very flat. In order for me to effectively type on this, I have to prop the top end on a book so that the keyboard lays on a slant.

- The keys are not sensitive to the touch, so I have to press hard in order for the letters to type.

- It’s difficult to determine when the keyboard is powered on. Many times I had to press and hold the power button until the light flashed as a simple press of the button would not work. The instructions say the blue light flashes for three seconds when on but this did not always happen for me. Sometimes the blue light came on steady indicating the keyboard was on. It was not always consistent. I wound up either pressing the pairing button to see if the pairing light would flash or just tried typing when paired with a device. Depending on whether the keyboard worked or not, I knew whether it was on or not.

On another note, when I registered this keyboard on the VisionTek site, I got a confirmation email with my username and password in clear text. This is poor security as passwords should not be sent in clear text over the Internet.

In summary, had I tried out this keyboard in a store, I would have never selected it. Unless I am typing a lot with my Nexus 7, this is just too difficult to use due to the effort that has to be used to type, the flatness of the keyboard, and the slightly odd layout. I love the feel of the keyboard and its compactness but other than this, I’m disappointed.

I want to give this 3.5 stars- 3 is too low and 4 seems too high, but I'll round up for now. I have mixed things to say about this camera. It isn't going to take stellar photos. They are either going to have a lot of motion blur or if you raise the shutter speed (sports mode) you're going to get substantial noise. The videos side is even worse. A modern cell phone or point-and-shoot is going to snap better photos and videos. BUT... you can take this to a water park and not care what happens to it, which is exactly what we did.
I'm including three examples shots here that I wouldn't have gotten without this camera (excuse the smiley face for privacy). One are kids about to go down a water slide, where I as the photographer am being rained on by nearby sprinklers. Then there's a slightly more epic shot of the giant bucket atop the slides crashing water down on me. This shot froze the droplets of water right before thoroughly drenching the photographer (me) a split second later. The last is from some of our underwater pool shots. These are all cases in which I would NOT have been comfortable using my real cameras or even cell phones- as waterproof as they claim some flagship phones are now, I wouldn't trust them to this. In my experience, even waterproof phones have trouble operating under water (the touch screen doesn't work properly), and we have ruined the charging port of another at a pool previously. But this is totally sealed and has real buttons that work just as well under water as above. For all those reasons, I actually LIKE this camera. It takes photos I literally would NOT have gotten otherwise.
Also, as a bit of personal experience, after going down a water slide and trying to video it, I actually dropped the camera into the pool at the bottom. I was able to run in and chase and grab it, and the entire time I was thinking I'm SO GLAD this isn't my phone!
I'm actually printing some of the photos as I write this and although they appear grainy on my screen, on 4x6 photo paper they look perfectly acceptable.
So why 3.5 stars? Well, the user interface is terrible. More than once I had to turn it off and restart to get back to photo taking because I couldn't figure out how to get out of the mode I was in. Also, it claims to have a 21megapixel mode, but I'm pretty sure it is just upscaling a smaller resolution. The noise at 21mp seems soft, like it took a lower resolution image and then scaled it UP to 21 mp. The 12 megapixels mode seemed much more true-to-pixel size, so that seems like a bit of false advertising. Then there's the video mode- keep it at 720 if you want any kind of normal playable frame rates. It also looks like less-than-HD that has been scaled up to fit, but at least it works at all. At 1080 HD, it was doing a variable frame rate thing that often slowed to a slide show and wasn't playable on my phone or laptop. I'm only able to play it back from the camera, which I wish I had known before I chose it for some things I wanted to remember.
Outside of those caveats, it is good for the specific use as a camera you can afford to get wet.

This is a combined review of two of the lowest cost “Active Noise Cancelling” earbuds on Amazon:
[[ASIN:B004K09H32 Audio-Technica ATH-ANC23 QuietPoint Active Noise-Cancelling In-Ear Headphones]]
[[ASIN:B00SA5JCWO Egghead 1010 - Active Noise Cancelling Earbuds with Travel Pouch]]

PRICE
The price difference as of May, 2015 was $14 with Audio-Technica being the more expensive unit.

IN THE BOX
Both products contain:
--Earbuds
--Multiple silicone earbud cups
--Airline headset adapter
--Carrying Pouch

Audio-Technica contains in addition:
--Battery
--Pair of foam earbud cups. Not memory foam, just normal foam. I have not tried these.

Egghead:
--Mute button: In addition to the ANC on/off switch, Egghead has a nice mute button that turns off Noise Cancellation while it is pressed down.

SOUND QUALITY
I am not an audiophile so the sound from both headsets were good to me but the difference comes when you factor in the fit of the earbuds.

FIT
Both sets sit deeply in your ear and from pictures of both products, you will see that beyond the earbud, they have a circular piece before the actual connection to the wires.
--Egghead: The earbuds are attached straight to the circular piece so the fit is actually straight out away from your ears.
--Audio-Technica: The earbuds are angled forward so the circular piece actually serves as an anchor that sits nicely in your ear lobe and further cuts out outside noise. The additional foam earbud cup may make the difference for some people when it comes to a comfortable fit.
--Kids: I purchased these for a trip that the family will take. The kids usually have a hard time with normal earbuds not fitting in very well but they were able to keep the Audio-Technica earbuds in using the smallest earbud cups. The kids are 6 and 9.

NOISE REDUCTION
Here is the main event. I want to make a few points about Active Noise Cancelling: --Noise cancellation filters are designed to cancel out lower pitched, repeating noises like airplane engine rotors and car tires on a road, but it will not cancel out high or mid-range sounds like human voice. The same engine rotor and road noise also contain components of higher pitched sounds so NC filters will not cut out the noise completely.
--Using Noise Cancellation often feels like being underwater with your ears popping. It is a discomfort that you would have to get used to. The greater the cancellation effect, the greater the discomfort. Be prepared for this if you haven’t used NC before.
--ANC only works IF the inverted noise wave can overpower the noise coming in. If you are using a lawn mower and the noise it makes overpowers the “anti noise” because you’re standing right in back of the motor, you will not hear a big difference in the Noise Reduction effects.

Ok, so on with it. The Audio-Technica claims to reduce 90% of noise. I don’t have anything to confirm the claim but if we assume the Audio-Technica(AT) to be at 90%, my own assessment of the Egghead’s (Egg) noise reduction effects would be around 50-60%.

--Computer Fan Noise: Egg reduces the noise to slightly audible but you’d need to use toggle the mute button on it to really tell. AT completely removes the noise.
--Clothes Dryer: Egg takes the “edge” off the noise produced. You can still hear most of the noise standing about 3 feet away from the dryer. AT takes the bass tones completely out of the noise while leaving the higher pitched metal friction and buttons hitting the tumbler noise. In effect, with the AT, standing only 3 feet away, it sounds like you are actually 20 feet away.

So in conclusion, you have probably guessed that I think the additional cost of the Audio-Technicas are worth it. In addition to the benefits mentioned above, I have recently been able to get a great deal on a pair of [[ASIN:B00UETOW4C Harmon/Kardon SOHO II NC]] on ebay. The noise reduction effects of the Audio-Technicas equal or maybe even exceeds those of the Harmon/Kardons.

I have a number of headphones and I have gotten quite fussy about them and how they sound and how they fit. I was interested in this set, as they resemble a set of Philips headphones I used many years ago and my experience with them was positive. The difference was that the Philips set I used was quite expensive and had active noise cancelling functions. These are a lot less expensive. While these are not the best headphones I have used they are well worth their asking price and I think they are a good set.

These are very striking-looking headphones and they really stand out. I have the blue set and they are by far the most eye-catching phones I have used. The paint is electric blue and the pads and headband are black. I like the overall design, The cord is long enough to make them useful for using at a workstation or desk without having to sit still, a problem I have seen with a number of headsets with very short cords.

There are two primary considerations I have when looking at headphones – comfort and sound profile.

The comfort is good. The pads are long and oval and they appear at first like they would pinch or otherwise not fit well enough to make a seal. I was mistaken. They are quite comfortable and they feel good when wearing them. I will say I personally prefer headphones that really fit tightly, and these are a lot softer than I prefer, but many people prefer lighter headphones so I cannot consider this a fault. They do get a little warm after wearing them for a while, though. Keep in mind that because these do not clamp down tightly, they are not the very best for noise isolation.

The sound profile is another matter entirely. The bass is strong and there is no problem there. The midrange is sorely lacking and as a result the music sounds like it is in a tunnel – this is a problem with many headphones and I specifically look for it. It can be corrected with an equalizer which is fine if you have access to such. I will say that it’s noticeable to me but I have worked with more expensive phones that sound a lot worse. The highs are fine and are clear. I have also noticed that as the volume gets boosted higher, the sound distorts.

Now, if these were expensive headphones I would be a lot more critical, but these are under $20. For a $20 set of headphones, these are just fine and they are very much competitive with others in their price range. They sound all right through they could be better, they are quie comfortable and I really like the price point. If you need an inexpensive pair of headphones, these are not a bad choice at all.

***The first part of this review is for the Red option***

I needed more than just a simple case for my Kindle as it pulls double duty serving as my tablet and my planner. I also needed something that would provide it with supreme protection as it accompanies me to and from work every day.

I purchased this case/portfolio in the red color in hopes that it would make it stand out at work. Many of my co-workers have Kindles as well and I didn't want mine to accidentally get picked up. The red is nice, but way too much for me. I have been considering exchanging it for the black and the following issues are what sent me over the edge and led to my returning the red case.

This case/portfolio worked nicely for my needs. However, I removed two stars for two reasons.
#1 The case stunk to high heaven. It was so bad that I thought a stink bug had gotten into my house. Though the "scent" did lessen over a few weeks, it was still very present after five weeks.
#2 The description claims that this case has the ability to put the Kindle to sleep when you close it up. Not true. After my battery died over night, I realized that the sleep/wake feature was not working in my case. I had to physically turn my Kindle off before closing the case (may not seem like much of a hassle, but it quickly becomes a time consuming annoyance).

There was one benefit to this case though. It is the first case I have had for my Kindle that does not have any issues with using the Camera App while still encased in the removable inner sleeve. This was a very nice feature, however not nice enough to get me to keep it.

**This is the review of the Black option**

So, I just returned the red case and opted to give the black version a shot. It arrived this evening and wow, what a difference!

It doesn't stink at all and the sleep/wake feature is functioning properly! I do, however, now have the ghastly on-screen message of needing to slide my Kindle up in its case to take a picture. But this does not bother me very much as I have not used my Kindle for taking pictures more than a handful of times in the month that I have owned it.

All in all, it is a nice, professional case/portfolio that offers the features for my Kindle that I was needing. It also has a fair amount of pockets inside, though do not expect to be able to store much bulk as you will run into two problems..
#1 If you add too many things to the pockets, you run the risk of the pockets bulging and possibly damaging your Kindle's screen.
#2 Also, if you add too much to the pockets, you will possibly not be able to close the case. And if you manage to close it, you may run the risk of stretching the zipper and ultimately damaging the case.

Personally, I keep a small stack (about 10) of my business cards, five gift certificates and a little cash in the pockets and the zippers still flow smoothly with no issues and nothing from the pocket side comes in contact with my screen. Overall, I would recommend this case, as long as you are willing to take a risk on getting one that has the features you are wanting/needing as it seems to be a completely random toss-up as to which case has which features.

On a side note, the included stylus/pen is a great idea, but it isn't executed very well here. The plastic tip leaves a lot to be desired - it takes more force than I care to apply to my screen for the Kindle to register the stylus' contact on the screen. I did some research and purchased [[ASIN:B00E0GV9IC The Friendly Swede Bundle of 6 Micro-Knit Hybrid Fiber Tip Universal Capacitive Stylus Pens 4.5" for Smart Phone Touch Pad + 6 x 15'' Elastic Tether Lanyards + Cleaning Cloth in Retail Packaging]]. These stylus' are VERY nice in appearance and easy to use without requiring much force on the screen at all.

I have been building computer systems and troubleshooting for a long time. I really enjoy taking parts in and out and programming systems to do what I want. I remember looking at a commercial for the new tablets and saying to my family- "What the heck would anyone want one of THOSE things for?" It was not long after they became bored with my insistence that tablets were a total waste that I had my chance to take my first tablet for a test run- the Acer Iconia A1-830.

The Acer was a fantastic little first tablet. It performed as well or better than a few Samsungs and older Apples that we had the chance to put it up against, and for the price, it was a great little tablet. I found some use for it and found myself reaching for the tablet when I didn't want to do work at the computer. It was more portable than a laptop and easier to do quick surfing and simple tasks on, and GAMING.

I thought that all was well until I began to have a few issues with the Acer. It was at that point that I saw a great price on the new Samsung Galaxy Tab S2. I was hooked.

WHAT IS THIS TABLET LIKE?
I plan to write this review to people who are not as interested in the detailed specs of this unit, but instead I will write this for an average user who might not be as technically astute. There are quite a few well done reviews that have lots of specs and details that will satisfy those who really need that information to make decisions.

SCREEN
One of the things that I did not like about the older Samsungs was the size. I preferred the more squared screen of the Acer than the Samsungs I had worked on. My daughter has one and although it seems nice, I just was not keen on the screen. This model has exactly what I wanted to have. The shape makes it easier to work on the web , use as an E reader, and play games. I find it easier to read than more elongated screens.

One of the things that I found to be frustrating is the slick surface of the screen. For web surfing or book reading it is fine, but games can really get frustrating as I find the screen to be very sensitive and it is easy to mess up.

As for the brightness, it is very bright. I have it turned down by about 75% and it is plenty bright enough most of the time. Also, the color contrast is breathtaking. The screen is very sharp and the blacks are BLACK and the colors are very saturated. This thing is eye candy squared! It is hard to look at other screens when I am done using this.

COLOR
This is not really gold in color. I would say it is gold tinged platinum in color. Do not expect a bold gold.

SMOOTHNESS AND UNEVEN EDGES
There are a few things which bug me about this tablet, but not that much. Getting a good case from Fintie took care of it. The button on the bottom of the vertical positioned screen stands out from the unit. That means if you are going to get a keyboard in the case, it could press on the button and cause problems. The Fintie case is raised enough to protect the button.

There is also the camera lens on the back that sticks out quite a bit. Again, the case takes care of that problem. The back itself might be plastic, but it feels like metal and looks like metal so it is not cheap looking.

SPEED AND FUNCTION
WOW is this thing FAST! I have to say that it really has blown me out of the water with the speed and smooth operation of everything I have tried to do. It works smoothly, load up is fast. I know part of that might be due to the inclusion of Lollipop but also the hardware and set up. I have not found it to lag at all. Great performance. I also know that this model is scheduled for the Marshmallow upgrade sometime this year which could change performance to be even better.

I have 32G microSD card in this right now but it is expandable to 128.

BATTERY LIFE
I was very concerned about all of the complaints about battery life. I was so concerned I almost didn't get this tablet. I am SO glad I did, however. I keep location turned off and bluetooth as well unless I am using it. The battery stuns me with how long it has lasted. I loaded that baby up to 100% last night and this morning about 11 AM I began to work intensely on the tablet, trying to back up files from my Acer and transfer them over to the Samsung via bluetooth. That means that the bluetooth was on all day, I was downloading and installing all day long. I have to say that I am shocked. It is about 12 hours later and there is still over 50% battery left. I had to recharge my Acer once during all of this time.

So, compared to what I am used to (which is about 2-4 hours of work on a tablet before recharging, including no location turned on) this tablet is dreamy for me. The battery is way beyond what I am used to with the Acer, so I am very happy.

THE BOTTOM LINE
I will update as I find things to tell you about, but I wanted to start off with the basics as that is what I was looking for when I was trying to decide if I should get this tablet or not. I still do not find tablets to be useful for all of my work, but they are great for smaller web surfing, quick look ups, apps for certain things and of course games and skype. As for the keyboard and typing, it is not really practical at least for me to use this for heavier loads of work- desktop or laptop are best suited for that.

Is it worth the price? At $300 it is a very powerful device with a screen that blows anything else I have seen out of the water. The colors are a feast for the eyes, the clarity is crisp, and the smooth operation is delightful. If you really enjoy having a tablet you can depend on, I would say that this fits the bill.

Could you do with something less expensive? Yes. But you might have more frustration with that lower price tag. The set up of this tablet is easy to work with, great operation and having two windows open at the same time is delightful. I am very happy with this and despite my misgivings after reading so many reviews with disappointment in them I can say at this point, I am very very glad that I went ahead and got it. It is a really great tablet.

Everyone is going to tell you this camera is awesome. It is. I'm going to concentrate on telling you some details you may not know:

- I'm an Electrical* engineer, but I am so impressed with the Mechanical* designs of this unit. It's amazingly small, but they've thought of everything to make it easy on the user, from battery pulltags, to grommeted permanently attached covers, to hold switches, mini displays, and options galore...

- ...and to keep it small, they actually had to make a separate tripod mount, that connects at two points, but only requires one screw (that you can screw with a coin), all because the unit is so small that it couldn't accommodate a full depth standard tripod mount screw...

- ...and then there is a baseplate that accepts that standard tripod screw, and once it is attached to that baseplate, you can attach it to either the flat or curved adhesive or Velcro-belt by a very strong friction clip. This friction clip is also accepted by the (not included) wristband offered by Sony, which does not come with its own friction clip (so don't lose the one that comes with the camera)...

- ...all this screwing and unscrewing could almost become annoying. But then you have the waterproof case. This case has a built-in tripod mount, but is barely larger than the camera with tripod mount attached, so why not keep the case on all the time for that extra layer of protection? I like the idea. And then you can keep that mounted where you want it, and remove the camera as necessary to charge or pull out the SD card.

- The strange thing about the case is, it's only rated (per Sony; they say "to their* specifications) to 5m deep water for 30 minutes. That's the same rating the camera itself has, but by looking at the case, I'd expect it to make it down to at least 10m for as long as you want with no problems. I think they're just being super careful, but I know from experience that companies don't like to make dramatic claims as to waterproofing because they end up with all sorts of warranty claims (both legitimate and illegitimate) to sort through. Even so, I love the double protection...

- ...Meanwhile, the wrist-mount monitor is rated down to 10m. Remember that Wi-Fi doesn't work under water, so this is probably only going to do you good at the surface anyway...

- ...The monitor works well, and picks up your camera right away after first connection. The buttons are fairly intuitive. Remember that the camera itself simply will not be as easy to playback/review as a regular camcorder simply because there is no room for all that mess on this tiny camera...

- ...And also remember that - even though this camera is totally awesome - it will not necessarily replace your camcorder if you care about things such as zoom, instant local playback, etc. Ideally, you'll have both for different functions, but if anyone can pull off the ultimate all-in-one a few electronic generations from now, it's Sony. The point here I want to highlight is NO ZOOM.

- You cannot record in XAVC S unless you have an (micro - it takes micro SD or the newest, smallest Memory Stick) SD card "greater than class 10". Even if you have a fancy class 10 SD card that claims to be faster than the rest, the camera will give you an error and you'll have to record to *.mp4. I didn't even know they had classes above 10, but the best they have out right now is UHS-3, which costs around $28 bucks for brand name 32GB, whereas a the same brand/size in class 10 is now around $15. I recommend getting the largest decent name UHS-3 you can find to accommodate this camera, which is probably going to cost $50-60 for a 64GB.

- The accessory options available for this thing are endless, from suction cup mounts for your car (exterior or interior) to your bike handles (the included curved base works on your bike handles, but not as perfectly as the vise strictly intended for that use), wrist mounts, snorkel goggles mounts, and the list goes on infinitely. Sony included two of these for my review, and - as you probably expect - the Sony branded stuff is sublime.

- At the time of writing, Sony's website does not yet have a full manual for download, but there is some barely helpful Q&A page you can get to with the link in the included paperwork. While there is tons of paper included with the camera, it's mostly useless; I wish they'd just give you the full manual and only include one language per box if they need to reduce paper use...

- ...I wanted the manual because I sort of expect there are more connections you can make with WiFi (i.e., connect to computer to download files) and other options that I am so far unaware of. Frankly, the best way for me has always been just to take the SD card to the computer and use the best freeware you already have on the computer (like VLC Media Player).

Conclusion: Sony products have always impressed me, and this camera (and included accessories) get me excited about the company in a way I haven't been since I bought my Z-series TV years ago. They clearly still make the best stuff when they try. Although this is not the perfect camcorder, it is the perfect action cam: the size, options, and quality speak for themselves.

Here are my thoughts on the machine itself--unrelated to the seller:

PROS
- Terrific resolution. Much easier to read screen text.
- Lots of variety in color configurations for different light environments.
- 32 GB of memory really makes a difference over my previous 4-8GB.
- SSD is likewise fast and the whole system is quiet.
- This list of pros is short, but they are the most important things to me. Everything else is small beans.

CONS
- It is unbelievable how hard it is to get to the USB ports, etc, on the back! I literally have to use needle-nose pliers to plug or unplug USB devices--and a flashlight and contortions. I've read it's because the speakers didn't leave a lot of options for where to put these, but it just ridiculous.
- The sound is not as good as I expected. My last Dell AIO had JBL speakers and I don't think I realized how good those were. To be fair, the sound is fine, I was just expecting to be blown away by the six speakers on the bottom.
- Poor webcam placement. It's on the bottom at a really weird angle. Will probably upgrade.
- Onboard mic is also worse than what was in the Inspiron 2320. Remedied by purchasing a separate mic. But on a system this expensive, the mic and webcam should be premium, not barely useable.
- The screen would buzz softly at anything less than 100% brightness. A workaround is to reduce brightness via Radeon Pro graphics board. SOLUTION: go through Dell community customer service boards to update the VBIOS.
- The color temperatures sometimes get really off after the monitor goes to sleep and wakes up. I put a shortcut to Dell Premier Color in the taskbar and just reapply the setting, and it's fine. Still shouldn't even be a thing that happens on a machine with this price tag.
- Not a fan of the included wired mouse and keyboard, so I swapped out my own. I'm guessing this was originally meant for a computer lab where you wouldn't want someone to walk away with the peripherals.

OVERALL VERDICT
It took a while to get everything sorted, some of which was my fault. But I did get it sorted. The lower price from the seller comes with the tradeoff of losing some of the warranty and it taking extra time to get the remaining warranty transferred to me. But it still cost thousands less via this route than it would have otherwise. So worth it, I guess, if you've got the time for shenanigans.

I really hate to use the word “cute” but there’s no way around it – this is a cute cam! It looks pretty much the same as the original Cube, but offers improved video and the addition of WiFi. Of the new features, the WiFi is the most significant, and makes this far more useful as a cam.

I also have the original Cube and the build quality continues to be very good. These are priced higher than the “no name” action cams, but after using (and breaking) a couple of those, it’s nice to be able to count on the Cube to keep on working. It’s water resistant, which makes it less worrisome when using it in bad weather or around water. It supports up to a 128MB SD card

The form factor and overall design is much the same as the original Cube. It has a magnet in the base that is more than strong enough to keep it well-planted. It’s not strong enough for significant activity (e.g., staying on a bike handle while riding) but it offers the benefit of tripod-like stability without the need for a tripod (providing you have something metal to fasten the magnet).

The biggest change is wifi on the Cube+. I found the setup to be straightforward – basically just download the app and follow the setup steps. I love that the app lets you use it as a live view – that’s a big improvement over the original Cube. It’s a very helpful feature for planning a shot, plus allows me to monitor how things are turning out without having to play the video.

Image quality has been impressive – zero complaints there. I was pleased with the resolution of the original Cube, and this is a bit better. Audio quality is OK. It’s not outstanding, but it clearly picks up voices. I understand that earlier versions of the Cube+ had very poor sound quality, but the one I have (got it in Dec 2015) is fine with regard to sound.

All in all, it’s a great cam with a fun form factor and look. Well worth considering if you’re looking for a small profile action cam with solid build quality and performance. While the price has increased over that of the original Cube, the wifi features are very useful and well implemented, making this version well worth the additional cost.

I like the basic design of this -- the small sleek size, nice layout of buttons, large display. The radio reception seems to be decent, although mounting it on the wall is not possible in my area, since I have to turn it various directions to get a couple of local AM stations. Weather band reception is OK, as is FM reception.

That's about where my positive feelings for this little radio end.

It is way too difficult to set up, NOT with regard to the physical aspects of hitting the correct buttons in the correct sequence, but rather in terms of deciphering and understanding the instructions. The instruction leaflet, such as it is, is written in such small type that it's nearly impossible to read. I finally went to the Eton website and downloaded the instruction manual there, then "zoom"ed it so I could read how to set the time, store radio stations, etc.

Then there's the issue of the S.A.M.E. codes. I had never heard of this technology before I got this radio. NO WHERE in the included instructions is there any mention of NOAA, or even the "S.A.M.E." designation. On the Amazon product page, there is a mention of "S.A.M.E." in one of the product features bullets, and "NOAA" in another product feature bullet on the product page here on Amazon, but nothing that explains what "S.A.M.E. codes" actually ARE. The instruction manual tells you how to "Select the county" -- OK, so what does THAT mean? The instructions don't tell you that "Select the county" really means "enter the NOAA S.A.M.E. codes." You're not "selecting" anything; you need to know the S.A.M.E. code(s) for the desired area(s), and then ENTER those according to the instructions.

This was my first weather radio -- and I'm generally fairly good at figuring things out -- but this had me confused for a good 15-20 minutes while I searched via google for "county code," "weather county code," etc. Finally found the NOAA site and the codes, and entered the one for my county.

And I STILL don't know what "Setting Defeat" means. I mean, I know how to set it, and I can read what the manual says, but it doesn't really tell me WHY I might want to enable or disable "defeat," and what, precisely, it enables or disables ("ENABLE: Alert when receiving a message. DISABLE: Displays the message on the LCD when receiving a message" -- does that mean that when it's enabled, you DON'T get a message displayed on the LCD when receiving a message? What kind of Alert happens when it's enabled? the flashing light? the siren? what, precisely, am I "defeating" with this??)

I have no idea if the weather alert part of the radio works. We've had one National Weather Service-issued high wind warning here in the Pacific NW since I received and programmed the radio, and it didn't set off the alert -- no light flashing, no "message," nothing. I intend to take this along on an extended road trip this summer (reprogramming the S.A.M.E. codes along the route), and I figure I'll probably encounter some sort of "alert-able" weather event along the way. I'll update this review then if that part works.

Meanwhile, I'm giving this 2 stars -- it works pretty well as a compact "clock radio," doesn't take up a lot of space, and has decent reception. But Eton REALLY needs to do something about the instructions. The ones included with the product are useless, and the copy on the website isn't much better.

I've only used Wyze, Arlo and Homehawk cameras, and without a doubt, this Panasonic software is the best of the bunch. 5-stars!

The reviews for this item are strange at best. I have a Nexus 7 (2013), so I'm doing some comparisons to that, even though I know well they aren't in the same league.
I bought this as a "family" tablet, so my son could play some educational/puzzle games without tying mine up and so my wife, less interested in having a tablet, could have access to some features I use mine for (controlling the KODI system, casting to the Chromecast, etc.) That said, the one feature that makes a FAMILY tablet has been intentionally turned off. The ability to have multiple user accounts on the tablet, which is a Kit Kat native option, is turned off by the manufacturer. They cannot turn it back on - according to their tech support. They did say if it was the right serial number, there was a software change they could send me, but since the serial number is on a sticker at the hottest part of the table, and where ANY normal use would require holding it, that number didn't last more than a week. This ONE missing feature is almost a non-starter, but since I bought it and it's not junk, it's really too late to not start. For shame turning this feature off. It seriously irks me. Suggested options include rooting. Good luck. I spent hours looking in the XDA and other android forums for a way to do it. No such luck. I found ONE thread claiming it was easy with xyz method. I didn't find that to be the case.

The Y88X is very light and very slim. It does feel a tad flimsy because of that and the fact that the shell seems like a slightly thinner than expected plastic. The screen is also not very hard. It flexes.

Charge life is ok. I'd say it should last a full day on a single charge with a few hours of gaming (not 3D/processor exhaustive).

The viewing angle in landscape mode is generally perfectly fine. The viewing angle in portrait mode is terrible. Actually, if you tilt it down, the angle is ok, if you tilt it up, it gives a posterized look to it. Not particularly visually useful.

The cameras are TERRIBLE. Really bad. My Canon Powershot from 1999 that only took .3M pictures did a better job that this, and I'm not exaggerating. Both cameras are blurry and slow. A secondary purpose for this was to use it for a wall mounted weather station with the capability to be a skype/video chat option for the house. I'm sure it'll suffice, but only just.

One nice thing was that it came with a screen protector already on it. Unfortunately, it wasn't put on with any care and has bubbles in a bunch of places. No one else in the house seems to care, so I'm not going to worry about it.

There is a problem with touching the screen around the edges. It's hit or miss at times.

My screen also came with two blemishes on it that are more noticeable when the background is lighter.

There is a bright side. It CAN be snappy with many apps. It streams netflix and casts to the Chromecast just great. Having access to a microsd slot makes the memory limitation it starts with not a big deal (wish the Nexus has one). The CPU seems perfectly capable of keeping up. I've not tried high needs games, but we don't generally do those on the tablets anyway. It does multitask, but the limitations show in the form of jolting screen changes and slow transitions. It is a low ram device, so this should be no surprise. Just kill some apps and move on.

My 5 year old doesn't notice or care about how it's not as nice as the Nexus, so that's fine to me as well. Some have described this as a good tablet for kids. I'd say it just fine for someone with lower expectations. Most adults I know with tablets are not power users, they just think they are. If the issues I brought up don't bother you, this is likely a good choice for you. I wouldn't specifically recommend it to a friend, but if they really only had $60 to spend, I'd say this is an option they can live with. If I had another $30+ to spend, I'd have looked for something else.

The company for which I work sent me this to upgrade my Levono T400. I was running out of space on the mechanical, 250GB SATA internal drive. Not to mention that the drive was starting to make alarming noises.

When this drive arrived I used a SATA to USB cable to connect it to one of my T400 USB ports, downloaded the free app that was recommended in instructions that came with the SSD drive, and cloned my mechanical internal drive to the new one. That process took about four hours since the old drive was getting very full.

While that was going on I went on Youtube and found a video that showed how to remove the original internal drive from the laptop. I was expecting a nightmare, but lucked out because the Lenovo T400's internal drive takes less than five minutes to swap out. Obviously your experience is going to be different depending on the computer that you are swapping the internal drive. This is the second "Creative" brand wireless bluetooth speaker with microphone, and so far, the sound quality has not been very good. The first, "Creative Sound BlasterAxx SBX10 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker with Microphone" was $127.04 (list price $149.99), and this one currently has a list price of $199.99. I cannot hear any discernable difference in sound quality, though this speaker is larger than the other. They are both OK for being usb powered, but there are better-sounding products out there for the same price if you are willing to sacrifice the speaker option.

I ran the same tests on this speaker as the other and got identical results:

This one gets a mixed review for the overall sound quality, but it does have some features that make it very useful. I will be reviewing its various features individually so you can better assess if this meets your needs or not. I used a decibel measuring app on my phone to determine when the speakers began to distort some of what I played.

Playing audio with Bluetooth or via USB with a computer:
-There is no noticeable difference with playback using Bluetooth versus USB connection to a computer, and it has a Very long range (I walked about 25ft away and it was still doing fine)

AUDIO

75 DECIBELS AND UNDER:
Almost all audio was fine: clear, undistorted, and with pretty good clarity (don't expect GREAT quality or clarity. Just Good.) Some types of music fared poorly even at this relatively soft volume. I used "Fortuna from Carmina Burana" to test the system's limits. (YouTube the piece if you want to know which song I refer to--you'll recognize it immediately) The chorus of singers sounded distorted. At higher volumes, even as lot as 85db, it was awful. Other types of music were fine (orchestra music, pop, hip hop, electronica), but sometimes the treble was a bit fuzzy.

75-85 DECIBELS:
This is the maximum volume the speakers can reach with the USB connection, so it can get loud enough for a small-medium party, but not Very loud.
It's hit and miss here. The treble and bass have some problems, especially treble. The clarity diminishes and any nuances in your music will generally get a bit lost or muffled. Choral music, music with higher pitched percussive elements, and some types of rock and orchestra music don't sound very good.

PHONE CALLS:
The voice of the person you are calling sounds a bit muffled--definitely not as good as headphones or the phone, but about on par with other Bluetooth systems I've tried.

The voice of the speaker (i.e. You) is actually clear! This part gets a solid review. With my built-in car Bluetooth system, as well as detachable ones I've reviewed, usually the person you are calling has trouble hearing you and can experience interference. Maybe that is because it is in the car and there's road noise, but in any case, the fact this one does, actually, sound clear to the recipient of your phone call is a BIG plus.

Overall, this is a good product when you compare it to other desktop laptop speakers. If you are comparing it to products specifically meant for enjoying audio, however, I would recommend the Pioneer Electronics Audition Series for a relatively inexpensive but high quality experience, or Bose if you are looking for something higher-end. The price of the Pioneer product is almost the same, and while it doesn't have Bluetooth unless you buy the attachment separately (about $70) and it only docks with the older iPhone and iPods, the sound quality of that one is stunning. If you want extra features like FREE Bluetooth and speakerphone capability, this one is ok for the price. Not great. Just ok.

Because this is basically the same as the "Creative Sound BlasterAxx SBX10 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker with Microphone", and the other is about $70 cheaper, I would recommend getting the SBX10 and saving your money. They are basically the same thing, so either pay more and get better sound quality with another product entirely, or pay less for the same thing.

My husband wanted me to go with the customized UE headphones as they are extremely comfortable and have the best sound quality ever. I tried his on to get a feel of the harden material inside my ears. So I ended up purchasing them from UE’s website. He has the most expensive ones and the sound quality is like listening to live music. So, UE was quick to ship the molding pieces for my ears. I went with the most expensive earphones, too (Over 1k). Well, after taking pics of my ears and doing the molding, it turned out my left ear, according to their techs, was outside the 95% range, and they suggested seeing an audiologist. Too much trouble, but they offered me a discount should I have gone. What I think may have been the problem was that I moved the left ear mold during molding process and that may have led to the final conclusion. However...

I can across these Fits, and though I was reluctant to try the molding method again, I purchased them knowing that Amazon has a superb return policy. Upon their arrival, I immediately prepared for the molding process. Now, I did run into technical errors. And this is just to share with you what happened to me and what I eventually did in case you should run into the same error.

After placing them into my ears, the UE Fits app popped up a message that the batteries were low and to charge for 5 mins for molding process. Now, I followed the directions, multiple times, as I kept getting the same error. And all while doing this I also had difficulties with pairing, repeatedly.

So frustrated with the app, and after 2 hours of charging and attempting to do the molding, I eventually reached out to the questions community on here. I received good responses but none of them helped. Even UE (Logitech) responded saying to contact their support line. I didn't. I figured it out myself. So if you run into the same error, you will need to delete the app and reinstall. Worked like a charm immediately. Pairing was difficult. Many attempts to pair, but one side would pair and then the other side would not connect. Eventually from Apple Iphone, I would get the message to forget device and re-pair. It's was a real pain but I eventually got them to work. So just keep trying should you run into the same issue.

So now the molding process. It is just like the customization earphones. You will hear music and then feel the earphones warming up. To some it may feel hot but just hang in there. Then the app tells you when it's complete. And then you are all set!!

I will say that these earphones are the best!! The material used to mold to your ears are soft and extremely comfortable!!! I can literally wear them for long periods of time without them causing left ear pain and they do NOT fall out!!! These Fits confirm that the customization ones I wanted I somehow managed to mess up. UE customized earphones do provide two sizes to try on, whereas these Fits only provide one size, but that worked for me!! I am excited that my search, and spending all that money on various earphones, has come to an end. They may not have the same sound quality as the customized ones I wanted, but these sound great being that they are moldable earphones!

I will have to update later regarding phone call clarity and such. I haven't had a chance to test them on calls.

In the meantime I hope this review helps!! I highly recommend these Fits if you do not want to spend thousands of dollars on earphones.

I recently purchased one of these laptops when I stumbled on it here at Amazon. I was very much attracted by the price but was a little wary - this was one of very few laptops with an Intel Core i7 CPU in its price range so I was unsure what compromise might have been made to drive down the price. After working with it and really getting to know it, I can say there were few compromises made - this is an all-around awesome laptop at a really, really good price (as I write, $799). There are a couple of minor things I personally would change but these come down to preference.

I will start with something that no one else online seems to mention when describing this laptop - the screen. From reading the specifications to digging around on the manufacturer's website I could find precious little regarding the screen beyond the dimensions. It's the glossy type, so please keep this in mind when shopping for a laptop. Some people prefer a matte finish on the screen to cut down on reflections so if a glossy screen is a problem then this laptop might not work for you. Personally, I like the glossy type of screen as it's easy to clean and since I work in a darker room most of the time I do not have issues with reflections. This laptop's screen is also very bright and clear, brighter than that of my Sony Vaio.

Another very interesting feature of this laptop is the keyboard. It has a full number pad on the right side, slightly separated from the main keys. I like that. It also happens to be the chicklet-style keyboard which in my experience has been better at keeping stuff from getting in the keyboard.

I made one unfortunate discovery when setting up this laptop - the power plugs into the middle of the left side of the case. That's a very awkward place for the power to be plugged in. What makes this particularly unfortunate is that the plug sits directly next to the output air vent where heat from the CPU dissipates. When not relying exclusively on the battery, make sure you move the cord in such a way to avoid that vent.

This laptop has three USB ports, all of which are on the sides and close to the front. This may cause some issues, as both left- and right-handed users may struggle with external pointing devices when using this system. If using an external monitor this may be of no consequence but it's important to keep in mind.

To my great joy, it is possible to turn the touch pad off completely. I dislike touch pads and on the occasions where I have to use the built-in keyboard I don't want to accidentally click on something or move the mouse pointer.

One final thing I would have preferred to see when it comes to the hardware - a lid latch. I do move my laptop a lot and I would have liked a locking lid. That's purely a personal preference thing.

My very first exercise with this system was to make restore media. This process was lengthy, taking about 2 hours and resulting in 4 single-layer DVDs. I then made a second set of restore media - something that some manufacturers expressly prevent users from doing. Once that was done I took a little time to explore the OS.

The "Windows Experience" numbers reveal a lot about this system. As expected, the Aero graphics are the slow point, but still the number sits around 5.1. This is driven by the Intel graphics chipset and reflects the kind of usage that would occur under light-duty such as word processing or generating email. The gaming graphics, powered by the NVidia card posted much more respectable numbers. The second slowest number was for the hard drive, and considering that Asus puts a 5400rpm drive in these units this is not too shocking. It is easy enough to put a faster/bigger drive in, so I am not terribly concerned with this.

There's a fair amount of vendor add-on software, most of which I am not likely to use. I was especially dismayed to see Trend Micro's security solution on there, a packages I personally dislike and will not use. Fortunately, stripping off all of the unwanted fluff is easy enough, but it represents a minor inconvenience.

After contenting myself with the Windows side of things, I completely wiped the hard drive and loaded up Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6. RHEL 6 is what I planned to run when I purchased this laptop anyway and it is where I can truly explore the system in detail.

The Linux kernel reports eight cores as expected. Since the Core i7 is a hyperthreading quad-core, this is exactly what I hoped to see. It also reports the full 6GB of RAM.

Boot-up time from pressing the power button to getting the log-in screen (under Linux using GNOME as a window manager) is less than 30 seconds. This is by far the fastest machine with which I have ever worked. Times would be even faster if the hard drive was a 7200rpm or an SDD-type, but it's plenty fast enough to please me.

Overall, I am delighted with this laptop. It has a lot to offer for such a modest price and it definitely delivers on its promises. There are a few minor design issues that may or may not matter when using this system, but considering how much machine you get for the price it's hard to pass up in spite of a few minor complaints. This is a great system, worth more than the asking price.

First let me get the positive out of the way. Very easy to assemble, sturdy, and I like the fact that I can secure the TV on the wall by the top as well as pop it free by unlocking the unit by pulling the two chains s on the bottom. It was very easy to assemble, and I like the fact that they gave you a leveler to make sure its straight. The images I posted is a 75-inch TV, the maximum it can hold is apparently an 80. However, the bigger you go, the harder it gets to reach behind the back to tilt it. There is still 2 1/2 space to run wires and reach around to turn the knob to tilt it forward or backwards.

Now the CON.

I was not planning on tilting this unit forward or backwards because it's a big tv. For those looking for a decent mount and plan on doing the exact same thing having it flat, with a little space behind it so that you can reach around and run the wires the two inches and a half for me of space was perfect. I secured the tilting mechanism to keep it facing forward. which are the two metal knobs as you see in my second uploaded image as well as Amazon's version in the photos. I figured that since it had two turning knobs it was the same as the previous one I owned that had a spinning knob that went forward unlock, and backwards lock. I installed some LED lights on the back of the TV and hung it on the mount 1 month later. However I decided to remove the LED lights on the unit without taking the whole TV off the wall because I can easily take those off by just pulling the lights off.

This is where the problem started and noticed the manufacturing or designer error, hopefully they can correct it in the future. When I pulled the LED off, it tilted the TV slightly upwards, no idea why when it was apparently secured facing forward when I tried reaching around to the side to turn the nob I noticed the little ball fell out of the turning metal nob. The ball that goes into the metal unit was super glued on and it's not a turning ball where you can put it in there, screw in to permanently secure it in place to metal rod.

This created a problem when I wanted to tilt the TV forward, I had to move the metal rod because now the ball fell off it and it could not be attached again because it was held in place by super glue when you turn the knob, the whole unit would slide through falling off. Also if you notice in the picture, it's three separate parts. Not only was the metal rod with the ball superglued on but the unit that you used to turn in place unscrews off because there's no resistance or warning mechanism when you're turning the knob you don't know which way to turn to tilt it.

Since I was trying to figure out which way to make it go forward and backwards I realized that the whole unit was unscrewing because I could keep turning it in a direction until the whole metal rod as well as the screw / nob came completely off. This means that I now had to reattach it back to the unit screw it back in as well as dealing with the ball that had fallen off the stick. I ended up just removing both of them and physically moving the TV by hand forward and upwards luckily it didn't require a lot of force and it must have been slightly loose.

Regardless of all that I would still recommend the unit. It is sturdy it's nice and I like the adequate space behind it or I can reach around the problem is that if you have a big TV and you plan on constantly tilting it forward and backwards before attaching it on the wall. it's probably better for you to tilt the TV and then attach it to the wall because reaching around the 75 inch TV it's a little bit more difficult easier to run a wire because you have more than enough space but harder if you want to reach the handle to tilt it forward and backwards.

Also in the setup video instructions, it's simply rotates the nob without saying counterclockwise lock, counterclockwise relock etc etc. There's also no resistance mechanism that would tell you it can't go forward. So what ends up happening is that you can unscrew the whole nob bar off by mistake leaving the screw on the mount and nob in your hand. Hopefully in a future revision. They use a ball screw to the nob vs super glue it and possibly secure the metal bar to the unit to where it can't be unscrewed off. But I think the best thing to do is it just properly aligned with television to your seating position and set it up like normal straight to avoid having to use the tilting mechanism.

I got these so I wouldn't yank my laptop off the desk when I get up. I got bluetooth, thinking they'd be easy to sync to my various devices. So, here's my breakdown:

Range
I can go upstairs and grab a few things or go two rooms away and I still get a signal. The range is pretty good on these.

Playback Sound
The playback sound quality is okay. Not blowing me away, but alright. I listen to music, no vocals, to block out the office noise and keep my head focused. The playback audio goes into tin-can mode when the mic is enabled. That's something I didn't realize as a limitation of how bluetooth handles the two signals. That took me a while to figure out.

Microphone
The mic is okay. It just flips me out that the playback goes into "phone mode" when the mic is enabled.

Battery
Well, I've only had these a couple of months. But, the battery seems to go at least as long as I can stand to keep them on my head. Max has been about 2 hours at a stretch before giving my head/ears a break.

Fit
I'm an adult and my head is average-sized, not large. After maybe three months these cans are still a bit tight. The cups don't quite fit entirely over my ears and get uncomfortable after maybe two hours --like, *ouch* uncomfortable.

Heat
These cans get pretty hot after maybe 45 minutes. Hot like I just got out of the shower and I need a towel in my ears hot. I don't think I've ever had sweaty ears like this before from a set of headphones.

Sync
I've easily sync'd these to Ubuntu 14.04 & 10, Windows 7, and OS X Mavericks.

Would I recommend these to a friend?
No. I like not having to carry a dongle around since bluetooth is in all of my computers (one has an $8 dongle that works just fine.) But, they get so hot, and are still not comfortable on my head and ears after maybe 100 hours of use. So, for the $50 price tag, I'd probably have to say no. If they were $25 and just to make the occasional phone call I might recommend them to a friend, but not to wear for any period of time. If they were just a bit more comfortable, and breathed a bit better, I'd change my mind. Maybe in the next revision, Photive?

Feiyutech is a brand that I've come to know for their camera accessories. Generally, their products have great build quality and is well-designed. I've had problems with their app working with LG phones but once I upgrade, that wouldn't be a problem anymore.

The FeiyuTech Official SCORP-C Camera Stabilizer is a 3-axis gimbal made for DSLR and mirrorless cameras. All of the axis arms are metal with high quality plastic in the body. The motors are quiet and there are plenty of buttons that control most aspects of the gimbal. There's even a video made by Feiyutech that explains the buttons very well. This SCORP-C model does not have an LCD screen.

The accompanying smartphone app is used to upgrade the gimbal firmware and for finer adjustments of the gimbal such as the follow speed and horizontal calibration. Control of the gimbal itself is also possible, but it is easier and faster to use the buttons on the device. It really is a good thing that the gimbal is designed to be operated without the need to fuss with a phone and app.

A few USB cables are included with this gimbal, which is designed to control the shutter of the camera that you own. Unfortunately, my Lumix GX8 is an odd model that just isn't well supported, even by Panasonic themselves. None of the included cables worked for me so this gimbal isn't able to control my camera. Not a big problem, though. If I really need wireless control of my camera, I can probably work out some sort of phone mount and use the Panasonic app. Just be aware that Feiyutech's list of compatible camera might be a little limited. They publish a compatiblity list. Just search for the term "Feiyu SCORP-C Lens Compatibility List"

With that said, the gimbal stabilization is great. Once your camera is balanced (search youtube for "Scorp-C Balancing" to see a video demonstrating this process), the motors are very, very quiet and the various follow modes help to create smooth motion in your videos.

Recently, I'm helping my daughter record videos and this gimbal has really come in handy. My camera doesn't support in-body stabilization for video and the lenses I have do not have in-lens stabilization. Gimbals are the best answers for my camera's limitations.

I like:
The weight. Even in the case it's very light, though if it gets much lighter I'll worry about it blowing away in a strong wind.
The size. It's not going to get much smaller without shrinking the screen.
The interface. I'm sorry, I like buttons. Call me old. I never bent back the spine of a book (horrors) so I can't compare the feel of this to that, but I can say it's nice for a long reading session. The touch screen takes a bit of getting used to, but the tutorial will guide a new user. The tutorial is intrusive at first, but provides useful information and goes away quickly. The lighting is now all but invisible. I was unhappy that you can't completely turn it off as you could with the Nook Glowlight, and turning it down casts an odd yellow light over the page, but it's so even now as to be so unintrusive I barely notice going from sunlight to tunnel on the bus home. With the Nook I'd be thrown out of the book to go turn on the light. With the Kindle, I can keep reading without a pause. It does not have adaptive lighting, but I'm not sure it needs it.
The download speed. I don't know if it's supposed to be faster than the Kindle Keyboard (the last one I had with 3G) but it certainly seems that way.
The battery life. Maybe with this thing going for months we'll finally hear an end to the "but my dead tree doesn't run out of power" nonsense.
Next in series. When you're almost done with a book, it tells you where the story continues. Now the next feature I want, and if it does this I haven't seen it yet, is an alert when the next book in a series I'm following is published. Yes, FictFact is great, but I'm greedy and want it right on the device.

I don't like:
It's not waterproof. There was a lot of hope it would be after the Nook went that route.
It's not solar, yet, but there are rumors of a solar cover coming soon.
It doesn't support Audible and the excellent immersive reading between ebook and audiobook. I have a weird love of that feature, seeing what changed print to audio.

I've always loved the idea of a Android powered head unit, I've seen aftermarket ones sold for popular car models, and I was hoping this would give me that functionality without having to replace my radio. But sadly, I can't use this.
For starters, it takes a long time to boot. That means you are first going to be greeted with your car's normal radio display, connected to my phone over bluetooth, and then once I've already pulled out of my driveway and started down the road, THEN it finally shows up on my display.
That is, if it displays at all. It seems to do this thing in which is boots up, checks for display info, then reboots in the proper resolution. The instructions even imply it does this. The problem is, most of the time my carplay radio will freeze up when it does this. Not only will it get stuck and not display anything, but my radio locks up and MY TIME RESETS. It's the strangest thing. After looking at reviews here, it seems at least one other reviewer said it make his car radio go crazy, so I don't really understand what this thing is doing that might cause that, but at least it isn't just me!
And even when it DOES work, it has a similar problem to other Android-powered adapters like this: it is a cold boot every time, with no idea what the time/date is. This is a major issue because if I don't supply an internet connection, the mini computer in this reverts to the wrong date/time on the display which is SUPER annoying. I will start by saying that I am typically not a fan of ear buds. I will also say that the very best headphones I have is a set of Sony active noise canceling ear buds. I have always had good success with Sony audio products and I regard the brand as an upper mid-range line. These buds are disappointing in that, while they’re comfortable for ear buds, the sound profile is lacking, specifically in the midrange.

This is a basic set of ear buds that work as you might expect. They do not have ANC functionality, there is no battery or battery pack and there is no Bluetooth functionality. These are straight plug-in audio gear with no fancy features. These will work with just about any device that provides a 3.5mm audio jack.

Most ear buds are uncomfortable to me, but these are surprisingly comfortable and I can wear these for a good bit of time. They come with several inserts of varying sizes so you can find the size that fits your ear canal just right. The included inserts are soft and do not irritate my ears as much as others have done in the past. I still very much prefer over-the-ear headphones which is a personal preference more than anything.

So, where’s the problem? The problem lies in the sound profile which is unbalanced. Having used literally dozens of sets of ear buds and headphones over the past 3-5 years I have developed a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Most ear buds have one of two issues, either way too much bass or almost none at all. These are surprising in that they actually get the bass just about right, not too heavy and not too light. The highs are very bright and clear, perhaps a touch too piercing for my tastes but not to the point of being unacceptable. The midrange, though, is flat. The result is that music sounds somewhat sterile and lackluster. This is similar to the issue I have seen with my Bose headset. These still sound good, but they fall short of where they could and should be.

Normally I would rate ear buds with a glitch in the sound profile a little higher, as they’re still quite usable and they sound decent. But, these are much more expensive than the average and I have heard less expensive buds with more balanced sound. Sony makes a number of sets of ear buds and headphones, but these are not among their best offerings.

Since there are some incredibly detailed and helpful reviews already I will focus on where these phones are best suited. I received mine as a review sample and have been using them for nearly a week to make sure I thoroughly test them.

For me these are best for critical listening, and especially raw mixes if you do recording. Of course they are not limited to that. The fact that these phones are fairly neutral across the entire frequency spectrum makes them ideal for listening to unmixed recordings, as well as music that you are studying or transcribing. The reproduction is so balanced that listening to albums with these compared to other phones - including some other Brainwavz models - is like night and day.

If you are listening to music that is heavily biased towards bass and drums these may not be the best phones for you. If you listen to acoustic music these are near perfect because you can easily hear every note. I tested it on a few jazz albums that I own as well as a broadcast of two friends from a local station that had been recorded directly from the sound board and it was wonderful to hear what was actually recorded versus what a biased pair of phones normally reproduce.

A few notes about comfort: these are light, do a great job of isolating ambient noise without totally eliminating it, and are easy to wear. I am not an IEM (in ear monitor) type of person, but these presented no problems even when I wore them for three to four hours straight. A big plus is this set comes with different sized foam ear pieces and a nice case (the [[ASIN:B00HPPL1M4 Brainwavz Hard Earphone Case]]).

While these phones may not be for everybody, they are perfect for those of us who spend a lot of time critically listening to music and/or transcribing it. If you fall into that category you will probably love them.

This is my first GoPro and I'm underwhelmed.

Starting with the good: The camera inside is great for video. It can record at 5.3K resolution @ 60 FPS, 4K @ 120 FPS, or 2.7K @ 240 FPS. The video quality is really good. Crispy and clear. Love it.

Now the bad: first off, this thing CANNOT shoot still photos (??), which is absurd. If you want a photo, you'll have to record a video and take a screengrab. No idea why they didn't include a photo feature.

The second-worst thing is that there is no screen, front or back. While I obviously knew this going in, not having any preview display has been a bigger annoyance than expected. It feels like this is being marketed as a more rugged version of the Hero 11 Black, but I'd rather just throw a case on a Hero 11 vs. not having a screen.

A couple other missing features, it doesn't have any scheduled capture mode or GPS. Neither of those are important to me, but I figure I'd mention them.

There is a flip-out cover that has a USB-C port and an SD card slot. It does not support an external microphone (!) and does not have an HDMI out. It's possible it'll support the GoPro external mic in the future after a firmware update, but TBD.

The battery is not removable, which I think they did to save (physical) size on the device. The battery is billed to give 60 minutes of recording time at max resolution, which feels about right given my experience. Lower resolution or FPS will allow for longer battery life.

I'd pass on this. Too many missing features to justify a purchase.

* 1080P native and extremely small, so it's very portable. The size is the whole reason I got this. It's for traveling and being able to project bigger screens in hotel walls.
* 300 ansi lumens, ALPD laser tech.
* 25000 hrs lamp life.
* Airplay, Miracast thru wi-fi.
* Aesthetically, very nice minimalist design.
* Picture quality is good, but I'm not a videophile. I do have a more serious Vava UST 4k projector in my living room, so all these portable projectors will never compare. They serve as a traveling device for me, and will not be the go-to video source at home.
* Very nice case is included to hold everything.

THE BAD:
------------
* Onboard 1W speakers are very weak to say the least. You will definitely want to hook up a portable speaker. It has a headphone jack, which is basically the same as an aux out jack. I hooked it up to a cheap little speaker and the sound improved drastically. Watch my video.
* No remote.
* No smart OS, so I have a chromecast connected in my video demo, and I just cast from my phone.
* No Bluetooth, so you must use aux if connecting a speaker.
* No mounting solution or tripod included. Depending on your situation, you might not even need it. Just set it on a coffee table and you're good.
* No built in battery.
* Lastly, the price. There are so many features lacking, so I do not understand the price point. If you're willing to spend $600, then check out the Nebula Capsule Max that's less than $500. It is also compact, the size of a coke can. It has a built in battery, 8w speakers, smart interface, bluetooth, and remote. The only thing it doesn't have is native 1080p, it is native 720p. But it's hard to even tell the difference with these little projectors anyway. So I am not sure that paying more money, and having less features is worth that 1080p. And if you have to also lug around an external speaker, a chromecast or fire TV, then it really defeats the purpose of being completely portable. With the Nebula, everything you need is inside a device the size of a coke can.

In conclusion, this is a neat little barebones projector, but the onboard speakers are so bad, you'll need to carry around a portable speaker as well, so it's no longer as portable as I anticipated. At its price point, I assume they're saying it's a premium to have a projector at this size that is 1080p.. But again, that size feature is almost negated by the need to bring along external speakers, and smart devices like a Fire TV stick. And if the Nebula Capsule products doesn't exist, then I guess this price point is justified, but the Nebula does exist, and it's a much better buy. I'm going 3-Stars.

Here are some tips for getting precise mouse control:

First of all understand that a low-DPI setting means your pointer doesn't move far when you move the mouse. This enables gamers to aim and target precisely in-game. It also enables artists to precisely move the pointers when working on graphics. How far your cursor/pointer moves is entirely up to you and can be adjusted in your control panel for pointer settings (or, depending on the game, possibly can be adjusted in your game settings).

In that control panel, uncheck "enhance pointer precision." This will turn off pointer acceleration, which can adversely affect control. If the software (or game) you're using overrides this (rare in graphics software, but more common in games), you may have to employ a fix. Just do a search for "Windows 7/8 mouse fix" and you'll find plenty of information on how to do this.

I wasn't expecting much given the price of this item, and I got pretty much what I expected.

The charging port is hard to reach and the LED charging indicator is difficult, if not impossible to see, without having to move the foam earpiece covering.

Setting up/pairing the device is pretty easy. Press the button for 4 seconds or so and you’ll hear a pleasant female voice say, “Hello”. This means the power is on. Continue holding the button and the device will enter pairing mode. You’ll hear the voice say, “Ready to pair.” When pairing is complete, you’ll hear the device say, “You’re connected” and tell you how much charge the battery has. So far, all I’ve heard is, “Battery full.” I have no idea what other battery indications the voice will give – perhaps only at 3/4, 1/2 and 1/4? Or maybe percentages?

The buttons are the biggest drawback with this device. Actually, it's really just one multi-function button on the right earpiece. The button functionality is not like any Bluetooth headset I've used before - very non-intuitive. The button has no label at all and the tactile feedback is nonexistent at times - I press the button sometimes and there's no "click" feeling. If a song is playing, it doesn't seem to matter where I press, the song stops if it is playing. When I press again, anywhere, it starts playing again.

There is no volume control on the headphones at all. You’ll have to adjust the volume from your phone/audio player. There is a bare bones EQ function. You control this by clicking the multi-function button 3 times in rapid succession. Each time you do this, the device advances to the next of 3 EQ setting – balanced, bass boost and JLab signature. The “balanced” setting seems to sound just like what it’s named – balanced or equal high, mid and low tones. The bass boos is decent – not overbearing. Not sure what the last one is, but if the pictograms in the manual are any indication, it boost the high and low ends. The EQ function does provide audible feedback – the voice announces each setting by name.

There's a next track function, but no function for going to the previous track. The next track function requires holding down the multi-function button for 2 seconds. There's no audible feedback for this function (other than a very short moment of silence). When you hear the silence, let go IMMEDIATELY. If you hold the button down for too long the Bluetooth connection will be severed and you'll have to reconnect.

Apparently, there's no ability to fast forward or rewind within a song or audio book. You'll have to do this on your phone/audio player. Pretty poor design if you ask me. BTW – I use this only with my audio player, so I did not test the phone/mic functions, but I’d be surprised if they were robust.

The instructions are minimal at best. The manual is one piece of paper printed on 2 sides. Unfolded, it's about the size of 2 business cards - about 4"x4.5" (10.16cm x 11.43cm). One side has instructions and the other is all promotions/disclaimers, etc. That's it.

Sound quality is acceptable - decent bass and stereo separation is good. I’m no audiophile though. The product description says it has "Noise Isolation", which is marketing speak used by all on-ear headphone manufacturers. It simply means the ambient noise is slightly reduced because the headphones cover your ears. Bottom line - there's no tech/function in this device that does any active noise cancellation.

The headphones are a little snug/tight, but not so much to be uncomfortable - at least that's my opinion after an hour+ of testing. Not sure if this will be true for something like a 3-4 hour flight. I’ll test this out in the near future and will update this review, if possible.

The charging cable that comes with the item is 9” long (22.86cm). Not very useful at all, but better than nothing.

On the plus side, the manufacturer did provide an extra set of foam earpiece covers - the set that comes on the headphones is orange. The extra set is black.

Bottom line, for $15 I wasn't expecting a lot - well maybe better button functionality, but hey, what can you do? As my granddad used to say, “You pays your money and you takes your chances.”
