[[VIDEOID:b21ba802df7fea83af659db90aa0851b]] Aside from one problem, these are perhaps the most useful, well-designed and economical C-stands I've ever seen.

Starting at the bottom, it's a turtle style, meaning the center column is removable. This allows for easy transport.

But here's the problem: the column's diameter where it slides into the turtle is NOT STANDARD DIAMETER. It's 1.095". It should be 1.125" (1-1/8"). This means standard accessories will not fit into the turtle base.

Nothing's more clumsy than a folded C-stand. The best way to transport a standard single-piece C-stand is with a custom cart made for the job like the [[ASIN:B01DMUNL28 C-Stand Cart (cart only, stands not included)]] for only $461. And you'll need a lift-gate truck to move the filled cart about.

With two-piece C-stands like this Neewer beauty, you take the center column off, fold up the turtle base and carry them separately on any cart. The turtle base folds using spring pressure detents. The legs, when in the detents, are splayed properly. They don't have a sliding "crazy leg" for uneven terrain like the [[ASIN:B003E4793K Avenger A2033LKIT Steel 40-Inch Sliding Leg C-Stand with Grip Kit (Chrome)]]. Use these on flat floors.

Because the turtle base does not accept a 1-1/8" column, it cannot be used as a low-boy stand. A gazinta like the Kupo junior-to-baby adapter [[ASIN:B006JHK80K Kupo Adapter, Junior to Baby, 1-1/8-Inch Stud to 5/8-Inch Stud, KG006312]], will not drop it into the turtle base. This is very disappointing. I actually bought a Kupo 20" column so I could have two different heights, but the Kupo will not fit into this Neewer.

Moving up is the unique center post. It has two strong internal springs that act like shock absorbers. If you have a heavy light up in the air or a backdrop suspended between two of these stands and some amateur loosens one of the lock handles too much without holding up the weight, the column will certainly slide all the way down. If he's lucky, he doesn't have his hand on the center post because a normal stand will pinch and/or crush it. This stand will stop short and bounce on the spring. The best I've seen on other stands is a thick rubber O-ring that softens the descent only a little. These springs may even save an expensive bulb's filament from damage as the lighting unit bounces off the spring, but does not bottom out. Other stands may have these features, but this Neewer is the first I've seen. Check out the video.

There is a neoprene sleeve for gripping the post. It's a good, thick, solid grip that should last.

The two extension sections elevate and lower smoothly, controlled by large friction knobs. The castings are solid and well finished with no sharp edges, secured to the center post by a large set screw. An Allen wrench is included should this set screw loosen over time or you want to take the column apart.

Moving up to the gobo arm, it's strong steel with a 5/8" spud at both ends. One spud end has a 1/4-20 thread on it and the other end has a 3/8-16 thread on it. With these two threads, plus the 5/8" spuds, you can mount just about anything. Both thread ends are protected by small rubber caps, which you'll probably lose after the first shoot unless you put them in your pocket.

The arm has two gobo clamps: one to adapt the arm to the stand and one for holding accessories like scrims, reflectors, softboxes or flags. Both slide the full length of the arm. You can add a set screw (not included) if you desire to lock them to the arm. The clamps have fine-tooth interlocking faces instead of a leather or composite friction washer. If you loosen the clamp knob sufficiently, the teeth will clear each other without wearing themselves off. Once locked together, I cannot imagine the gobo arm sagging and changing its angle, no matter how much the light weighs. Both clamps are nicely finished and have large, easily gripped locking knobs. The tightening washers are well-greased to prevent galling and are shaped like miniature tripod ball mounts -- a cup-shaped bottom fits into a matching cup-shaped hollow in the clamp. This allows the two halves of the clamp to move to accommodate different diameters of flag pins, but still tighten securely. Easier seen than explained.

Packaging was excellent: bubble wrap around every piece, then into Styrofoam shipping blocks, then into an inner cardboard box then two of those boxes into an outer cardboard box. I pity the UPS guy who had to deliver the thing, but both stands arrived in perfect condition. I set them up in a few minutes.

For about $105 each, the only way I'd be more pleased is if the turtle had a standard socket size. Had to take a star off. And now I have to send back my Kupo 20" column %^$#$$!!

A keyboard used to be a rather boring, under-appreciated, rectangular attachment to your computer, useful for typing stuff, and for catching stray staples, bits of paper from your paper punch, dust and assorted DNA particles.

Now here comes the Wave Pro, with a sensuous curvy design, and a whole lot of kewl features that you never knew you needed until now. This model comes with an MX1100 Cordless laser mouse, both sharing a common USB micro-receiver.

Features:

Cordless Keyboard

1. Windows Vista Flip 3D button, that helps you to switch between application windows easily. With XP you get a pop up list of your open windows, but with Vista you see your windows in 3D view, and then use your arrow keys or mouse to choose your next destination page.

2. Zoom keys to get that paragraph to a size you can read, even without your progressive lenses.

3. Special Vista keys that bring up all the Vista features, and all your picture files, each with the click of one button.

4. Navigation keys for multimedia - volume, mute, play, pause, stop, fast forward, skip back. This is a very handy feature - kind of like a monster sized remote control

5. One button to bring up your Media Player

6. One button to bring up your Media Center, where you can listen to music, or watch a movie, tune in to the television, view your picture files in a slideshow, check out MSNBC.com and more.

7. Call up a handy calculator in a jiffy

8. Sleep button

9. Fn key to give each of the function keys a second job to do, such as launch Word or Excel, your favorite website, your IM page or e-mail or favorite search engine.

10. Battery status indicator.

11. Contoured keyboard with palm rest for comfortable typing. This design works very well for people who can type with the proper fingers, but also does the job for the two-fingered corn-pickers among us.

12. Displays actions on your monitor for a few seconds so you're less likely to accidentally hit your Caps button without noticing it.

Cordless Mouse

See: [[ASIN:B001DJ64C0 Logitech MX 1100 Cordless Laser Mouse]]
(NB) On its own this mouse uses 2 AA batteries, but when packaged with the keyboard it uses a rechargeable battery.

Cons:
1. The keyboard is pretty big (albeit understandably so) and takes up quite a bit of space on the desk. I'd get around this by typing with the keyboard on my lap and my feet up on the desk, but they tell me it's not good office practice.

2. The mouse uses rechargeable NiMH batteries - good for saving on dead batteries, but a real pain to keep track of the charger, which you'll need once every six weeks.

Conclusion:

The "Ayes" have it - regardless if you're a whizz at data entry or a two-finger wonder, this keyboard makes a lot of functions easier, and the Media Center and handy navigation keys put it way ahead of other keyboards.

Add it to your own Christmas list this year.

Amanda Richards, November 3, 2008

Got these for my hubs and I. The stands have 3 height settings to make it easy to adjust to whatever height you need. Easy to assemble, just push the legs in and you're ready to go!

PROS

1. The silicone band is very comfortable. Apparently if it breaks, it can be replaced, though I’m not sure where or how you would buy a new band.

2. The appearance is sleek and modern, and the size of the watch face makes the digital numbers easy to read.

3. It has a rechargeable battery, which may have a longer life than the non-rechargeable batteries of most sports watches.

4. If you want a smart watch that is far cheaper than most brands, this might work for you.

CONS

1. There are three primary functions that I use a sports watch for: to instantly check the time, a stopwatch, and a timer. It irritated me no end with this watch that, after only a few seconds of being lit up, its face goes dark. While this might save the charge on the rechargeable battery, there are plenty of times when my right hand it not free to punch the button on this watch to light up its face, and I can’t quickly and conveniently check the time! It is also a hassle trying to use the stopwatch and timer functions.

2. I absolutely loathe the way this watch’s battery is recharged. Instead of using a standard C cable, the charging cable attaches magnetically, and it becomes detached far too easily. There is also no warning when the battery of this watch is about to go dead.

3. I don’t like the software this phone uses. It is a major hassle to learn for what I personally consider very little useful return. Why? Because most of the functions offered by this watch that are of any interest to me I can get through my smartphone. I use my phone and a Bluetooth for phone calls, texting, music, and hearing alarms. I check the weather by looking around me when outside or looking at weather apps on my phone. I use my phone for photography.
The rest of the functions this watch offers I personally find to be useless. I do not need a watch to tell me how to do a deep breathing exercises. As a healthy individual with no heart issues, I do not need to monitor my heart rate 24/7. (And if I did, I would use medical equipment that is far more reliable than this cheap watch.) I don’t need to obsessively monitor my sleep. (And, again, if I did, I wouldn’t trust this cheap watch to do an accurate job of it.)

4. Its pedometer function might have been of use to me, but unfortunately, it is inaccurate.

CONCLUSION

I dumped this watch and went back to a regular, inexpensive sports watch.

I've had my AKG K701 headphones for many years, so I didn't really notice the breakdown of the (original) pads until right after I washed them a month or two ago. Soon after, the headphones were increasingly uncomfortable to wear and I realized that my ears were resting directly on grill covering the drivers - that's how degraded the pads had become. I considered ordering new OEM pads, but honestly I've now replaced the driver on one side of these headphones, resoldered the connection, repaired the wire and chewed up the outer cups in the process so I supposed it didn't really make a difference. I just needed my headphones to be wearable again.

These fit the AKG K701 perfectly. The material itself is not as nice as the OEM - you'd probably have to pay ~$80 for a pair of similar pads - but it is sufficient. Cushioning is okay, a little firm at first, I'm guessing they'll break in over time. They are still fine for people with glasses, like myself.

The one thing I didn't expect is the boost in sound quality, which is truly remarkable. Improvements across all frequencies, everything is crisper and clearer with these new pads, enough that I feel like I'm wearing a new pair of headphones. I suppose people who know headphones well probably see this as obvious, but for me it was a very pleasant surprise.

Would recommend for basic replacement pads for the AKG K701 headphones.

It says it fits a Nikon D800, but when mounted, the D800 is too tall, barely fitting under the overhead grip arm.

The overhead arm does not extend forward enough to allow the camera to balance, even with the camera mounted all the way to the rear of the baseplate. Thus, even when I'm holding just the front two inches under the hot shoe mount, the camera when mounted with a heavy zoom lens like the 24-70 f/2.8, tilts down. A lighter, shorter lens works better, but you still cannot hold the unit by the foam grip handle without your knuckles scraping the camera's hot shoe mount.

The entire device is of molded ABS plastic and is somewhat flexible in a "springy" way. It appears strong, but remember, your multi-thousand dollar investment is hanging by that little joint in the back of the base plate. If it breaks, it's curtains. You might want to have a safety lanyard attached to a neck strap lug that attaches to your wrist, just in case.

The sleds on the bottom are nice. When you put it down, it's stable, although I had to re-superglue one of the padded inserts on one of the sled rails.

The camera mounting screw is well designed and easy to use, but for some reason, is too long. The threads bottomed out in my camera and would not hold the camera tight. I had to remove the thumb screw and add a washer on the underside of the base effectively shortening the threads. I could have ground off 1/16" or so, too. Not a big deal, but out of the box it didn't work.

One thing's for sure: you need a strong arm to hold this for any amount of time if you have a heavy lens attached. If you are working with a lightweight SLR and a lightweight lens, it's much easier. And seeing the viewfinder is a real problem. And forget about focusing. If you mount a remote electronic viewfinder on the upper hot shoe, it's much easier to see what you're shooting, but now you've added even more weight and your arm will die. (True steadicams went with vests and spring-assisted arms for this reason years ago.)

Overall, the sled is a simple, inexpensive method to hold a camera from above and does smooth out motion well. It's a worthy gizmo to have in your bag.

UPDATE: I attached my Canon HFS-100 HD camcorder to this sled and have never taken it off. It is absolutely the best accessory ever! Perfectly balanced. The overhead handle allows excellent control and fabulous low angle positioning when capturing kids or animals on the floor. The camera's flip-out viewfinder is the key, something the D800 sorely lacks.

I was researching televisions for MONTHS and could not figure out which one to buy. My boyfriend is better at this stuff, so after I spent countless hours comparing TVs in Target, Wal-Mart and PC Richards, (and even securing a pre-order for a Coby, [which I quickly cancelled after hearing bad things]), I told him to see what he could find on Amazon. He found this TV and after sorting out what could be "insider reviews" from genuine ones, we decided that it sounded like a great deal for the money, and though the name is not exactly a household one yet, it was worth a shot, as another buyer said the same thing happened with Vizio a couple of years back.

So, we bought it for each other as a joint Christmas gift, figuring what the hey. If it wasn't as advertised, we'd send it back. And it had a lot to live up to, considering this was essentially our only gift to each other this year. It has been over a month now, and we LOVE this television.

Pros:

- No side glare - you can see the picture well, even if you are sitting on the side of the television.
- It is lightweight and super thin, so it is easy to transport.
- Very clear picture.
- Decent enough sound - you don't really need a sound bar if you don't have one, especially since there are options to change the sound (i.e. "music", "film", "surround sound", etc.)
-Provided you are not signed in to a game system (which you can change the video input from your remote), there is a setting where the TV will automatically shut itself off after 10 minutes of lack of use. This is very helpful if you have a roommate who tends to fall asleep in front of the television.
- There are plenty of settings to customize the picture and sound, as well as "label" your game systems with the pre-loaded options so you know which video input to select for your X-Box or PS3 (for example, I have the PS3 set to "Blue Ray", whereas the X-Box is set to "Game").

Cons:

-It is not a "smart TV", if you are in the market for one of those. It's a simple design, which was perfect for us.
-There are no buttons on the TV itself, so if the remote ever breaks, I have no idea how we are going to turn it on and off, aside from buying a new remote.
-There are a shortage of plugs in the back for cables. For example, I can hook up the cable box, X-Box and PS3, but there is no room now for the sound bar. Not a huge deal, but I could see where some people might find that to be annoying.

This television lived up to all of the positive reviews it received here on Amazon, and I am so thoroughly satisfied that we decided to go with this one that I kept reminding myself to write this review so I could help others who were as in the dark as we were about which TV to buy. I didn't get the dreaded "green screen" upon turning it on, as some people have experienced, and the packaging didn't overly give it away that it was a TV, (though we got the 48" one, so I'm sure people could figure it out).

Bottom line: If you are in as much doubt as we were about which TV to buy, trust us on this one - TCL rocks!

The app also has a bunch of adjustments to the level of noise cancellation, equalizers, many soundscapes, like rain and pink noise, that work well with the cancellation to block out the world. The button functions can also be rearranged, which is nice because every brand seems to be different, and it's nice to be able to switch it to something personally intuitive.

I ended up connecting them to both my tablet and my phone, and now when I put them on, they say, "two devices connected" If I'm playing audio on my tablet, and then pause it and play audio on my phone, it seamlessly plays whichever is running, though not both at once. I like that I should be able to listen to my tablet and then take an incoming call. I'm not an audiophile, but the sound quality seems excellent to me. I've tried a couple expensive brands with noise cancellation, and it's interesting. It doesn't remove background noise very effectively, but it does a bit. I think it's more that when it's turned off, they use the mic to pump in outside audio so it's almost like you aren't wearing them. Neither mode is especially effective, so I wouldn't buy them for that specifically, but It's a small benefit. It's best suited for making your audio your focus or your situational awareness your focus.

I tried them on a call and it went well. My first time using earbuds for a phone call, and I have no complaints.

The other problem is range. Range is average, but when I tried walking out of range, instead of announcing the problem and handling it, they just cut out and turned off. I had to actually put them back in the case before they would go back to playing.

Overall, even with a few minor quibbles, these have become my new favorite earbuds, after having about seven (from good brands) in my family's stash to try. They fit well, audio quality is very good, the app actually functions and they are just a very solid, comfortable offering.

This crystal-clear screen protector film is very easy to apply. It's pre-cut to exactly fit the Kindle Fire touch screen, and it presses on without any need for additional adhesive. After the film is applied, there is no loss of sensitivity in the touch screen.

The application process is very simple: (1) clean the screen thoroughly, using the included microfiber cloth; (2) use the #1 tab to remove the plastic stiffener/shield from one side of the double-sided film; (3) position the uncovered side of the film on the Kindle Fire screen (holding the film by the #2 tab, starting at one corner, and allowing the film to fall gently onto the screen); (4) use the included smoothing card to get rid of bubbles; (5) use the #2 tab to remove the remaining plastic stiffener/shield; and (6) use the smoothing card again to get rid of any bubbles. The whole process took me less than 10 minutes.

Whenever I apply screen protector film, I usually have to try two or three times to get everything right. With this kit, the first application was successful, because the film adhered properly at the edges, and all but one tiny bubble smoothed out. Now, should I ever need to re-apply the film, I have the second shield in reserve.

It's probably worth noting that the Kindle Fire has a larger screen than an iPhone or iPod Touch or camera viewfinder, so that the risk of getting dust particles under the film during application to the Fire is higher. Also, it may not be necessary to install protective film on the Fire at all, because the touch screen is supposed to be made of particularly tough, scratch-resistant glass.

MY HISTORY WITH THIS PRODUCT:
I've owned this headset for almost a full year. Technically, I've had two of them, since the boom mic snapped off the first one and had it replaced. I use these every day, for multiple hours and a variety of uses (VoIP calls, gaming, music, and movies).

PROS:
The audio quality, when it is working, is good. The bass in 7.1 mode is great, and the overall surround sound is pretty convincing. They are comfortable and rechargeable via USB.

CONS:
The biggest problem here is the wireless connection. Both headsets I owned suffered from this same problem - they would frequently just restart or lose the signal and reconnect. The process takes about 3-5 seconds each time, and sometimes you get multiple restarts in a row. It doesn't sound too bad until it happens when you're watching a movie and you have to quickly pause or rewind a bit because you suddenly couldn't hear anything they were saying (which also completely pulls you out of the movie), or when it drops out in the middle of a phone conversation, or drops out at the worst possible moment in a game... It happens probably two dozen times a day, if not more. At first, I didn't care too much about it, but the first time you have it drop out 3 times in a matter of a single minute, it's simply maddening. Imagine going randomly deaf for several seconds throughout every day of your life, and you'll get a sense of what it's like.

If I could simply plug the cable in and it would use the USB cable to transmit the audio instead of wireless, that would be perfect, but when it's plugged in, it simply charges the internal battery - you still get audio interruptions all the time. The interruptions will also reset the "mute" status on the mic, which can be troublesome if you're intentionally muted on a conference call and suddenly your mic is on and people hear you eating lunch.

Second problem is that the power button is a bit flaky. If the headset is plugged in via USB and powered off, sometimes it will not power on unless you unplug the headset and THEN power it on (and then you can plug it back in to continue charging). I thought it was a defect in my first headset until the same thing happened with the second one.

A minor third problem is that the boom mic is a little flimsy on the construction. I am careful with my toys, but it still cracked and finally snapped off one day when I was lowering the mic to use it, and that was only a few months into owning it.

OVERALL:
If they would fix the wireless, I would rate this 4 stars in a heartbeat. If they fixed the power button, it would go up to 5. That said, the G35 seems to be the G930 but wired, and cheaper. The number of times that I've wanted to really make good use of the wireless (go to another room and keep the audio going) is far less frequent than the dozens upon dozens of times that the audio cuts out, so it's just an unacceptable point for me, since that is what this headset is about.

I ordered the ‘1More True Wireless ANC in-Ear Headphones with Microphone’ for review and would like to share my thoughts.

I have been looking for a true wireless earbud with true ANC which until recently have been pretty hard to find. I have a few different earbuds that claim “Noise Cancelling” but really they just “Isolate” the background noise. I have had these 1More earbuds for some time now. I have tried and tested several other brands both before and after receiving these and I have to say that these have become my Go-to earbuds for many reasons including their true ANC features. I will lay out my Pro’s and Con’s in no particular order.

Pro’s
* TRUE ANC - Yes these actually are true ANC earbuds with two different level settings. Is it the best ANC I have ever tried? No, but these 1More earbuds are the first True Wireless ANC “earbuds” I have tried and for me, I am impressed. The ANC does not work as well as some of the over-the-ear ANC headphones that I have, but that is to be expected. Again, for my use and in my opinion, the ANC functions beautifully for such small True Wireless earbuds.

* SOUND - These are the best sounding earbuds I own. The Bass is a bit on the heavy side but not to the point of becoming muddy which I appreciate. The Mids are well balanced and the Highs are crisp and clean.

* PRESENTATION - 1More did an incredible job on the presentation and unboxing experience with these.

* DESIGN - This may be my favorite thing about these earbuds. The case that both houses and charges the earbuds is a beautiful small metal matt black pill shaped case that not only looks great but feels nice and solid in the hands. The lid stays closed via a satisfying strong magnetic click which in my opinion is the best option and design. I have had others that use a flimsy plastic tab to click closed, and they tend to break after only a short time which then you need to use rubber bands to keep the lid closed so the buds charge and don’t fall out easily. Speaking of magnets, the buds snap satisfyingly into their respected right and left sockets and hold quite tight with no worries that they will fall out unless you take them out. The design of the buds themselves were not as impressive initially. They seemed to look a bit awkward compared to the other buds on the market which are more sleek. However after using them, I quickly changed my opinion. They poke out a bit from the ears and are not very “stealthy” so to speak, but I actually really like the look. Plus unlike other earbuds that are hard to figure out how they position into your ear, these 1More earbuds are as simple as popping the case open, pulling the bud out and putting it into your ear the same way it was positioned in the case.

* PAIRING - I had zero issues pairing these to my Android device. It was quick and easy and once paired, they will quickly and flawlessly connect every time I take them out of the case. I also love that everytime I take them out of the case, they pair back up using the same volume level that I used last when wearing them even if my media volume is turned all the way up or down before taking them out of the case.

* CHARGING - I love the fact that these not only charge via USB C but they will also charge wirelessly which really surprised me. While I am talking charging, these also retain a charge for several weeks which is most definitely a Pro. I have had other buds that will not hold a charge while stored after a week or so. With these 1More buds, I can give them a full charge and know that they are ready to go even after several weeks of no use.

* SINGLE BUD USE - I love that you can use just one bud at a time. It doesn’t matter which one you take out first and put in your ear - it will automatically pair and be ready for use as a single bud. I use this feature a lot as I will put just one in my ear while I lay on my side in bed.

* BLUETOOTH 5 - This is huge if you like to watch any streaming media. I have other earbuds that only offer Bluetooth 4.2 and there is an annoying sync issue with these. With the 1More earbuds I do notice a slight sync issue right at the beginning of the video for maybe a couple of seconds. After that, they sync up perfectly and continue to stay synced up throughout the video. If you happen to pause the video then unpause it again takes a few seconds to sync back up, but this really isn’t an issue considering that once synced, they stay that way during the rest of the playback.

Con’s

* FIT - Though they fit well and there are several bud tip and wing sizes included to choose from, I have not found the “perfect” combo to where they are totally secure in my ears. Don’t get me wrong here, they do fit well but after a while I find myself pushing them back into my ears. This is usually if I am, say just doing housework and bending over a lot. If I am just standing upright and walking, there are no issues.

* APP - there is a 1More APP for these and it works great for updating the firmware or changing the ANC or passthrough settings but other than that, there isn’t much to it.

* TOUCH CONTROL - Now I have had these for a while and I still struggle with the “conveniently located button” on each bud. Sometimes I can get them to work and other times I can’t. For me this is probably the biggest con although I did not take away a star rating for this because it very well may just be me. I love tech and usually am pretty good about figuring things out but the touch controls on these are a little tricky or perhaps just a little finicky.

To sum this lengthy review up, in my opinion the Pro’s far outweigh the Con’s. This is an amazing quality product and well worth the price. Are they better than some of the other Top brands out there? I really don’t know for sure, but so far in my experience, they are the best True Wireless ANC earbuds that I own! They look, feel solid and sound amazing! I hope that this was helpful.

Normally when I receive a review sample I can do a thorough evaluation and write a review within two days. This one took longer. The reason is that it took me a while to hear the differences in this model versus the [[ASIN:B00G4UQ6U8 Brainwavz S1 In Ear Headphones]], which also impressed me (and I also own).

After going through a pile of albums to try to understand what the product description meant by smoother bass I finally found an album that allowed me to hear it: [[ASIN:B00492ANTS Portrait In Jazz]]. When Scott LaFaro's bass came in on Autumn Leaves I started switching back and forth between this and the S1, and also hauled out some studio reference monitors. These phones are capable of going down in the 18Hz range for the low end, which is lower than most in ear monitors and phones that are usually in the 20Hz range at the low end. I am not sure my ears can discretely detect the differences between 18 and 20, but I was able to detect nuances that the lower end provided.

These also go up a little higher than more phones, which are usually in the 20 KHz range, Again, I am not sure I can truly hear sounds at 24KHz, but there is a discernible difference. I tested that end of the frequency spectrum with a few Ahmad Jamal albums since he tended towards the right side of his pianos.

One other thing that took me some getting accustomed to was the over-the-ear way of wearing these. I am use to in-ear or the old fashioned over-the-hear phones and I had to play around with these before I figured out how to place them in my ears perfectly. If you are use to over-the-ear you will probably not experience the learning curve that I did.

A few other features that I have come to expect from this brand are here: extra tips of different sizes, a hard case ([[ASIN:B00HPPL1M4 Brainwavz Hard Earphone Case]]) and a 1/4" adapter. I love the flat, tangle-free cable that is tougher than it feels. And it has an adjuster like a chin strap on a cowboy hat that aids in keeping these firmly in place with the over-the-ear way of wearing them.

This is definitely a five star set of phones (according to my way of grading, anyway), and one that I will not hesitate to recommend to fellow musicians. We tend to spend a great deal of time listening to music and these do an excellent job of reproducing it. My advice, though, is to take your time when you first get them because their true power is not immediately apparent. When you do start hearing the difference you will understand why I rated them so highly.

Their admin's are nowhere to be found and finding an article on something as basic as the nut that needed to be changed is impossible. Peer support is your best bet for either product.

I've had the opportunity to review three different G.G. Martinsen players, and of the three this one is my favorite. I brought two of the players, pre-charged, to review at my sister's where I am staying a week while she had and recovers from surgery, and the one thing I can say right off the bat is that I wish the charging cable was of the ubiquitous Micro-A type and not the mini type, which I did not think to bring with me. The [[ASIN:B016F4AGLC other player]] handles like the [[ASIN:B0173CW2CQ first one]] I reviewed for G.G. Martinsen, but I will have to wait until I get back home to do anything other than test the recorder and FM radio on this 16GB player because I have no cable to copy music onto the player with!

Anyway, unlike the other two players, the controls on this one make sense and handle more like what I'm used to. The instructions that come with this (that I also left at home!) were well-written in English, unlike so many products coming out of China these days. But I haven't needed the instructions to figure out how to use this player or change the settings. The first thing I did was set the Power Off and Sleep settings to 0 so the player won't shut off unless I flip the manual switch to turn it off. I have been listening to this player while I've been writing reviews, and I have had absolutely no cutouts with the FM radio even though I'm in a condo sandwiched on all sides by other units and this place is bad with reception of cable TV and other radios. I like that the station stays selected even when you power the player off and on again.

The control dial is easy to see, with a top Menu button, left and right arrows, and a pause/play button on the bottom (something the other players did not have). The round button in the middle has a good tactile feel, and even in the dark it's fairly easy to feel where to press for the different functions. I'll have to re-read the instructions to understand fully when to use the center button and how.

The little piece you can thread a lanyard into is plastic, but I don't think it will break easily unless you put a lot of stress on it. The player comes with a pair of original Apple-style earphones, which are great for walking outside where you need to be able to hear sounds around you while listening to music. The headphones are not the best in the world, but they are a nice additional feature and good to have in situations where you wouldn't want pricier headphones to get ruined (the gym, outside should it start raining). Of course, your listening experience will only be as good as the wired headphones you plug into this player. It really is a whole lot of bang for the buck and an attractive little player. I have the turquoise color, and it's really nice.

I put links to the other two players I have reviewed so you can compare them. What I like about this one is it doesn't have that gimmicky bubble-gum type selection screen but, rather, just has a list of the different features and functions. The list is easy to read and looks more businesslike and professional than the more cartoonish screens of the other two players.

I am not the target demographic for this device: middle-aged empty nester who loves to watch sci-fi, thrillers, and horror. I have a number of these brilliantly simple, highly configurable lights. They are perfect in the bedroom where, depending on our intended mood, a variety of different colors or modes might be appropriate. I have two in the living room, hiding behind tropical plants at a 3' height, on either side of the big screen, about 5 feet away on each side. I have a routine set up to turn off all the lights in the room and engage campfire mode in both lights at 45% brightness with a single keyword. Voila--instant torchlight in the jungle (or romantic candlelight - take your pick). I am a colossal LOST fan, and this lighting is perfect for watching LOST, or anything scary or dark. And if I need a different effect, that's only a few words away.

The simplicity with which these set up and configure themselves is so good it makes Apple products jealous. If you have an Alexa on your Wi-Fi network, simply plug the Glow in to a power source, open the Alexa app on your phone, and the light will auto-connect to your network and add itself to Alexa. It will then prompt you to configure it with a name and add it to any groups, etc. Utterly simple. If the setup fails, it might ask you to scan the barcode on the back of the booklet it came with to get it going, but this has not been my experience - they have all self-configured and join the network seamlessly.

For those of you complaining this does not have a mic and speaker - folks, it works WITH an Echo device. It is a light - that's it. If Amazon built Alexa mics and speakers into this it would cost double--and I am positive they are developing just such a light ...for which you will pay $60+.

Normally, these are $30/ea, but they were 45% off on Prime Day, so I added a few more. There are indeed cheaper (and much more expensive) smart mood lights on the market, but if you run Alexa at home, this is hands down the best way to do it. Seamless.

It baffles me that Amazon does not have a whole range of lighting products which work exactly like this. They easily could. Give me one of these on a larger scale (12-15") and make it weatherproof for outside on the patio, please.

I can't imagine someone making them longer (moving it down a few notches) as I'm 5'9" and the bottom of the bag is already pretty close to the floor when I hold it to my side.

What I mean by that is when I have all of my stuff in here (I use this for my work bag so that includes laptop, notebook, mouse, charger, lunch/snacks, and purse things), it can become pretty wide quickly and bulges out a bit.

With all that said, for the price, it is an excellent bag. I ordered many others off of Amazon before settling on this one and for the price, this one blows them out of the water.

This is why I'm knocking of a star but, again, the problem is not with the headset but with my own anatomy!

With that caveat aside, I love them! For a gardener who wants to listen to something outside while working, the FM radio works just fine and the yellow rubbery cord keeps them around your neck even if you do knock them off. The U.S. Military-grade protection features (against dust, moisture, and shock) make these headphones stand out from the pack.

The Bluetooth pairing and sustained connection with these is better than any other Bluetooth device I've ever used, although I tend not to use Bluetooth unless I'm up and about in the house doing chores. I also don't make or get a lot of phone calls, so we don't even have a cellphone account and depend on the occasional VoIP to get the job done. Meaning I haven't tested the headset features at all.

But the sound is crisp and clear, without mud, more like monitoring headphones used in the music industry. I feel no pressure when wearing them (holding them to my head with my hands, of course, to keep them from falling off of my teensy ears), and I know they would be very comfortable for me in daily use. Maybe I can come up with something to rig them with so they don't fall off. Because I really do like them.

I ordered the ‘adidas RPT-01 Bluetooth Sport On-Ear Headphones - New’ for review as I am a sucker for wireless headphones. My initial thoughts right out of the box were that these are solidly built, lightweight and beautifully designed headphones. They look and feel "high end". I’ve now had these for nearly a month and feel that I am ready to share more.

First I would like to comment on the fact that these are touted as “Sport” headphones and my idea of “Sport” headphones are more of the "in-ear" earbuds, which fit much more securely and do better in the “head-shake” tests. I honestly don’t see these working for anything more extreme than jogging. Don’t get me wrong, they do fit well and are lightweight but just don’t quite pass the “head-shake” test haha. These are IPX4 Water Resistant which is a bonus, and the padded ear cups are removable and washable which is nice (though I have not been able to figure out how).

Pairing was super easy and they sound really good for “On-Ear” headphones which leads me to comfort of “On-Ear” headphones and wearing glasses. I wear glasses and I have issues with “On-Ear” comfort in general. These are no different. Though they are very light and comfortable at first, within only a few minutes of wear they get quite uncomfortable for me. With that said, my Son who does not wear glasses has zero issues with comfort and says that they are really comfortable to him. Also speaking of comfort, personally (after about 30min of wearing) my ears tend to feel like I am wearing Winter Earmuffs as my ears get quite warm. This isn’t a huge deal but I thought it worth mentioning.

Now on to my absolute favorite thing about these headphones. The single Toggle Button on the right earphone. This is so simple to use and can control pretty much everything. Long Press to turn the headphones On or Off. Toggle forward or back to go forward or back a track. Toggle up or down for Volume Up or Down. Short press to Answer and End calls. This innovation is absolutely incredible and makes this the easiest pair of wireless headphones I have ever used. The button on the Left Earphone has the ability to assign three different functions. For example a single click could activate your phones default assistant or double click to play your favorite Spotify playlist and three clicks could play a different Spotify playlist. So basically the left Earphone button can only be used to use your default assistant or play Spotify. My guess is that Adidas could eventually add other apps to this button (with a firmware update) but for now, you only have the two to work with. In my experience so far, this button is a little tricky. First off, the button does not protrude much and can be harder to get it to click, especially if you have large fingers. Once you figure out how to get it to click, the next issue is that you really need to click fast to get the triple click to work. I've gotten to where I can get the triple click to work nearly 80% of the time. It's not a big deal because there's really only two apps it can control. I did notice that if you use this button to start playing Spotify, the Spotify app does not actually open on your phone which kind of freaked me out. This means that the headphones will be all that you need to use to quickly start playing Spotify. If you need to access it for anything else (on Spotify) you'll need to actually launch it from your phone.

USB C charging! More companies need to get on board with USB C and I appreciate the fact that Adidas have included USB C charging which makes for super fast charging of the Adidas RPT-01 Headphones. I have not fully tested the advertised 40 hour runtime but I can say that I have used these a couple hours here and there over my time with them, and I have only had to fully charge them once.

The Adidas app is pretty basic but it does offer some nice eq presets with the option to customize your own. Personally I like to start with the Adidas preset which is "flat" by default. Then if you prefer, you can customize it. The sound is amazing but not quite comparable to some of the other higher end noise cancelling headphones which I won't name.

Overall, I do love the Adidas RPT-01 headphones and they definitely have a place in my collection. Really the only two complaints that I have is, the comfort issue while wearing glasses, and I feel that at this price point they should have come with a nice protective case.

This review covers two different models of the Arctic fan:

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>Model with USB hub:
I have been using the original ARCTIC Breeze for a while and have been very pleased with its performance, and especially pleased with how quiet it runs. The Pro model builds on that and adds a few more useful features.

Unlike the original model which had a bendable stem with a USB plug on the end, the Pro has a base so the fan can be positioned away from the USB port on the PC. The attached power cord is a little over 5 feet long, making it possible to put the fan on my desk and plug it into the PC on the floor.

The base also has 4 USB input ports, so it works as a USB hub. It has a 5V power input jack if you want to turn this into an active hub. The power adapter to do so is NOT included.

Unlike the single-speed original version, this has a knob so you can vary the speed. It's not precise, but there is a somewhat noticeable difference between low and high. It's a continually variable speed - you can turn the dial to whatever speed you like.

Best of all, it's just as quiet, if not quieter, than the original model. That's the biggest plus for me by far, since the cheap USB fans make a racket. This just makes a low-pitched hum. The build quality is solid - the base is sturdy, and the bendable arm holds its position well.

One negative: the packaging. It's in a clam shell package that is a major, major pain to open!

While it's more expensive than the original, the added benefits of being able to position it on a desk and use it as a hub makes the upgrade worth considering. Highly recommend.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>USA EDITION:
I've have (and use) a couple other Arctic USB fans and have been 100% satisfied with them. This new version (their "USA Edition") has a couple of improvements over past designs.

The base is a metal plate which increases the fan's stability when you're bending the stem to point the fan. The on/off/speed dial switch no longer has a lit LED ring around it. I never found the lit LED ring to be bothersome on the other Arctic fans, so having or not having it is not a big deal to me.

The base also does away with the USB hub connections that other models have. That's keeps the base more streamlined and allows it to have a lower profile. It also does away with the clam shell packaging, instead using a very easy to open box.

The build quality of this, like the other Arctic fans I have, is excellent. The stem is bendy by stays put where you want it; the operating sound is pretty hushed; the on/off/speed control works well. The overall design is attractive, with a red/white/blue color scheme and graphics.

It moves a surprising amount of air. No, it won't blow your hair back as a Vornado fan will, but this makes a noticeable difference in circulating air. The size makes it very easy to find a spot on your desk to position it.

While I can't speak to the long-term reliability of this as of yet, I expect it will last for some time. I have an Arctic fan similar to this that I've been using almost daily for the past 1+ years, and it still works as good as it did when new.

Looks good, works well, and easy to use. Highly recommend.

One of the problems I have seen with the latest crop of notebooks and Ultrabooks that have come out is a lack of USB ports. There's usually a need for more ports than these systems have and it gets frustrating. A small USB hub like this is a good solution. That said, this particular hub does not have a separate power source so some consideration must be made when plugging in power-hungry devices.

From a design stantpoint this is a solid unit, shaped to be accessible without being huge. It has a little weight to it and this is helpful for keeping it stable. The addition of Velcro strips in the package to secure it in one place is a welcome inclusion and makes securing the hub very simple no matter what your configuration is.

The hub provides four USB 3.1 type A ports. Let me state what should be obvious - this will not convert a USB 1.1 or 2.0 port into a 3.1 port, so plug it into a 3.1 port if you want the speed across the hub. For my specific uses, it does not need to be a high-speed hub and I am find with using it as a 2.0 hub, but admittedly that's slightly wasteful.

There is no power port on this hub and there is no DC adapter in the box. So, any power that the hub needs comes through the onboard port into which it is plugged. That's fine for low-power devices like mice, keyboards, memory sticks and so on, but if the intent is to plug in such things as USB hard drives with no external power supply this can cause some headaches. No, one drive isn't going to overload the hub, but if you have multiple drives attached there may be reliability issues when they starve one another for power. When the device plugged in has its own power supply (like a big backup drive), this has little impact on the hub.

The point is, plan carefully how you intend to use the hub.

I like this hub and it does a good job for what it is. It has given me three extra ports on an Ultrabook I use which is all I could ask for. The ability to power this hub with it's own power supply would be the only area for improvement I could find.

Before writing this review I glanced over some reviews of earlier models, and whatever issues previous editions of the Bose SoundTouch speakers may have had seem to have been worked out with this SoundTouch 10.

Setup was simple with the SoundTouch app (available for iOS, Android, and Kindle Fire devices). We had the speaker set up and operating in less than 5 minutes using an iPad. You'll need your home network security code to connect to WiFi and that's about it.

It comes with a remote, but most of the controlling is done from your device (tablet or phone). The remote is handy for adjusting the volume when you're using your device for other things.

The speaker is about the size of a cereal box. The sound that comes out is impressive for its size. I think there's a wee bit of case resonance in the mid range, but that's just me -- everyone else thinks it sounds terrific. It doesn't rival a huge stereo system but it's really, really good.

Now excuse me while I get on my soapbox about monaural. This is a single speaker system, not stereo, and that, to me, is a good thing. I'm a fan of monaural. It solves a lot of issues about speaker placement (trying to make sure they're equally distant), and you hear the full mix as the producers and artists intended. You can move anywhere around the room and not have half the mix disappear. And if you like oldies, particularly from the 1960s, this fixes the problems caused by common pan/mix practices from that era (for example, drums and bass panned hard left, guitars and backup singers panned hard right, lead vocals in the middle). If you listen to mixes like that in headphones, you pretty much have to mix the music down in your imagination since bass/drums are exclusively in one ear and keyboards in the other. Some devices don't support mono audio output (I'm looking at you, Windows phone), and as far as I know no one makes a dual-ear mono headset for phones either. So a mono speaker solves the issue. Okay, that's it for the soapbox. Back to the review.

The only tone control available in the Bose app is bass volume. But since the sound is well engineered, it's adequate. And bass is very audible. Not subwoofer level audible, but it's very present.

The SoundTouch app itself is impressive. It really does make setup a breeze. And the listening options are VAST. Hundreds of radio stations from around the world on WiFi, streaming music services, Pandora, Spotify, and so forth. I used to do a little shortwave listening, and if you're a DXer, this exceeds the capability of SW by far, and every station is digitally clear. And you can connect directly to play music straight from your device.

Just to be clear, the speaker itself needs a wall outlet to power it. It's not battery powered. But everything else is wireless. More speakers can be added, but it's so easily unplugged and moved around that one speaker can easily be sufficient.

You are able to record 4K, 10 bit @ 4:2:2, but you have to run it to an external recorder. If you do a lot of green screen composites--you'll want this 4K capability (the more resolution, the easy it is to key); talent with long, flowing hair keys perfectly... Also, if your project export will be 1080, for interviews, shooting 4K is a must. You can get the feeling of a two camera setup, using just this camera. For example, you can have a nice medium shot; and punch in for that emotional close up (200%) without any loss of resolution. A few other nice features are the recording format options available (MOV, MP4, AVCHD). It's nice to have options and what works best for your post workflows. And lets not forget the awesome Variable Frame Rate @ 96fps. The 96fps at 24p is so smooth! Love it. Finally, focal peeking. See exactly what areas in the shot are in focus--a great built in feature!

I would also recommend picking up the 64GB Class 10 U3 SD memory cards. This class of memory card is exactly what you need to be sure you're capturing at the fastest rate possible. The max bit rate on the GH4 is 25MB/s and the Class 10 U3 cards are rated at 30MB/s.

The build quality, hands down, is solid. You will not be disappointed!

Can this function like old school speakers if I don't care for all the tech? So I simply used the 3.5mm connection method from my dell to the logitech, but there was NO SOUND. So you have to at least power up the wireless controller for the first time. Because under the controller is a button to switch from bluetooth to wired. Press the WIRE option, and you will then get audio. After this, if you remove the batteries and take away the wireless controller, the speakers will continue to work as 3.5mm connected speaker. You just have to turn on the wireless controller on the initial set-up. So this is good. My concern was what if the wireless controller is lost or damaged? If that happens, then you would like the speakers to go on like old school speakers connected simply by 3.5mm. So I'm happy to report, this will function without the wireless controller module. I'm not even sure turning on the wireless controller in the initial set-up is absolutely required. Your PC my pick-up sound the moment you plug in the 3.5mm jack. For me, I had to turn on the wireless controller during the initial set-up.

Another thing I wondered is if I connect a bluetooth device, say my smartphone, to these speakers, then disconnect, will the speakers automatically revert back to wired? The answer is no. To connect to a bluetooth device, you have to press the bluetooth pairing button under the wireless controller, and it will stay in this mode even after you disconnect. You have to press the "wire" button to get back to 3.5mm.

I bought and installed the Pogoplug on my LAN for the purpose of sharing photos over the Internet.

Right out of the box I had misgivings. There is no documentation or technical specifications. That immediately raised serious questions in my mind about it being vulnerable to hacking or opening access to my computer and personal information. You have to attach it to your modem/router and allow it to go out on the Internet without knowing what it is doing. I decided to take it on faith that the company was legitimate and not going to install a backdoor into my system.

I attached a Seagate USB external hard drive as my main memory device. I have also used USB memory sticks for temporary storage. All are USB 2.0.

Initially I had issues with people accessing my files. The Web access used by outsiders does not show any indication of activity. If you have a couple of hundred photos like me, it can take a couple of minutes for anything to appear. I have also had people report 404 and other errors fairly frequently. My workaround was to create more folders to compartmentalize everything. They load quickly enough for people to see something happening and know that they are connected.

Once you get inside the folders, people see a filmstrip and a large image like they would see in Windows. It is a serviceable but not glamorous interface. It is also not customizable.

Once I established that people could access my photos over the Internet, the next step was to fill up the hard drive. To do so, my plan was to push the files over my 10/100 MBps LAN. The Pogoplug shows up as a drive, so all I have to do is drag-and-drop. The problem is that it is incredibly slow. I normally get about 30 kBps. That is dial-up modem slow.

This exposed the second big problem. Remember the total lack of documentation? I had no FAQ, troubleshooting guide, technical specifications or other information to go on. I had to contact technical support via the Pogoplug web site. The Web site is slow and not always working, but I did get to someone, and they gave me the obvious suggestions like turning everything off and back on, dismounting and remounting the drive, trying a different drive, etc. After several iterations, I still had a slow connection that was now unreliable, a bunch of tech talk gibberish on ports and processes to open and close, and a closed out support ticket.

Doing more research, this appears to be a known and frequent problem. It is a deal breaker for me. I am going to be looking for a replacement. As an interim solution, I will attach the USB HD directly and transfer my files on an as-needed basis. However, I am looking for an alternative now.

So, to summarize, the concept is great, the implementation is okay, but the tech support and the LAN connection are not good. If you are serious about file sharing, this is not the device for you.

I was given one of these units as a gift and I have been working with it for a couple of years now. I upgraded to a more capable and more expensive unit but I still use the eTrex Legend frequently. It is a fine entry-level GPS receiver (GPSr) for most applications.

First off, this is not a large and bulky unit but rather it fits nicely in the hand (or in a front pocket if desired). It is lightweight and the curves/shape do not make it uncomfortable to use.

In spite of being fairly small, the display is large enough to read clearly and the controls are fairly easy to use. There are a few buttons on the side of the unit as well as the "click stick" that facilitate navigating the menus and displays, but it is a good idea to read through the manual to get some idea of how these work. I took the unit out of the box and had no idea what to do or how to use it, but once I leafed through the manual it made good sense.

It takes some time to acquire the satellite fixes it needs to facilitate navigation. On average, it takes about 45 seconds to acquire a lock, which may or may not be acceptable to some people. For my purposes it is fine. That said, it does not take a lot to lose the fix - heavy canopy cover or even obstructing the reception by holding the unit with one's hand over the internal antenna can cause it to lose track, after which it cuts off to conserve battery power. So, this unit performs best under open sky or light cover, though I have had success even in very heavy cover.

The accuracy on this unit is quite good. I have seen it accurate to within 6 feet, which is excellent. It usually holds its accuracy fairly well, though sometimes it struggles when there is magnetic disturbance or heavy cover. It have difficulty in the car unless it is on the dashboard or near a window.

I use this unit almost exclusively for geocaching, and it has proven to be excellent for that purpose most of the time. It can hold up to 1,000 points and it has functions for managing waypoints. That said, my family and I connected it to the computer on a trip one time and used it to navigate from Virginia to Indiana, and it did a nice job of keeping up with the roads. Also, the batteries lasted from Washington DC to Indianapolis, under continuous use, about 12 hours.

The base map within is fine for *general* navigation but it is not very helpful for pinpointing. It will get you down the interstate and to major roads, but that's about it. Still, for a unit in its price range, that's reasonable. There's 8 MB of memory in the unit so more detailed maps can be loaded.

This unit has been dropped, stepped on, knocked off desks, sat on and otherwise abused, and it continues to work.

There are more powerful GPSrs that have more functionality, have a better display or have better reception in areas where this unit fails. Those units cost more. This is an entry level unit and it does quite well in that role.

I have a small stand similar to this one that I use for my phone when I am at the office. It allows me to see who's calling when the phone lights off and it gives me a very consistent place to keep my phone where it is out of the way and in a safe place – no more misplacing my phone. The idea is good, and the design is good, but I have one issue with this stand that keeps it from being ideal.

This is a small, aluminum S-shaped stand with a plastic kickstand, designed to hold a tablet, phone or e-reader upright so that you can see the screen without holding it. The kickstand is adjustable with the push of a button and it has almost 360 degrees of movement (though it does not really need much beyond 100 degrees to be useful). It has rubber grommets to make the surface anti-slip and to keep it in place. So far, so good.

In the tray of the stand is a rubber insert that serves two purposes. First, it also provides slip resistance so that your device does not move easily. Second, it prevents damage to your device's screen which is important – metal on glass is usually a bad idea when the idea is to keep away scratches. I have used another stand like this that does not have the rubber insert and the first time I put in my phone the metal lip caught the screen protector and cracked it.

Be aware that there is not enough clearance between the tray bottom and the surface on which the stand is set up to allow plugging in the device without either cocking it at a weird angle or turning it on its side (or upside down). This is typical with this type of stand and I cannot count this as a flaw.

The one issue with this stand is that the rubber tray insert is not permanently attached and it is not secured in the tray at all. When the stand arrived the insert had separated completely and was loose in the box. It does slip back in without issue, but it won't necessarily stay there when you move the stand in transport. Without glue or some other method of modifying the stand there is no way to secure the insert more securely, and this is an unfortunate design flaw. It's not a deal breaker, and it does stay put when the stand is set up so the stand is very usable, but care is required to ensure the insert does not fall out when moving the stand.

Other than the tray insert not being securely fastened to the stand, the is a fine little stand and it works well. It's small, easy to pack and move and it provides a stable and easy way to set up even a larger tablet so that it is upright without having to hold it it place. It will see regular use in my house.

This is why I like VA panels, the black levels and the contrast. I've always bought IPS before and they're still great obviously, but after having a VA television, I started to personally prefer its benefits. There are obviously a few downsides when it comes to VA monitors, but this particular model solves most of them.

I have 2 IPS displays on both sides of this, and I can tell you the colors look excellent. It was also close to perfect calibration right out of the box, which was a nice change.

One review mentioned Gamma Mode 1 as closer to 2.2, but another comment mentioned Gamma Mode 3. Mode 3 seemed closest to me when calibrating, so I would recommend it.

Viewing angles:

The viewing angles aren't very good, as expected, but it doesn't affect me as I'm always right in front of my monitors. There is some slight vignetting when sitting close, so a curved screen could have been nice if implemented well.

Backlight bleed:

Having no IPS glow or backlight bleed is another benefit. With larger VA tvs there can occasionally be some slight blobbiness when in very dark settings, but this panel is very uniform with no BLB that I can see.

Size/pixel density:

I personally love bigger monitors, and don't have an issue with the pixel density here. Some people who are more sensitive to that might not be completely satisfied, but I personally would choose the increased immersion of a larger panel. Regardless, 1440p is awesome.

Ghosting/input lag:

In terms of ghosting, it's surprisingly almost nonexistent. Here's some comments from other people:

"I played some Doom last night, and literally did nothing but rapidly move my camera all over the place to see if I could notice any ghosting or bleeding. I couldn't find anything objectionable..."

"Also there is very little ghosting in the monitor which is super rare for VA panels."

"...even in dark games like Outlast 2/Doom, the ghosting is so hard to see that you have to intentionally find a worst case scenario to try and induce it."

"Ghosting is slight, about on par with 165 Hz IPS gaming panels from my testing. Only TN is faster really."

In terms of input lag, tftcentral says: "We measured a total display lag of only 6.40ms. With approximately 4.15ms of that accounted for by pixel response times we had an estimated signal processing of just 2.25ms, which was next to nothing. This is in keeping with other G-sync screens we have tested, as the absence of an additional scaler (and presence of the G-sync module) allows for extremely low lag."

This monitor is exactly what I've been waiting for. The circular light bar on the back is a nice touch as well, although it could be a bit brighter. I also would have preferred a sharpness slider, but it's not entirely necessary.

FYI, it can be freely moved in basically every direction, including 90 degree rotation - if you need that for some reason.

So if you don't have issues with viewing angles/slightly higher pixel density, this is an excellent choice as it excels in basically every other area.

I've had a number of Bluetooth headphones and the overwhelming majority of them have an "audio interface" that makes sense - some bare bones, some quite pleasant. This interface is in the form of sounds the relate to each of the functions - power on/off, paring, etc. These headphones have a TERRIBLE interface. When you power them on an annoyingly loud series of tones blares in your ear. The tones rise in pitch. When you continue to hold the power button, to access the paring mode, all you hear is an extremely brief, muffled tone. Apparently, the makers thought this was enough of a signal to indicate you're in paring mode. Believe me, it is NOT obvious at all. When you power off the headphones, you hear the same annoying loud series of tones. In this case, the tones do not decrease in pitch, which one might expect.

By comparison, the audio interface of my other Bluetooth headphones are a joy - unfortunately, they do not have volume controls or skip and rewind. When powering them on, a pleasant female voice says, "Hello", and when you enter pairing mode, the same voice says, "Ready to pair." When pairing is established, the voice says, You're connected", then tells me how much charge I have - either full, medium or low. These Cootree headphones do none of that. You'll be lucky if you're able to tell if they've been turned off properly.

In terms of sound quality, they're okay - nothing exceptional. In terms of fit, they're okay as well. Again, nothing exceptional. To my knowledge, they do not have an active noise cancelling function, other than what little noise they may happen to muffle by covering your ears. I mention this only because the rating form asks about it.

This is exactly what I wanted. I have set up two different activity-based logitech-type remotes. Neither really did everything I needed them to do, and even though both had lighted buttons, they were of limited use to me with my bedroom set up, because I still needed my glasses to do anything with them.

Why I like this (and who will most likely feel the same way): I have reasonably new components in a reasonably common configuration in a smallish bedroom. When I started this particular set up, my dish joey remote did everything I needed it to do: turn on the tv and joey, turn off same, adjust channel from the cable guide, set dvr, control volume on the tv, *MOST IMPORTANT* fit on my bedside table. As time went on, I acquired a sound bar and a FireTV, neither of which was controlled by the dish remote. The dish remote also would not change the input on my tv, so I had to have that out as well if I wanted to use the FireTV. I have experience and patience with the logitech set up process. My husband and I both have smartphones (and mine is already on my bedside table at night). Set up took a bit of time and patience, but resulted in a universal remote AND smartphone app that control everything I need them to control (and I can use accessibility features on my smartphone so that I don't usually need my glasses to find the buttons). That's a lot of problems for one device to solve, and this one did it.

Also, if you have wanted an activity-based universal remote and haven't wanted to pay hundreds of dollars for a product from this manufacturer, this is an awesome choice.

Who may NOT like this: People with devices that are not 100% controlled with the logitech app/program. People who don't have/don't like smartphones. Senior citizens who are uncomfortable with technology (although I would not be above putting the app on a big bright tablet for a parent or grandparent who is open to the idea, especially since many tablets can be made to play a sound that will let you find where you set them down). People who are fine with having/using a few different remotes or who really don't use more than one or two remotes. I mean, this thing is really cool, and I love it, but if you're not having any problems with what you're doing, you may not want to spend money to solve a problem you don't have.

I like layering tanks under shirts and even dresses, but it can be difficult to find high-quality tank tops for this purpose. This Ultimate Slimming Tank Top from Nudwear is definitely excellent quality. The combination 84% Nylon/16% Elastane was substantial and opaque, even in the white version. Furthermore, the fabric was smooth with plenty of stretch.

Unfortunately, the fit was more of a disappointment. Because I wear a small or medium in most tops, I ordered a medium (given the stretch, I didn't want the top to be TOO tight). This tank definitely fit me close to the body. I wouldn't say that it was bandage-tight, but at the same time, it was clingy enough that I would wear it alone as suggested in the description.

Despite the close fit through the torso and waist area (keeping in mind that I'm pretty slim there--my natural waistline is only about 27-28"), the straps on this top were a bit too long and too loose on me. Although I did like thicker-style straps, I did NOT like that they weren't adjustable like tanks with spaghetti-style straps. Furthermore, I was disappointed that this tank had NO shaping around the bust whatsoever. A final fit issue I had was with the wide waistband. Although I believe this was designed to keep the top down, I actually found that it caused it to ride up! The only way this top stayed in place is when I had it tucked into my pants.

In the end, I think the description of this top as "slimming" is misleading; perhaps "smoothing" would have been more accurate? I would have found this tank top to be MUCH more practical if it had an actually slimming panel in the tummy area--a built-in bra would have been nice as well (or at least some sort of shirring or other enhancement to the bustline). Perhaps this tank will work for others, but I would not recommend it for a woman of my similar shape and size.

I have worked with a lot of headphones, active noise canceling (ANC) phones in particular. ANC phones are interesting in that while they are good at stripping out white noise they frequently do not sound quite right because they twiddle the sound profile, usually in the bass range, to compensate for the sound frequencies they filter out. Also, there are varying levels of ANC, the standard to which others are compared is Bose. This headset by Jabra came as a huge shock to me, both for the very balanced sound profile and the aggressive ANC function.

This headset is on-ear, not over-the-ear. Usually I am a bit wary of on-ear headphones as they tend to be a little uncomfortable. These have very soft, leather-like pads and they are actually quite nice – for a while. After about an our of wear they start to get slightly uncomfortable for me, though taking them and shifting them a little makes them fine again.

The ANC function is VERY aggressive, approaching the same level as Bose but not quite. It is able to wipe out the sounds of the A/C, a fan, engine noise and more. Like Bose, when these are first turned on the ANC gives the wearer a sensation of pressure on the ears. Using this without feeding in noise, it is possible to enjoy relative quiet when traveling, reading, studying or enjoying similar activities.

The sound profile is on point. The bass is present and unmistakable, but it is not pushed forward so much as to dominate the whole profile and drown out the midrange. The midrange is bright and warm, giving music the right depth instead of making it sound like it’s either in a tunnel or in a barrel. The highs are very good – solid but not piercing. Jabra has nailed the sound profile where a lot of others have screwed up.

This is also a headset for talking, and call clarity when using with a mobile phone is very good. I have had excellent results using this headset and it has worked extremely well for me. There is a caveat, though – because this headset covers both ears, it is not suitable for use while driving in many jurisdictions. It’s great when in the office, but know your local and state laws if you plan to use it in a motor vehicle.

There are two ways to use this headset and connect it. It has built-in Bluetooth and it pairs and connects very quickly with my phone. It also has a USB dongle for connecting to a PC, though it can be connected to the PC via Bluetooth too. My observation there is that volume levels are reduced when connecting to a PC via Bluetooth.

The headset comes in a crush-resistant case and includes the USB dongle and a USB cable for charging.

I can find little about which to complain with this headset. It does get slightly uncomfortable for extended wear, but it has great ANC and a very balanced sound profile. As a headset it works great for talking, too, and the Bluetooth pairing is fast. This has already become my favorite set of headphones for streaming music, though because of laws where I live I cannot use it as a hands-free set while driving.

Thank you to all you wonderful Amazon reviewers. I'd never purchased a Bose product before, with the exception of possibly headphones at some point in time. Like many other reviewers, I have trouble understanding some dialogue on TV. It's fine as long as there is someone around to annoy endlessly by asking "what did they say," but watching TV alone, I miss big chunks of the story & plot. The doctor says it's just "one of the vestiges of old age." Oh. Another one of those. Thanks, doc.

So, I wondered if the Solo speaker might help, and thanks to all my hard-of-hearing contemporaries here (or should I say THANK YOU), I saw all the reviews promising that I wouldn't have to ask "what?" every 2 minutes any more. I could jump for joy after hooking up the speaker and giving it a listen, although my doctor would probably advise against it. On my TV, unlike some others mentioned here, the TV speakers work along with the Solo speaker, so it's easy to mute the Solo and hear the difference between it and the TV speakers. It's amazing. The sound is rich, and big, and crisp in a way that my surround-sound system isn't. Most importantly, in answer to my wildest hopes, I can understand every single word of dialogue, even Christian Bale mumbling behind his Batman mask. No kidding. The Bose speaker took 20 years off my age, and reduced my waist by four inches. Ok, I am kidding about that.

As if all that isn't reason enough to get one of these gems, it has to be the simplest piece of electronics to hook up, set up & operate. It's simply two cords, one to the power outlet, and the other to the TV. They include all the cables in the box: digital optical, HDMI & RCA. Plug, plug, power. That's all. The remote is four buttons: power, mute, up & down volume. It's hard to believe that such intricate, complex sound can come from such a simple device. Thank you, Mr. Bose, wherever you are. Not only would I highly recommend this to my friends, I think everyone with a flat-screen TV owes it to themselves to get one. Seriously. This is the audio-visual experience I thought I was already having with 5.1 surround system.

Basically the whole thing is a button and depending on where you push down on the pad it either depresses the left or right button. You can also pinch to zoom, which is a nice feature for looking at smaller text, though it does become a bit blurry.

Performance is amazing. The Solid State hard drive is amazingly fast and quiet. From a full shut down windows boots to the login screen in under 5 seconds for me.

This comes with windows 8, so steep learning curve aside, you can use the screen as a touchscreen when you are using the tiles or anytime for that matter. For regular use, opening Facebook or shopping on Amazon, you can use the touch screen to scroll, zoom, highlight and click, simply by touching the screen. I dn't use it much, but did find it fairly responsive when viewing web pages, but even more so in programs meant to be touch screen. Scrolling through tile screen is the windows menu is surprisingly fun.

Overall this is a great computer. It is sleek and beautiful, with a wonderful screen and so so buttons and touchpad. Most of the latter comes down to preference. Myself, I like how they are as I've used other devices that behave similarly.
