I've been using a clip-on light for my Kindle Touch when reading at night. It works, but I don't like that there's a separate piece of equipment I need to keep track of. This all-in-one solution has proven to be an effective way to light up the Kindle without having a separate light.

The case itself is nicely made. The cover is soft and cushy; the interior is a nice "suede" type material that wont harm the screen. All the stitching is even and tight. The Kindle fits in easily and is held securely. The cover has what I assume is a magnetic closure. It works well, and keeps the case closed in transit, but opens without having to undo any snaps or zippers.

The light is attached on the back of the case. When needed, you undo a protective flap (has a snap button), flip the light over the top and secure it in place with a "hook" that's built into the top of the case. The on/off switch is on the side of the light housing. Takes only a couple of seconds to get it into position.

The light is more than adequate for reading is a dark room. It uses 2 button batteries (CR 2032).

IMPORTANT: my case came with a plastic protector on the batteries to ensure the batteries remained fresh in transit. This must be removed before use or it will appear that the light is non-functional. Unfortunately, there are no instructions about this (I guessed it was the issue when the light would not turn on).

While it's great to always have the light as part of the case, the downside is that the light housing creates a bulge on the back side of the case. That makes this more cumbersome to toss into a briefcase since it increases the width. But, for me, it's a fair trade-off since I don't have to remember to bring the light with me.

I'll give this 5 stars, but 4.5 is a more accurate rating since it should come with instructions with regard to the battery. I also think the battery cover should be thicker (no problems so far, but it's a thin plastic) as well as the lens cover (very thin plastic that bends easily). Those quirks aside, I'm finding this to be an excellent case for my Touch.

The same applies to cable or satellite. All you do is surf the guide, click what you want to watch or record, recordings are automatically saved to your hard drive. I've recorded hundreds of over the air, free, broadcast shows and movies, most of them I was totally unaware of until I bought these tuner cards and set up media center with TV guide. An IP camera is an inexpensive and straightforward way to add a little extra security to your property, whether it is watching a door, monitoring a hallway or even just keeping an eye on the dog while you’re at work for the day. This is one such camera by Foscam, and it seems to work fairly well in my testing. There are a couple of minor issues I have seen, though nothing that I would consider a showstopper.

This is a small and lightweight camera, about the side of a baseball, and it is hinged such that it can be angled in a range of about 300 degrees of coverage if it is placed properly though in practical use (meaning, when it is placed on a wall and anchored to it) it is likely to be positioned more like 70-90 degrees. It also rotates on the base, so it can be configured to point to just about any target from where it is anchored.

The base itself is detachable and the whole camera can be popped off the base with no tools. To me this represents a concern. It means that someone can simply take the camera from the mounting place if it is low enough, using no tools. I like being able to rotate the camera on the base but I also like knowing the camera is not going to get taken easily.

Setup of this camera is very easy and I was able to get it connected to my network without too much effort. That said, I struggled a little bit with the Foscam software and it took me a little while to get the software talking to the camera. I have had this trouble with another Foscam camera, and the problem seems to be the software - very specifically the IP Camera Search Tool utility - and not the hardware or the network. I was able to find the camera in the monitoring client.

Once the camera is connected and available it can be logged into directly. There, the user has some control over a multitude of settings including firmware updates, login credentials and more. I like the interface even though it is somewhat basic as it is easy to navigate and is completely accessible from a web browser.

The monitoring client software allows for more control, which includes concentrating on a single camera if there are more than one connected, scheduling, playback and more. In addition to the software that runs on a computer, users can connect to it via smartphone if they have an iPhone or an Android. Windows phone users are unfortunately out of luck.

The camera resolution is very good and is detailed with fairly accurate colors. This certainly is not the same as a camcorder, of course, but it is sufficient to recognize faces even at a fair distance. The night vision (infrared) is excellent and is sufficient that I was able to read a sheet of instructions that was held in front of the camera.

I do not like the LEDs on the camera, though... It is very hard to place the camera inconspicuously and have it remain unseen in the dark when it lights up with a ring of LED lights. This is the one major issue I have with this camera that I think needs improvement. What makes this drive different from all other drives? Two things.

First is the rather useless ability to control it with a touch. You can set two functions, one if you touch the panel and one if you keep your finger on the panel until the program you've selected pops up. Although there are a few drop down options, Explorer, which I would think is the most obvious, isn't one of them. Point to c:\Windows\Explorer.exe to set that program to a touch or a hold. It's awkward to take your hands off the keyboard and mouse and reach over to launch a program. After the novelty wears off, you won't find any use in this.

Second is the really useful ability to partition it for multiple platforms in the setup utility. This is great if you want to use the machine for a Mac and a PC or a Windows box and a Linux box. For the sophisticated user with multiple environments this is a fabulous drive. I can find none better.

The good:
It works for Linux, Windows, and Mac.
It's fast.
It's easy to format for NTFT without having to run Microsoft's convert utility--useful if you're going to be storing larger files.

The bad:
The finish feels uncomfortable to touch. It's not smooth.
The set up is a little buggy and I had trouble getting Windows XP to recognize it.

If the drive isn't recognized, or even if it is in disk management but you can't get a drive letter mapping, start with a reboot. That worked for me. If that doesn't do it, go to control panel->Administrative Tools->Computer Management and then click on Drive Manager. In drive manager you should see the drive and can format it from there. This will, of course, erase the set up utility that lets you partition this so nicely. It's a last resort to get the drive working. Once the drive is formatted, either manually or by the utility provided, it is recognized easily by the next computer.

I selected this hub/docking station for a new laptop that did not come with an SD card reader, a tool I used almost daily with my older system. As I looked for options and features I began to realize that I can use extra ports and interfaces too, though the card reader was the main consideration. After doing a good bit of research I settled on this hub and I am very pleased with it so far.

This is a small device, about the size of a deck of playing cards. It’s shelled in an aluminum casing so it is durable enough to handle getting battered around my desk a little which is a good thing. It comes with a USB-C cable, but I have not used the included cable, opting instead to use a cable that is able to handle higher wattage and was purchased at the same time; I’ll keep the included cable as a spare.

I had no issues with connection and my Windows 11 system was able to see it and set it up automatically with no manual effort at all. It quite literally has been plug and play for me.

The card reader works flawlessly for me. I have used it with two different cards and the system sees the cards as soon as they’re inserted into the reader.

I have not tried all of the other interfaces this device offers, but I did plug an external USB drive into the hub and it worked exactly as if it was plugged into one of the onboard ports. Speeds are excellent and I have had no problems with time-outs or stalls when moving large amounts of data across the interface.

What I have not tried yet, because I haven’t had the time, is connecting to my Linux system. My Linux system has an odd issue with the HDMI port (a known hardware issue with the graphics card model), and I want to see how well this hub addresses the conversion from USB-C to HDMI. If this solves the issue with that system’s HDMI connectivity when I try it, I’ll be buying another one. Once I have tried this I will update my review. If it doesn’t work with Linux it’s okay – the product description does not mention Linux as a supported platform, so if it does happen to work it’s a bonus.

My experience with this hub/dock has been very positive and for me it has been worth the expense. It’s expensive when considering I just needed an external card reader, but when considering everything else it does it’s a good investment for my system.

I couldn't get it to connect to the AT&T network.  I live in a major metro area, so I'm sure there has to be coverage here.  In fact I don't know how the device was able to be activated if it didn't see the network, as activation is through the internet.  I called tech support and they said that it might be because my wireless router was interfering with it.  I switched off my router and still could not connect to the AT&T network.  I also wondered if my wi-fi router interfered with it, wouldn't others also interfere with it?  The tech support person said no, because I wouldn't be that close to them.  Makes no sense to me.  Seems like any signal that could be picked up strongly enough to detect would then interfere.  I don't have the time to mess with this any more, so am giving up for the time being.  Another thing that I did not like is that it appears that the device is always on.  The screen blanks out automatically after a few seconds, which is good.  It also has an on/off switch, but even though the switch appears to function, it seems like it just turns the display on and off, but the device continues to eat up the battery life.  I don't think the battery will last as long as they claim.  I had the device charged up 100% last night and it still seemed to be charged 100% this morning, but in trying to use it today, it has already dropped to 90% and that's probably from only a few minutes of use.  If I ever get this working, I'll update the review.  At the moment I really don't feel that this is ready for prime time. I was extremely skeptical upon receiving this speaker because I mean after all, it is a tiger head with the speakers located in the eye sockets. Okay. Then I plugged in my Iphone 4 - and played Evanescense, Ennio Morricone, and John Barry. Totally blown away.

My biggest complaint with them was that they were too large to drag in and out of the house and just not portable enough for my needs. But since I wanted good sound, I'd put up with the inconvenience. Till now.

I know you won't believe me because I can't even believe it myself, but this little speaker packs quite a wallop in the sound department. No need to adjust knobs for bass and treble (there aren't any), because the balance is excellent. Put in 3 triple A batteries, adjust your smart phone to the highest volume setting, plug it in the already attached adapter cord, and flip the little switch at the bottom of the tiger's head. There is a sliding volume control on the side of the head which you can then proceed to raise or lower according to your needs. That's it. The sound is rich and deep without the tinny trebble or heavy bass you get from other models. It even sounds terrific when I switch to my Pandora app.

The only drawback is that there is no where to plug in an adaptor for charging my smart phone. But big deal - now I can use my more expensive, bigger speakers to do that. Cause this little guy can be held in one hand along with my Iphone and I can go from room to room playing my music and setting it down anywhere I want.

Please give this little guy or one of the other animal heads a try. You'll be as surprised and thrilled as I was to discover such a cool, useful and perfect little speaker buddy.

I've been using this speaker every single day since I got it. The sound is still amazing for such a small, clever design and the batteries seem to last longer than I'd originally believed. I have wanted a Blu-Ray player for a while and I have had reason to suspect that my DVD player is dying. I have a flat-screen Sony television so I figured this player would connect and work with it without too much effort. I was right and it has worked very well for my family and me.

I popped in a disc and it loaded up to the menu. That’s exactly what I expected to happen. In operation using the remote it has worked very much like my old DVD player – remote is laid out a bit differently but the operation is the same and it provides buttons to stop, fast forward and reverse, pause, eject, select the root menu and more. The remote had given us no issues so far, though it does need to have near line-of-site with the player in order for the player to see it and respond.

The footprint is much smaller than my older DVD player and required a bit of rearrangement in my entertainment center. The whole unit is smaller than a ream of paper and weighs next to nothing.

It has built-in WiFi and makes it easy to access online streaming services. However, I will confess that I haven’t yet tried this as I try to keep my WiFi device list small. I will experiment with this when there is time.

So far we have seen no issues with playback – no skips or stutters or freezes. I have a couple of discs that I know to cause issues for my DVD player that I will try in this player and see if it fares better, though I believe the discs are actually bad.

So far I have had a positive experience with this player and based on that I am happy to recommend it. It seems to work well and it is easy to understand and operate. It isn’t particularly expensive either which is a big plus.

If you want faster speeds on Windows, you should go into Device Manager and find the device labeled "USB 3.0  SD Card Reader USB Device" under Disk Drives. I selected this keyboard/touchpad with the idea of using it with my tablet. Admittedly I mistakenly thought it was a Bluetooth keyboard which would have made it suitable for my tablet but this turned out to be a misunderstanding on my part. That said, it has proven to be a very handy keyboard in more ways than I had originally planned. In particular, in addition to working with Windows and Linux it works with Raspberry Pi which opens a whole world of possibilities for this keyboard.

This keyboard is very small, barely bigger than a Hershey bar, and it has a full set of keys as well a touchpad and mouse buttons on the right side. This is sufficient for doing pretty much everything you’d want to do, including surfing the web, text editing and software development. Granted, the size makes it less than ideal for some of these functions but it does work as a full keyboard/mouse combination if you want to use it that way.

Right out of the box, the switch was on and the keyboard had completely drained its battery so it had to be plugged in and charged overnight. This was a surprise but was not a big deal, just unusual.

When connected to a Windows 8 system the OS recognized it and immediately it was usable. It required no special drivers, no configuration changes or anything else – just plug it in and turn it on. It worked the same under Linux as well.

The real test for this keyboard/mouse was on a Raspberry Pi system. The keyboard connected and worked without a glitch – expected since it worked fine with Ubuntu Linux but not guaranteed as the kernel was known to work but the hardware was not yet tested. With a second external keyboard connected it was possible to type on both at the same time and also to use the other keyboard as a regular keyboard and the other just as a mouse.

There are a number of other SBC types and designs out there, and there is no reason that this device should not work with any of them that have a Linux-based kernel. Embedded Windows system should also support it as well.

Though I have not really tested the full range it is good to at least 10 feet. At that range the system still recognized input from the keyboard and touchpad without any issues.

So far I have found only one issue with this keyboard and that’s the space bar. I habitually press the space bar in the middle, and on this keyboard the press sensors are on the ends. The spacebar is not quite stiff enough and when pressed in the middle it bows instead of pressing down on the sensors, thereby not registering the press. To get it to recognize the press I have to press on the ends specifically. This is a minor irritant and is a very small price to pay for what this device offers.

This is a very small but fully functional keyboard/touchpad combination that works with multiple configurations. It connects easily and so far has given no real operational issues. Keep in mind that this thing is extremely small, though, which is great for portability, mobility and economy of space but less pleasant for systems that aren’t being transported anywhere.

These are nice speakers for a ceiling (or, possibly walls). They will take up the entire 3.5" cavity inside drywall walls, so don't expect to be able to use these with plaster and lathe unless you're using them in a ceiling.

They attach sort of the way an "old work" plastic electrical box does - with tabs that you tighten from the front via screws. Those have enough depth for plaster and lathe, but the speakers themselves are close to 3.5" deep. You can take the grill off from the front to spray paint it.

This is my second pair of in-ceiling speakers, so I can tell you the two I've installed are both about the same installation-wise. And they both sound similarly good, but deep bass is left to be desired, so plan for a subwoofer if you desire and can. These things are looking for a restricted environment, so they sound better if you can put some insulation above/behind them or ensure the area they are enclosed in is relatively tight (think of a subwoofer box you'd make for a car and how each has a specific volume recommended - I didn't see a manufacturer recommended volume for these, but you can guess they want to be enclosed).

Overall a very nice product.

A friend told me he acquired a "fluid ball head" but I hadn't used one. The idea intrigued me, especially for video use.

Though this 6664H head has mixed reviews due to inconsistent manufacturing quality, I took a chance and bought one in December, 2012 -- 18 months ago -- and it's still working fine.

I had purchased the [[ASIN:B002SXMRQM Induro CT-214 8X Carbon Tripod 4 Section 61-Inch Max Height 26lb Load]] and it needed a head. The compact and extremely lightweight CT214 is simply amazing for field or studio still work.

For serious video work, I rely on a much larger and heavier [[ASIN:B003VQXWZA Manfrotto - 504HD,535K - Tripod]] that pairs a Manfrotto 504HD fluid head sitting on Manfrotto 535 carbon fiber legs. It's much lighter than older video tripods, but the combo is relatively giant and heavy, though it has a 75mm ball head for horizon adjustment and sliding base plate and counterweight springs for better balance.

As camera technology get smaller and lighter, the supporting equipment technologies are becoming lighter and stronger. Aluminum and steel are replaced by carbon fiber and magnesium.

This 6664H head on the Induro CT214 is surprisingly good for video! I first discovered this when I wanted to shoot video with a Nikon D800 at a balloon festival. Who wants to cart around a monster tripod, lenses and a heavy camera body?

I grabbed my "still" tripod/head (the Induro CT214/Fancier 8886H combo) that weighs all of 5.9 lbs, is only 27" long and 5" in diameter in its Induro nylon carrying case.

Amazingly, with a 70-200mm f/2.8 Nikon zoom on the D800 (and with a [[ASIN:B00D3551NU Brand New Photography & Cinema VF-4 Universal LCD View Finder WITH Extend Bracket]] loupe on the back of the camera to boot) I found I could actually pan the 6664H smoothly, even without an "official" head and pan handle. I was smoothly tracking ducks swimming in a marina with a doubler on the 70-200.

Yesterday I had to shoot a sporting event at the beach, this time shooting 4K with a Panasonic GH4. The GH4 is even smaller and lighter than the D800 rig and was even easier to pan and carry. The whole thing was a bit over 6 pounds! I carried it all over the beach for five hours. I was able to move rapidly amongst hundreds of people with minimal intrusion.

There are four knobs on the head:

The top one is for locking the Arca Swiss-style plate onto the head. The plate itself has a flip-up lever that allows attachment of the plate to the camera without a screwdriver or coin. It holds firmly. A safety button stops the camera from slipping off the head should you loosen the locking knob. You must positively press the button in while sliding the plate to remove the plate from the head.

Three unmarked knobs on the lower body control the head itself (kind of wish they had labeled their functions, but I can do that):

1. The large knob locks the ball solidly from rotating in its socket.
2. The small lower knob locks the panning motion
3. The small knob opposite the large one controls drag

In operation, I fully loosen both the large locking knob (#1) and the small lower pan lock knob (#2), then snug up the #3 knob to adjust the amount of drag. Panning works amazingly well, especially if you're not zoomed to a long focal length. Simple pans with normal/wide lenses are quite effective.

I realize the fluid movement is achieved via some viscous grease that may fail over time, but the head still works pretty well in my opinion in reasonable temperatures. I have not used it in extreme cold where the grease might become too thick -- but I have used it in very warm temps and it still worked well. The grease has not leaked out at all.

As you can see from the picture, it has a marked base in degrees, should you wish to pan incrementally for time lapse or panorama shots.

No bubble level, but there's one on the Induro and the artificial horizons generated by the D800 and GH4 are great for getting the camera level in a hurry. With the right amount of drag, I just push it into position and it stays for the 15-30 seconds I need for any given video shot.

For such a reasonable price, the 6664H is very hard to beat.

I gave my father my old Zune a while back, since I moved onto the Sansa Zip Clip+ years and years ago. He has some trouble seeing, so the larger screen helps him out. However, it is an older device, the battery was dying in 45m, and I wanted to freshen it up a bit. So I figured, while I was replacing the battery, I'd replace the HDD with an SSD - mostly for the reduced weight, power usage and access times, rather than the increased storage size.

As others have said, it works great, first time in. What I did was carefully remove the little plastic bezel in the bottom of the Zune, remove two tiny Phillip's heads, gently pried the two halves apart, removed the battery by unclipping the cable, removed the HDD case via four tiny Phillip's heads screws, gently pried *that* up, starting from the end opposite where the battery was, gently pried the HDD from the cage, removed the ZIF cable from the HDD, inserted it into the SSD, put the SSD back in the cage (with shock absorbers attached, they fit the new drive), then reassembled the whole thing. It took about 30m total, moving at a very careful pace.

After reassembly, I reconnected the Zune to the computer, had to reinstall the firmware, then resync the Zune to the collection. This was a bit tricky, as the old Microsoft servers are no longer active, but there are guides online (search for ZuneUpdate for more info).

For reference, the original HDD is about 47g, the SSD is about 32g, so you are looking at a 30% savings in weight there. If you forgo the shock absorbing pads and the HDD case, you could probably save another 10g, Probably not worth it though.

It is a bit pricey, and there is a 64GB version for ~$30 less, but from what I understand, the KingSpec is one of the only drives that reliably works for the Zune upgrade. Converters, ZIF-SD for example, also don't seem to be reliable.

I'll leave an update if my father has any issues, but so far, I am happy.

I've been obsessed with fully wireless earbuds for years and have tried out at least a dozen different ones throughout.

I fully support some in the $30 range, I had a pair of old soundcores that worked great. I've also tried the more expensive Samsung Galaxy Buds (2018 version), which worked well enough. I've also tried some mid-range ear buds in the $70 range. Earbuds have gone through some growing pains with drop off issues between the left and right buds and battery life. In my experience, I believe the $30 buds are great value and >$100 buds are worth it only if they have good sound and good app support. For me every one of the $70 buds that I have purchased have broken down in less than three months, so I'd say stay away from those.

Now on to the review:
The Cleer Audio, Ally Plus II True Wireless Noise Cancelling Earbuds are in the >$100 range (although just barely) but in the last few weeks that I've used them, I truly believe they are worth their asking price. I will of course update this review if they break down in a few months.

There are so many wireless earbuds being produced these days, which most imitating the airbuds with their ugly stalks in one form or another, Cleer has gone with a tear-drop shape and capacitive controls that I appreciate. I purchased the tan-colored buds and they don't stand out like a pair of white or black buds would. There is only a single dim light on the earbuds to indicate charging status and they are the in-ear-canal style of earbuds.

Features:
- Light-weight.
- Charging/carrying case supports type-c connection as well as wireless charging. Interoperable with products designed for airbuds wireless charging.
- Long battery life. I listen to audiobooks and they have lasted for hours while I worked on chores around the house.
- Passthrough with good app support (more on it later)
- Active Noise cancellation
- Can be used as a single earbud without having to pair each separately
- Touch controls: Only tap, double tap, and triple tap are supported. Configurable through the app.

The App:
When I first received the Cleer earbuds, the app was unimpressive. There was a single slide bar that changed the balance between noise cancellation and passthrough, a equalizer with no presets (and no reset for that matter), and there was limited control over what the tap functions did.

Since then, the app has been updated and the earbuds had a firmware upgrade. While the app still has room for more improvement, they did separate the passthrough, normal, and noise cancellation modes into separate controls. Passthrough now has a slider to control the strength of the surrounding noise and the noise cancelling has a "smart noise cancel" mode. In addition, a new personalized audio feature was added. The app takes you through a hearing test and adjusts the sound to your hearing levels. Quite cool.

The limited controls over the touch function is still there and the barely passable equalizer is still there but I'm hoping that they will be improved in future updates.

I am pretty good at making things work with computers. Peripherals often need some kind of coaxing or tweaking to make them work well. This, however, was beyond help. Let me explain..

WHAT IS THIS KEYBOARD LIKE?
LAYOUT
This keyboard is what I thought I had been waiting for for years. I have been using my third PC Concepts Ergonomic keyboard that I have used since the early 1990s. I used them because they are set up far better than any of the Microsoft ones. The problem is that they are not USB so I have to have an adapter to use it in USB slots.

TOUCHPAD
This keyboard is set up almost exactly like the other keyboard I have been using. The only difference is the touchpad is in the middle of the keyboard instead of on the right side like it is on mine.

SETTING UP
I was VERY excited to try this. I put my hands on it and was so excited- the spring in the keys and the way that they worked in typing was fast and effective. I could not wait to plug it in! Surely this was worth the VERY long wait for a keyboard like this.

HOW DID THIS WORK?
The box claims that this is plug and play. I plugged it in and ..nothing. WHAT? First the system claimed that there was nothing there. Okay, so I changed USB ports. The mouse signed in haltingly, but no keyboard. I removed all drivers, and then re-installed them. Nope. Nothing. First the touchpad would stagger and no keyboard. Then the keyboard would work but no touchpad. It was very erratic and no matter where I tested it, it would not work correctly.

I tried everything to troubleshoot this thing. Finally I figured out that somehow it appears that thistouchpad/ mouse driver shares the other mouse driver that is in the system. That means that my Wacom pad was no longer working as well as usual. It seemed to be fighting.

Finally I got the keyboard to load up. I began typing. I even considered keeping the keyboard and not hooking up the mouse (probably not possible). Then it happened. I began to type the word "keyboard"

Here is what came out..
keybooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooard.

Did the key stick? Nope. It sprang back. I tried again. Typed fine. Suddenly it happened again. oooooooooooooooo

WHY DIDN'T I JUST GET THE KEYBOARD WITHOUT THE TOUCHPAD?
I got this because due to a wrist issue, I have NEVER been able to use a mouse. Touchpad is all I can use. I also do not have the room on my desk for a mouse pad due to my Wacom tablet. Using the Wacom tablet is not convenient most of the time for regular touchpad use (non-graphic) or I would use that. When I want to do productive work, I want the touchpad in my keyboard.

BACK IT GOES
I tried EVERYTHING to get this to work correctly. I was really hesitant to try another one because at THAT price it should not be this difficult to use. I even tested it on another machine. It worked but had occasional hiccups too.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Other reviewers will probably cover the wi-fi setup, but I got this for another reason. I hate wi-fi because it can be slow, too many things can interfere with the signal (such as microwaves) and there is always a security concern. In addition to being a wi-fi extender, this works great for extending the range of your router's wired connections, which is how I am using it. There are two parts to this; one is the sending end, which you plug into your router via included ethernet cable and then into an electrical outlet. The receiving end of this has 3 ethernet ports and you can connect up to 3 devices by ethernet cable. If you use it this way, there is no setup at all. It truly is plug and play and worked immediately for me. The setup sheet doesn't make it clear that it can function this way, but there is a picture on the box showing it. Also, I was very pleased with the fact that both pieces included a pass-through outlet, which is a great feature. It would seem that this would keep you from losing an outlet. Maybe and maybe not. Here's why. Both pieces are quite long. If you plug them into the top outlet of a typical 2 part outlet, the devices will cover the second outlet. So just plug them into the bottom outlet, right?; then the top outlet is free. Maybe. The problem is that the devices are just a little too tall and you cannot fit a 3-prong gounded plug above them. You can use a 2-pronged plug and it will mostly likely fit. You would think someone would have tested this when they designed the product. It's that slight design flaw that caused me to knock one star off my rating. Other extenders of this type that I have seen are small enough to fit with another 3-prong cord above them when plugged in to the bottom of a 2-part outlet.

If you have a large house, it is possible you might have more than one main electrical circuit running through your house. This only works if you plug both devices into the same master circuit. Of course that is not the fault of the device; that will be true of any range extender of this type.

These power plug range extenders have been on the market for a while, but nice someone finally decided to include a pass-through outlet, but too bad that the device isn't just a little smaller so that it doesn't partially block the second plug in a 2-plug outlet when plugged in at the bottom. Note these do need to be plugged directly into a wall outlet; can't be used off a power strip. That could be an issue if you are short of outlets, as I am.

The connection speed wasn't quite as good as I expected, but it is adequate. The units heated up a little, which I didn't like, but not uncomfortable to the touch. I also have experience with standalone extenders that don't use the powerlines in your home; they work just about as well and some of them also have ethernet ports; the only difference being that you are going Wi-Fi to the extender and then going back to ethernet if you want to use a cable, whereas with a powerline extender, you are going through wires all the way. Those standalone extenders only require one outlet too.

I have used other TP-Link products and generally they seem to be of good quality, so I don't hesitate in any way to use their brand. Made in China, which is common for electronics products.

Sound quality is excellent. I was impressed with the bass in particular because it sounded natural. Many speakers I test have a bias towards bass, which is great for a lot of contemporary music that is bass-centric, but sounds artificial playing music that is more acoustic in nature. Since I listen to a lot of jazz piano trio albums these speakers are perfect for me.

The high end will not break up at the highest volume, but does sound a little compressed. Again, that is not necessarily bad because high frequency compression makes some music sound better. The mid range is very rich and one of the reasons why these speakers sound so good to my ears.

Volume is more than sufficient for a 20x30 foot room. There are no controls on the speakers, so you need to control the volume and EQ from whichever device you plug these into. My phone, tablet and laptop all have hardware/software to do this and chances are so will your devices.

My laptop's spare USB port was sufficient to power these speakers, and the big plus is you do not need to worry about batteries, wall warts and the such. I was able to also test these with my phone connecting the USB cable end to a charger. To be honest, that is a little inconvenient because the cables are hardwired into the speaker master unit. I would have much preferred separate ports and cables for the 3.5mm and USB, which would have allowed me to purchase cables of specific lengths for my own needs, as well as easily replace one or both of the cables if they were to become damaged.

Despite the cable issue I mentioned above these are nice, compact speakers that sound great. More importantly (to me) there are no batteries to worry about, and they take up very little desk space.

Two members of the family just told me that they had broken their headphones with this product came up to get. I decided it was worth a try, despite some previous experiences not being too great with cheaper headphones. Let's see what happened.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These headphones make some claims. They come in a great box who for Carlos fans will be a thrill. It is well decorated and presentation is fabulous. That means they would be a nice gift in that respect.

LEATHER?
The case says that these are leather padded ear cups and underneath headband. I am still not sure about this. Perhaps it is that bonded leather that is made from leather residue chopped up and blended with binders to remake it into sheets which are printed with leather look imprinting. Technically that can be called leather, but it really is not as much leather as I would like.

EAR CUPS AND HEADBAND
Having said that, these white headphones are comfortable. I can wear them longer than some others that I have had which are a bit rough after only an hour. These can be worn for several hours without a problem.

CORD
This comes with a cord which is only 38 inches long. That is a bit short for me. I find it is annoying and not quite as long as I would prefer.

SOUND
The sound of these is surprisingly great. The bass is really good, and the mids and highs are definitely clear and not muddy.

CONTROLS
The controls on the white pair are awful in that they are nearly impossible to read. The buttons are white and the markings are just very thin raised white on the buttons. It should really be colored with marker- which I took care of. Using a very fine permanent marker I colored just the raised areas. The up/down and play pause buttons are separated by the noise cancellation button which is good.

ADJUSTABILITY
These are very adjustable. They go longer, tilt in and out and rotate from side to side.

COMPACT?
These do fold flat and compact if you need to travel with them or store them in a smaller place.

SOUND CANCELLATION
THAT is where we part ways with these headphones. The noise cancellation is awful. It barely works. When it is turned on, the sound gets really compromised too. It becomes almost muffled in a way.

OTHER FEATURES
The ability to know how much power is left on the headphones while using the phone is nice, but it does not help if you are not using it with a phone and some other bluetooth device. Calling, people hear just fine and we can hear them too (several of us tried this feature with our phones)

THE BOTTOM LINE
For the price, these headphones are a step up from what I usually get when I try them. The sound is very good and well balanced, the folding up for storage is great, and the comfort is also on the upper level. The only disappointments are noise cancellation, short cord for corded listening, and the hard to read buttons.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. If the noise cancellation worked better, these would be over the top amazing. As they are, they are still pretty great. I love the white color- it stands out from the rest, despite getting dirty faster. They are a great gift to yourself or someone else and are some of the nicer headphones I have used.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

If you are new to home security camera systems, I recommend going with wired (non-WiFi), NVR or computer based recorders run with systems such as Blue Iris. This type of system is infinitely more secure and stable. While initial setup costs are a bit more the security it affords is worth every penny. It always pays to research the products, discuss them with those in the field, understand vulnerabilities and PLAN YOUR SYSTEM PRIOR TO PURCHASING ANYTHING. If you are at all tech savvy at all you can do it. While there is a bit of a learning curve it is not awful and in the end you will be thankful for the time you spent in the beginning as it will save you time, money and endless frustration.

I have set up, tested and reviewed more security systems and individual products than I can possibly remember. Without question my go to solution for home security solutions is a computer based, Blue Iris system with POE cameras run off of quality POE switches. This type of system is not only easy to operate but is highly secure.

As with any component there are a host of factors to consider. In terms of cameras more megapixels is not always better. For instance 2MP cameras often perform better in low light while 5MP will allow for more detail when lighting is good. One disadvantage of higher megapixel cameras is the recordings will take up more hard drive space. Depending on the number of cameras, this can become a larger concern.

Highlights of this camera include:

Lens: 3.6mm HD Lens provides a viewable angle of 80 degrees

POE: Power over Ethernet allows for one wire to be run to the camera that will handle everything - not only making installation easier but vastly more secure

Images are excellent and even low light images are better than most similar cameras in this price range

Set comes with what you will need (except Ethernet cable and system) to be hung in host situations

PoE compatibility - 802.3af - critical for using with software such as Blue Iris

Great build quality - this camera is well built and will hold up outside in all conditions

Issues I’ve discovered with this camera:

An issue to be aware of with all bullet style cameras is spiders love spinning webs in front of the lens. Just be aware of this so if this were to be hung in a difficult to reach location that will be an issue. With that in mind, any security camera should be hung no more than 8 or, at max, 10 feet high. Capturing a person that can not be identified committing a crime serves little purpose.

Setting the angle of this camera is a challenge - this is done with an Allen headed bolt that is exceedingly hard to access.

Audio is not available with this camera.

With all things considered this is a quality bullet style camera at an outstanding price. The sensor is decent quality, the build is solid and will hold up to years of outdoor use. The lens produced clear, crisp images both during the day and at night. POE wiring is easy and the most secure way to go.

While this camera won’t perform as well as more advanced cameras it is perfect as an extra camera for hard to reach locations. It connects to Blue Iris with no problem and has proven to be very dependable.

These are some very impressive headphones. The sound is incredible – full, natural separation; clear tonality throughout the full range; clean bass that properly complements the sound without being muddy or overbearing. Truly some of the best sound I’ve ever heard out of a set of headphones, even ones that cost three and four times as much as these.

The key word when describing the sound is natural. No, you won’t get booming bass that drowns everything out and rattles your eyeballs. What you will get is music that sounds as close to what the musician created as you can get short of a live performance.

The headphones are very elegant looking. The ear cups are clad in a gray-toned metal with a brushed finish. It looks nicely understated and modern. The ear cups are cushy and comfortable. The ‘phones come with an extra set of ear pads, which is a nice touch. The cups totally surround your ear providing excellent sound isolation. You won’t hear any ambient noise with these on.

The headband is well padded and comfortable. My only comfort quibble is that they grip my head pretty tightly. Not painful tight, but tighter than I normally prefer. But, since these are ear surround headphones, a tighter than normal grip does have some benefits.

The headphones use a Y cable, with inputs on each ear cup. The set comes with 2 cords – one with a 3.5mm jack; one with a standard 1/4 inch jack.

They come in a very nice hard case (that is also available separately). The case is excellent – very high quality materials (including a zipper that works very well) combined with practicality. My favorite feature of the case is that it has a zippered pouch that holds an ample number of cables. The pouch has Velcro on it, so it can be removed entirely from the case. Plus, it can be positioned anywhere on the inside of the case. Someone was actually thinking when they designed the case, rather than have it be an afterthought.

These are undoubtedly the best value in a high-end headphone I've ever come across. The sound is nothing short of spectacular – far beyond what you might think you’d get at this price point. Spending more will get you some nicer materials (such as real leather and wood accents), but you won’t get better sound unless you spend a WHOLE lot more. Huge recommendation!

[[VIDEOID:9452f3f4fe85561cedb2616d98f18348]] I have worked with many different Bluetooth speakers, and most of them are very similar in design and sound profile. The iDea Taco is a bit different and is the most innovative of the speakers I have used, not so much in the shape but more in the way it projects sound.

This is a pill-shaped speaker that is angled off at the sides and styled to look like a taco, though it is deceptive to that end. The sound does not come out of the ends but rather it comes out of the bottom. When the speaker is powered on and playing, the sound is reflected off the shelf or desk where it sits and this somehow enhances the sound (I am no expert in acoustics so I can't really explain).

I had no troubles with pairing or connecting. It advertises itself as "iDea Taco" and I was able to pair it to my phone and also to my computer (at different times). I had no trouble streaming to it and it was very responsive.

The sound profile is good, though not perfect. The bass is very good though it is not artificially boosted like with so many other speakers (overdriving bass is the current trend and it drives me crazy as it drowns out the rest of the sound profile). The midrange is full and as a result the music sounds warm, not like it is hollow or in a tunnel. The highs are the soft spot, with very slightly muddied sharps but still mostly clear and warm. The sweet spot for the sound is when the speaker is sitting at approximately a 45 degree angle from vertical, with the actual speaker facing down. It's at this point that the sound is best. This design decision is a bit more innovative than with most speakers I have used which project either straight up or straight out.

This is a solid little device and seems to be assembled well. It has a slight heft to it and it feels very solid - no give in the housing and no noise when shaken.

Overall this is a nice little speaker. It's designed a bit different than other speakers I have used and so far I am very pleased with it.

After a month of painstaking research on machines, I finally settled on this ASUS Zenbook when my Mac died. Several positive reviews (this was as of December 2013), and several negative ones. I figured they had worked out the kinks with this machine, so I took the plunge!

It was beautiful. Probably the most spectacular laptop I've seen. Keys clicked wonderfully, the screen was super high resolution, the casing itself was gorgeous.

The problems began almost immediately. After I got the whole thing set up with updates to Windows 8.1, updated internet drivers (some said they had problems with internet and new drivers fixed some issues) and installed my favorite internet browsers (Chrome and Firefox).

The ASUS had issues with scaling and screen resolution of many apps including the desktop itself, Chrome, Firefox, and Adobe programs. By this I mean that every time I opened the laptop after it "sleeping", the scaling and resolution were different than I left it, usually microscopically small, and I do mean TINY. Not just 10 point font and if you squint you can read it (I'm 25 by the way, so I'm not an old person when it comes to reading small font)...more like 2 point font. It was ridiculous.

With this ASUS, the internet connection was spotty and would go out periodically (like every 20 minutes I had to restart the internet connection--sometimes it fixed it, sometimes not). My husband is a computer guru and tried everything that the ASUS forums suggested, from uninstalling and reinstalling to updating the drivers, and turning off settings that I never would have been able to find on my own.

So as much as I loved the way it looked, I had to return it.

Now, the machine is just fine in quality, I'm sure. It just has SUCH a high resolution screen that programs are not yet equipped enough to handle it, making the font very very unpleasant. And whatever kept switching my sizing while it was asleep...that was a problem.

The internet issues, on the other hand, are very very real. While searching for the solution online, my husband found that this is an issue that ASUS is still trying to work out. I’ve spent the last month using and playing games on the Lenovo IdeaPad Gaming 3. It’s a decent entry-level laptop. I wouldn’t consider it a dedicated gaming machine, but more aimed at daily use plus some gaming.

The laptop includes 3 free months of Xbox Game Pass, so I’ve played games available through that library. Games like Moonlighter, Moonglow Bay, Tunic, Sims 4, and Hades. The laptop handled all of those just fine, but many are older games and/or not very hardware intensive.

However, I don’t think 8GB of RAM and a 256GB SSD are enough. In my very first day of downloading games, I filled more than half the hard drive (and only ~236GB is available to start). As for the RAM, my 5-year-old laptop has 8GB of RAM and I’m feeling it. A laptop from 2022 should start with at least 16GB.

The Quad Vent fans vent in the back and on both sides of the laptop. I wish there wasn’t a vent on the right, because it’s right where the mouse sits. After maybe twenty to thirty minutes, my hand gets sweaty, which isn’t great when playing a competitive game.

There are 2 USB-A ports, one on each side. The back has an HDMI port, Ethernet, USB-C, and the power input. I actually really like the power input being on the back, as that way the cable isn’t in the way when using the mouse. But I’d like another USB-A port in the back, because I can see using a hub with this laptop.

The keyboard is not my favorite. On the plus side, it’s a full keyboard. I can’t remember the last time I saw a laptop with a numpad. The keyboard has backlighting, but only one color option: white. The keys are flat on top and somewhat slippery. The keyboard itself feels cramped, especially when gaming with WASD.

The laptop is heavy, about 7 or 8 pounds. It’s not something you’ll want to tote from class to class. The battery lasts about an hour if playing games, and about 3 hours for normal use.

This is an great value in a light panel. While the size limits the amount of light output (compared with larger models made by Bestlight) the size makes this far more workable on smaller cameras.

I've used a couple of their larger models, and they are fine for hefty DSLRs. But, when put on a smaller camera it makes it so top-heavy that it topples over. This one, however, is so small and light (it is less than 2.5 inches wide and weights only 2.1 ounces including the battery) that it worked fine on my Powershot without making it top-heavy.

Now, the size does limit the light output – this is nowhere near as powerful as their larger models. It also does not have variable light output as the larger models do. It just has an on/off switch. But for general lighting tasks, it works very well.

It comes with an internal lithium battery that is rated at 1200mAh and a charger for the battery. The battery is small and adds little weight to the device. I find that to be a big plus, since many of their larger models don’t come with a battery. On the downside, this will not run on AA batteries like their larger models do, so when the battery is dead you’ll have some downtime until it recharges (unless you buy a spare battery).

It has a hot shoe attachment for mounting on the camera. It can also be mounted on a tripod or light stand. The mount is plastic but reasonably well made. Note: although it has a hot shoe, it does not communicate with the camera in any way. You have to manually turn it on/off.

It does not come with filters, so the color temperature is limited to 6500K. That's a good point for general use, however.

This is a great choice for smaller cameras or for when you want to add some light but don’t want to deal with a larger unit. It’s easy to toss into a camera bag and carry along. The performance is excellent and the build quality is quite good given the price (especially since a battery and charger is included). Highly recommend.

A warning to first time users, you may experience the microphone picking up background noise. It's very sensitive. Be prepared to set-up an area for recording if you are wanting to get clean audio. The VIMVIP USB Condenser Microphone came in a fairly plain box with a large hard foam protective insert. This microphone seems to be a great starting point for anyone interested in a higher quality microphone. I can whole heartedly recommend it.

The VIMVIP USB Condenser Microphone is a USB interface microphone that is a large step-up in quality to those used to the basic microphones that come with many web cameras. It provides a higher sensitivity to sounds; enabling both a greater ability to pick up lower volume noises and the ability to comprehend higher volume ones.

The lower volumes it was able to obtain included whispering, including the mouth noises associated with ASMR videos, and keystrokes from a non-mechanical keyboard roughly 6 feet away [With it's recording volume turned down to 50%]. On the higher end of volume it is able to accommodate singing, yelling, and screaming; by not topping out what it able to accommodate this allowed for wide arrays of vocals and would assist with those wanting to record instruments. I did many different experiments to test the range at home on different days.

The VIMVIP USB Condenser Microphone came with a short stand and pop filter that is attached to the stand by goose neck. The stand and metallic goose neck are both adjustable to assist with angling, but it is not vertically adjustable. The microphone, when pointing directly up, is about 26 cm / 10 in in height to the top of the microphone. It has a rubber ball footed desktop tripod for stability. The microphone can also detach from the included stand and be mounted to a standard size tripod or any other compatible stand, making the pop filter necessary depending on setup.

I had a great experience using VIMVIP USB Condenser Microphone to audition for a voice acting role organized by fellow fans of an animated series. The VIMVIP USB Condenser Microphone certainly made me sound much better than my webcam microphone is able to do. I have been using this for cooperative game-play online as well. This is a great value, especially at the price point.

After using my MacBook Pro all day, I always have a short adjustment period when I pick up a Chromebook. Compared to a normal Mac or Windows laptop, a Chromebook is very basic, very slimmed down on what it can do. Basically, ChromeOS is like turning an Android phone or tablet into a computer. ChromeOS runs on Google: Google Play for apps, games, books, etc., Google Drive for word processing, spreadsheets, etc., Gmail for email, Chrome for web browsing, and so on.

I know schools use Chromebooks but I don’t have kids, so my review is from the perspective of someone who uses a Chromebook for light browsing and streaming. For that purpose, it’s good.

The battery on this HP Chromebook lasts about 10 hours for watching shows and movies. I like that I can just grab it, watch for a few hours, and only have to remember to charge it a few times a week. Unlike some other Chromebooks, this one has only the standard laptop form factor, it doesn’t tent or fold. It also doesn’t have a touchscreen, which can be frustrating when trying to use Google Play apps on it.

The display is just okay, not very bright compared to my MacBook Pro, but then, that’s an unfair comparison to make. The sound quality (Bang & Olufsen audio) is good, making up for the display. The keyboard is not backlit and is missing some keys, like Caps Lock for a Search button.

The screen of the Chromebook has a black plastic edge that sticks out slightly from the white shell of the lid. I’m pretty gentle and careful with electronics, but I notice the black plastic edge pressing back into the white shell whenever I open the laptop. This is right where the webcam is. I’m worried that overtime, this area could break, since it’s already giving a little and I’ve only had the Chromebook for a few weeks.

The Chromebook charges via USB-C. It has two USB-C ports, one on either side, one USB-A port, an audio port, and an SD card slot. It has Bluetooth and WiFi; without an internet connection, a Chromebook is almost useless.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

If you are new to home security camera systems, I recommend going with wired (non-WiFi), NVR or computer based recorders run with systems such as Blue Iris. This type of system is infinitely more secure and stable. While initial setup costs are a bit more the security it affords is worth every penny. It always pays to research the products, discuss them with those in the field, understand vulnerabilities and PLAN YOUR SYSTEM PRIOR TO PURCHASING ANYTHING. If you are at all tech savvy at all you can do it. While there is a bit of a learning curve it is not awful and in the end you will be thankful for the time you spent in the beginning as it will save you time, money and endless frustration.

I have set up, tested and reviewed more security systems and individual products than I can possibly remember. Without question my go to solution for home security solutions is a computer based, Blue Iris system with POE cameras run off of quality POE switches. This type of system is not only easy to operate but is highly secure.

As with any component there are a host of factors to consider. In terms of cameras more megapixels is not always better. For instance 2MP cameras often perform better in low light while 5MP will allow for more detail when lighting is good. One disadvantage of higher megapixel cameras is the recordings will take up more hard drive space. Depending on the number of cameras, this can become a larger concern.

When I saw this camera at this price point I knew it was something I needed to check out. I appreciated the fact it was 2MP because with this lens you are not going to want to be eating up the hard drive space required for a 5MP.

I was able to get it set up within my Blue Iris system after playing with it for a while. Typically this takes me no more than a couple of minutes - this camera required much more extensive programming in order to have it functional.

Once I did have it up and working image quality is substandard even compared to other cameras with similar specs.

I figured it still could be utilized as a tertiary filler camera but it kept going offline for absolutely no reason. When a camera is connected via PoE to Blue Iris this simply should not be an issue unless there are issues with the camera itself.

While the price point is excellent on this camera, unfortunately this is an example of getting what you pay for. In my four months of testing this camera has proven to be unreliable, difficult to connect and keep connected and the images captured are far lower quality than expected from cameras with similar specs.

This is a product to pass on.

This is a rather unique take on a traditional power strip. Rather than be designed as a strip, it’s a tower, with two outlets on four sides, plus a bank of four USB outlets in the front. The design is perfect for plugging in “wall wart” transformers, since even the largest ones allow you to have access to all 8 power outlets.

There are three on/off switches. Two are on the top, with each controlling four of the power outlets. The third one is below the bank of USB outlets. Thus, you have a lot of flexibility in turning on/off outlet banks. That’s a big plus for me, since I use this as the power source for my Li-Ion chargers, and don’t like to leave them in use overnight. The independent switches allow me the flexibility to turn them off, but still leave 4 outlets on. The same for the USB outlets – I can turn them off rather than have to unplug the device being charged.

The outlets and housing feel pretty sturdy. Where the build quality could be improved is the base and the switches. The base has some measure of non-slip padding, but it’s still a bit slidy on a smooth surface. It would benefit from better grip plus a wider base to give it more overall stability. The on/off switches for the power outlets feel (and sound) rather cheap. They have a positive click to them, which is nice, but the feel is really “plasticy.” They work fine (at least so far) but the way they sound and feel don’t give me the warm fuzzies about a long life span.

The USB outlets output a total of 2.1A. That’s fine for a single item or perhaps two, but the charge speed drops way down if you have more than 2 items plugged in that have a high draw.

The only feature noted on the box is that it has overload protection, which appears to be some type of resettable breaker. As noted in the product guide:

"When power socket overloads, the protector -- a white or black pin -- will kick in by popping out automatically and cut off the power. When this happens, please unplug power socket, unplug the high power consumption device that connect to it, then reset the overload protector by pressing the overload protector button back."

I didn’t factor the potential omission of surge protection into my rating, but did factor in the build quality issues. Those bring my rating to 4 stars. Still, it’s a very useful and novel design that is a great way to have access to 8 outlets while using “wall warts” and not have it take up much floor or desk space. The multiple on/off switch options are also a big plus.

It does what it's sold to do very well. I've tested several types of ebooks (PDFs, epub, doc, txt), mp3 files of various quality, pics, and vids (avi, x264, and x265) - it read and ran everything well and smoothly.
Basically it's a low-end phone running an old distro of Android. It's super locked down and there's no internet access, so there's no updating and no adding of apps - this includes bluetooth tethering. That being said, a few of the apps are ones I've used for ages and (obv) I like them: specifically moon reader, the ebook reader - it really works well on this device. And I believe the video player is MX Player, also an old fav. Moving files via TF card was a bit of a pain, as the older version of android only supports up to 4GB at a time, but otherwise it moved everything without error. I tested the reader with several cards, from a generic 32gb to a samsung 512gb u3, and they all read well, so you can easily have a large library of media at hand. There's no cam or wifi; and there aren't any sensors, so it can't tell tilt, ambient light, etc. The screen is tiny but looks surprisingly good. The speaker is decently loud, but it def sounds like a phone speaker, still though, it's better than expected.
If you just want a simple media device with some neat features (FM works really well btw), this is great. I both would and wouldn't recommend this for kids - you can't add any educational apps (or games, lol), and they wouldn't be able to access things like their school portal or wiki; but if you only want your kid to have books, vids, and audio with a few tools (calc, calendar, alarm), this is right up your ally. Heads up though, they can swap out the TF card if they have a media collection you don't know about, and Moon Reader supports requiring passwords for opening the app.
If you want something you can do more with, I'd suggest foregoing the 50% off coupon and getting a burner phone at this device's list price. A burner probably won't work as smoothly (because it will have more hardware/software), but it'll have wifi and an app store and updates.
I plan to use this as an extra/backup media device. I'm one of those weird people that has a TF collection in my bag with tons of movies, tv, games, etc. I'm going to put one of those pockets on the back for credit cards, and use a TF card organizing card to hold my cards, so I'll have all my media together and with a device that can play them, in case my phone is AWOL or dead. IMO, after the coupon, it's worth the price as long as you know what you're getting.

This is my second purchase of a Sony Walkman. My first one was for my husband for our anniversary. I bought him an 8g player (NWZ-E438) and once I got that up and running, I realized that 8g really isn't that much when I realized that he has a whole bunch of cd's and videos and pictures. But the reason why I bought the 8g of that model was because it had an equalizer. Now, let's talk about this beautiful S545 model - WOW! It's 16g and what a beauty. the sound quality is A-Mazing, and the picture/video screen is clear and crisp. AND it has an equalizer - 5 settings, plus 2 custom settings = 7 equalizer settings. I bought mine at Walmart, and it was $119. I also got it in red - the red color is a nice color, not faded or pastelie. The sound quality from the exterior speakers will surprise you. Keep in mind that you will not be able to host a large dance party with it, but it is just perfect for a personal experience, let's say in your room or something like that. The sound from the speakers is quite nice, and I would compare it to the speaker from my Motorola RAZR2. My phone can get a lot louder than the Sony Walkman, but the quality of sound is just as good. I was not in any way disappointed with the quality. The only thing I would change on this player is the placement of the speakers - they are on the back, not the front. The picture of this player might fool you to think the speakers are in the front, but they are not. I also learned that this player will not be able to download podcasts. The higher-end Sony Walkmans do.

Another thing is that the software for the player comes loaded in the player, instead of including a cd in the box. It worked really great, it was simple and just way too easy to use. It was much easier to set up on the computer and get going than the one I bought for my husband. With the software, "Content Transfer" all you have to do is drag a song, or a picture or a video right to the Content Transfer window, and POW - it's there, and it knows right where to put it (music, pictures, video). So you don't even have to fuss around and click into the different files. I already have 1,926 songs in WMA format in 48Kbps, 38 videos, and 223 photos, and I have 10g left. Right out of the box, because of the software itself, there is 2g being used for the player, and you get 14g to play with.

This player will also record voice recordings and FM radio recordings (song, advertisement, talk show or whatever). It looks like they give you 99 hours and 59 minutes of recording time.

The FM player will only work if you have either your headset plugged in or your speakers plugged in. The FM won't work with the external speakers - it needs to use the wire as an antenna. And I didn't think the FM was bad - worked and sounded just fine to me.

So, if you are looking for a player, you just might want to consider this one.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

I have tested and reviewed many wireless doorbell systems. Typically I always advise to avoid any wireless cameras due to the inherent security vulnerabilities but this is often not possible with doorbell cameras. That being said there are key components I look for in wireless doorbell cameras: clear picture that provides a wide viewing angle, it either be hard wired or have excellent battery life, when chime button is pressed alert is sent and app can be opened and responsive in a quick time, 2 way audio communication is clear on both ends, motion sensitivity is adjustable and accurate.

I have thoroughly tested this product over the last 4 months and in comparison to the others on the market around this price point this product has proven to be clearly the best.

In terms of what is excellent - the internal battery is long lasting and dependable - I have found that it will last nearly 2 months on a single charge. The vast majority of wireless doorbells use proprietary batteries which forces users to purchase secondary batteries typically costing $30-$50. This factor is a huge bonus.

The camera is quite good. Images are clear and the wide angle provides a full view of the area in front of the doorbell. The AI Smart Human detection is without question the best I have found. This is a huge feature that helps prevent constant false alerts.

The base station holds up to a 128GB SD card for video storage. This is awesome for multiple reasons. If the camera was stolen the evidence will be saved on the base station within your home and all of your recordings are stored locally. This is an outstanding system.

Unfortunately, as with many similar products, while the hardware is good the software needs some work. As is typical, I can not find any way to force this doorbell to work with better software. It is obvious this was designed on the Tuya platform though I have not found any way of integrating it. I would much rather use the Tuya app where I have the bulk of my automation set but this will not migrate.

The lag from the time the doorbell button is pressed until you can see who is there is mediocre. The FASTEST I’ve been able to get this to work is 18 seconds - and I’m using an iPhone 13 Pro Max with 512GB on a super fast 1G mesh WiFi with a node located within feet of the doorbell inside the door.

The 2 way audio is spotty. It sounds like ordering through a drive through where every 3rd word is audible. Since I don’t use these to have in depth conversations it isn’t a huge deal but should be noted.

This is definitely among the best wireless doorbells I have tested for a while. It is not perfect, the sound leaves room for improvement as does response times but overall this is a quality unit.

While the vast majority of the doorbells I tested I advised to avoid all together this one is one worth using.

My mom ordered 2 of these thinking she'd be able to play music out of both of them at the same time from her iPhone. They come in the mail and we cannot figure out how to do this at all, and the instructions that came with them were unclear, as well as what we found online.
After a few hours of trial and error, this is what we figured out:
Pair both of the speakers to the iPhone
Make sure *one* of the speakers in connected (the other may not show anymore/doesn't have to be connected)
On the *connected* speaker, press the play and + buttons simultaneously (a sound will play)
On the other speaker, press the play and + buttons simultaneously (the same sound will play with some additional beeps)

Play music and they should work! This worked best for us when only one iPhone was connected/paired with the speakers at a time.

Hope this helps someone else!

This is a high quality camera, but you must take time to read through the owner's manual to understand how to get the best pictures. You can just grab it and point and shoot using it while in the "automode" setting, but the resulting pictures may leave you a little disappointed depending upon the photographic conditions. To get the highest quality photos you must become familiar with how this little beauty works. Unfortunately, you might have to print out and tote the manual with you when you find yourself in situations where your pictures aren't what you'd like, or you can't figure out how to do certain things like know what's behind the flashing icon error message, or how to simulate different types of film, or can you choose between clarity, reduced noise and dynamic range? This is not really a simple "point and shoot" camera and all images will turn out great. You will have to study it, practice with it, and most of all have patience and you will be pleasantly rewarded for your efforts. Though the indicators vary with camera settings, there are 23 different indicators just for shooting mode, and 12 for playback mode, not to mention the date/time stamp, battery level, and indicator. It can get confusing.

Although a basic manual booklet is included with the camera, a much more detailed manual must be uploaded from the enclosed CD and then all 125 pages can be printed out or read from your computer monitor. The manual covers all the material in the booklet almost page for page but includes much more information about features the booklet leaves out and the booklet will refer you to specific pages in the manual for more information. Also, in the manual are about 50 FAQ's that are very useful. I am a manual reader, (having written many technical SOP's) and appreciate having well-written and well thought out manuals that are understandable and succinct. Though I would have preferred a manual that I don't have to upload to my computer, it is well-written and many useful pictures are included.

This camera is loaded with many different options/features but accessing and understanding many of them will require reading the manual. For people who don't want to be bothered with all the bells and whistles this camera may be more than they need. I can see very serious photographers using this camera. Reading through the manual I have compiled a list of some of the various modes, options and features available:

Digital Zoom
Movie Mode
Silent Mode
Variable ISO settings
Image size selection
Aspect Ratio selection
Intelligent Face detection
Scene Position
Shooting Modes
EXR Mode
Film simulation
Dynamic Range
White Balance
Continuous Photography
Photometry - multi, spot, average

Playback Options:
Erase
Slide Show
Red-eye Removal
Image Rotation
Protection from accidental deletion
Crop
Resize
Voice Memo
Print Order
Time Difference
Format

Pages 37, 67-68, 86-87, 97-103, and 104-107 would be good to print out and keep with your camera as they contain tables of various camera functions and a trouble shooting chart.

I have taken many pictures and movies inside and out, light and dark, with this camera set on various settings. And though I have practiced with it now for several weeks, I still need to often refer to the manual when I choose to vary from automode. Some things I have found especially desirable are:

Silent Mode - I attend classical music concerts where flash photography is prohibited. This mode will silence all beeps and flashes.

Large viewing screen on the back of the camera. It is exactly 5.5cm x 4.0 cm.

Digital Zoom - extremely good. I attended a local minor-league baseball game and sat far away on the grass well beyond the playing field. I was able to fully zoom and still get good, clear, close-up shots of the players with no blurring.

Movie Mode - Completely surpasses any other I've experienced so far. Images are clear, colorful and the sound quality is excellent. Camera noise was heard and recorded while using the "zoom" function in Movie Mode though it was not very loud.

Multi-frame play back function is very useful to quickly scan for a particular picture.

Fine Pix Viewer Program was very easy to install on my computer. I use Windows XP.

Very good photography in low-light conditions.

Also some things I did not find particularly desirable but are not major flaws:

I cannot directly burn a CD using the Fine Pix Viewer Program which comes with this camera. I have to use another camera program, import the pictures into it and then burn a CD.

Very easy to accidentally turn it on or off and easy to get misfires.

The zoom lever is too sensitive. I have learned with practice to barely move it very slowly.

The camera does not give helpful suggestions on how to get a better picture as does my HP R717.

Not HD capable.

The higher the ISO the grainier the picture though a higher ISO is desirable when shooting in dim/low light levels. I have set the ISO level to 200 and that seems to produce the best pictures so far.

Almost too many options, modes and functions to choose from. Though you can immediately begin to take pictures using Automode, it will take time to fully understand the many other aspects and features this camera has.

In Summary:

I can find no major complaint concerning this camera. It takes excellent clear and colorful photos even in situations where I least expect it - indoors with no flash. Any poor quality pictures I have taken are not the fault of the camera but due to the photographer's ignorance of how to use/understand properly the many features of the camera. The basic mechanics of such things as battery and memory card installation are very easy. Battery charging is a very simple process and battery life seems long. The manual is detailed and covers more than I would probably care to know. This is almost more camera than I need, though I will continue to use it and will update this review as necessary.

UPDATE 2.9.15 - Been using this camera all these years and now it's beginning to show it's age and giving me some problems. The viewing screen on the back has a vertical big black bar but it doesn't appear on the actual pictures. And the lens cover doesn't always completely open when the camera is turned on. I still use it but it might be time to think about a replacement. It's been good though so I really don't have any complaints.
