There is always a run on headphones in our house. Not only are they being lost or dying, but everyone is on a constant quest for the best design and sound they can find in a bluetooth headphone. Let's see how these measure up.

WHAT ARE THESE HEADPHONES LIKE?
These headphones have a long sturdy neck band which means they will fit a variety of neck sizes. Each ear piece has a magnet on it so that when you are not using them, they will close in front of you so you won't lose them. The controls are at the end of the neck band on the right side.

ON/OFF BUTTON
Play, pause, on/off, pair can be done with this button.

VOLUME
The minus and plus of volume control is also used for skipping songs- + skip forward, - skip backward.

ANC
There is an ANC button on the right side directly behind the negative volume button which makes it easy to press them both at the same time. It does do noise canceling, but it is frustrating because it is easy to press the ANC button by mistake when also pressing the middle button.

CHARGING PORT
Charging port is on the edge of the control button area.

AI INDICATOR VOICE
The automatic voice is very dysfunctional. It only says part of words, and seems to be a bit mean sounding which makes my daughter say it feels creepy.

NOISE CANCELING
The noise canceling works beautifully on these headphones.

SOUND QUALITY
The sound quality is awesome. Highs and mids are where they should be. Bass is very good. It is not overdone but it is in balance and does not distract from the music. There are not any breakups in sound unless you walk away from the device.

BLUETOOTH RANGE
The bluetooth range seems to be good up to about 35 feet or so.

PHONE CALL QUALITY
The calls go through very well and people can hear just fine on phone calls.

BATTERY PERCENTAGE
There is no physical light indicator to tell you how much battery power you have left.

THE BOTTOM LINE
If you want a good solid set of headphones to use with phone and music that work well, are in balance, and great for listening. The controls are not as convenient as they could be, which can be frustrating at times.

MY RATING
Four stars. If the control area was set up just a little more conveniently so that you can not accidentally press the wrong buttons all of the time, they would probably be five stars.

I really love the Moshi iVisor "black border" screen protectors. Because the screen protector is stiff, you can pick it up easily for do-overs until you're completely satisfied with the positioning.

As other reviewers have noted, this crystal-clear MOSHI IVISOR SCREEN PROTECTOR FOR KINDLE VOYAGE is highly reflective. I don't like matte-finish screen protectors at all, so I don't mind this. When I'm reading under a lamp or light source that causes mirror-like reflections, I simply adjust the angle at which I'm holding the Voyage. (In truth, you don't really need a screen protector for a Kindle Voyage or Paperwhite, if you have a simple case that protects it from scratches, such as the [[ASIN:B00MVUR3DY OMOTON Kindle Voyage Smart Case Cover]], or the [[ASIN:B00IU7CLD4 Incipio Top Folio Cover for Kindle Voyage]]).

My biggest concern when I installed this screen protector, was whether the stiff plastic would interfere with the Voyage's haptic page-turn feature. (A feature that you don't know you need until you experience it.) Happily, it does NOT. The Voyage's haptic page-turn continues to work perfectly after the protector goes on.

This screen protector took me about 10 minutes to install, including several repositioning do-overs. If you want to remove the protector for any reason, it leaves no residue behind. A microfiber cloth for cleaning the screen prior to applying the screen protector is included in the package.

THE GOOD:
--------------
* Aesthetically, a very cool looking laptop. Looks menacing, looks high tech. Makes me think of Alienware.
* Ram is not soldered, and is upgradeable.
* SSD drives are upgradeable too.
* Windows 11 Home out the box.
* Comes with 3 months of Ultimate Game Pass from Xbox/Microsoft. Doesn't say this anywhere in the listing, so it was a pleasant surprise for my kid. You find this out during the process of setting up the laptop.
* Advertised for gaming, but hardcore gamers will find it a little light. But for a child using it as a school laptop, this is perfect. Much better than the Chromebooks, and for Roblox and Minecraft, which is all my kid does, this is more than enough.
* Nevertheless, if you want to boost the ram and ssd, you'll need to know how to remove the bottom cover. Search YT for, "Lenovo IdeaPad Gaming 3i (15", 2022) - disassembly and upgrade options." Click on the very top search result. The video is by LaptopMedia. They disassemble several similar models, but this is the term you want to search to get to the exact model. However, keep in mind that he's disassembling the intel version which uses DDR4 ram, you'll be using DDR5 for this Ryzen model.

THE BAD:
------------
* Screen is only 1080P.
* Ram is only 8GB, but again, you can upgrade this.
* If truly using for gaming, you'll need more than 256GB. My son will mainly use it for school, so this won't be an issue.
* No touchscreen.
* Regarding power supply... Not necessarily a bad, but a tip. If you have children, then you know when they take their tablets and notebooks to relatives or friend's house, the power supply goes too. Instead of constantly unplugging the one that is supposed to be stationary at their table, I always buy a second power supply. For this model, it's a 170W with the Lenovo rectangle usb head. You can buy any 3rd party, just make sure it's 170W with the rectangle head.

Despite listing some items in the bad list, I understand it's par for the course in terms of the price you're paying. If you want all of those features included, your price would go up. My kid loves it, we'll go 4-Stars overall for now.

Any wire should be inserted parallel and adjacent to the grounding rod itself through the two holes of the clamp mechanism. The wire should also be inserted through the two holes in the clamp opposite the screw side, This allows the tightening screw to put presure on the rod directly rather than having it try to clamp down the wire against the rod.

I was looking for some replacement headphones for two sets in my family when I had the opportunity to try out some of the new Carlos Santana line of headphones. Let's see what happened.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These headphones come in a great box which will appeal to fans of Carlose. It is well decorated and presentation is done so well, it would make a great gift. These are the black ones, and there is also another set available in white under a different listing.

ARE THESE REAL LEATHER?
According to the case,t these are leather padded ear cups and the lower half of the headband. I am still not sure about this. It is possibly bonded leather. Bonded leather is made from leather scraps chopped up and blended with binders. Sheets made of this mixture are printed with leather look imprinting. Technically it can be called leather, but it really is not leather as I define it..

EAR CUSHIONS AND HEADBAND
These black headphones are comfortable. I can wear these headphones longer than many others I have used. My daughter who ended up with these, uses them constantly and raves about them. These can be worn for several hours without a problem. She has sweaty ears and these are not nearly as frustrating for her as many others.

CORD FOR CORDED LISTENING
This comes with a cord which is only 38 inches long. That is a bit short for me. I find it is annoying and not quite as long as I would prefer, but my daughter does not use it so I guess it is not a problem for her or if you are like her, you won't mind either.

HOW DO THESE SOUND?
We are all surprised at how really good these sound. The bass is well defined and clear/strong, and the mids and highs are definitely clear and not muddy. The bass is not overwhelming either, which is a problem with some headphones.

HEADPHONE CONTROLS
The controls can be a bit difficult to read, but once you know where they are, you can figure it out pretty quickly. The +/- and play/pause buttons are separated by the noise cancellation button which is good.

HOW ARE THESE ADJUSTABLE?
These adapt to all sorts of comfortable positions.. They go longer, tilt in and out and rotate from side to side.

ARE THESE ABLE TO FOLD TO BE COMPACT?
These do fold flat and compact if you need to travel with them or store them in a smaller storage area.

CASE?
This did not come with a case.

SOUND CANCELLATION PERFORMANCE
The noise cancellation is awful. It hardly works. When noise cancellation is turned on, the sound gets pretty compromised. It becomes almost muffled in a way and the base definitely goes down.

OTHER FEATURES WITH THESE HEADPHONES
The ability to know how much power is left on the headphones while using the phone is nice, but it does not help if you are using these some other bluetooth device and not a phone. During phone calls, people hear just fine and we can hear them too (several of us tried this feature with our phones)

THE BOTTOM LINE
At this price point, these headphones are a step up from what I usually get when getting headphones for this price range. The sound is well defined and well balanced. Compactness for storage is great, and the comfort is also very good. The only disappointments are noise cancellation, short cord for corded listening, and buttons being a bit difficult to read.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. With better performance from noise cancellation, these would be really really good. As they are, they are still pretty great. They are a great gift to yourself or someone else and are some of the nicer headphones I have used in my journey through headphones of all sorts as well as those the family has obtained. They are not B&O or Turtle Beach, but they still are pretty good.

This Cat6A nylon braided cable is designed to be thin, but don’t let that fool you into thinking that it lacks capacity - within the thin flat nylon braided package contains aluminium foil shield, 4 shielded twisted pair (STP) of copper wires, with upgraded PVC protection for super fast transfer speeds.

The connector bases are reinforced at each end of the wire which really help hold all of the wires in place even if you have to bend and twist it to fit it within the plug. The plugs have a protective rubber boot guard that protects the clip on the plug - this becomes very important when snaking the cable through walls and tight spaces. Prior to doing this I wrap the boot and plug with a small piece of electrical tape to make sure I don’t unintentionally snag anything.

I love the nylon braided shielding on this cable - not only is it durable and will help the cable withstand damage but it just looks great.

Instead of using old discs, I downloaded the most current drivers for my (wired) Samsung CLP printer, (wireless) Canon Pixma IX 6800 printer, and (wired) Fujitsu ScanSnap S1300i scanner. So easy and smooth, no issues. They all worked like happy family members who could all finally be in one home now (not enough USB ports on previous machines for them all).

My first experience with Windows 10. Blech. Lots of deleting, uninstalling, and Cortana was exorcised before the immediately offered Windows update was at 2%. Mine turned on with version 10586 of Windows. It offered an update to the most current (15063) which would take up a gulp-inducing measly 40 plus GB. Sigh. They do this right at the beginning so that you're rendered more accepting and ambivalent by the amazing display.

It is gorgeous. Enormous. Sharp. Extremely bright. As others have discussed, changing brightness is annoying as it is not available through settings or as a hard button. You have to access it by opening Lenovo Nerve Center -> Display Settings. I'm not sure if a keyboard dedicated button would work, my keyboard's volume buttons work but it doesn't have display buttons. You can uncover a keyboard shortcut eventually in the Nerve Center: Alt + I increases brightness and Alt + D decreases. At the lowest setting it is comfortable even for my tired, dry, sensitive eyes, in the dark.

It is as fast and peppy as I had hoped. I can multitask writing emails, viewing huge digital radiographs ("xrays"), downloading/uploading photos or video, watching movies, and transferring gigs and gigs of files all at the same time elegantly. The radiographs look better on my screen then they do at work on the actual radiology viewing screen, and instead of crouching and angling myself to examine them I can smoothly and with the touch of a single finger, tilt this screen to the best angle.

Photo editing is amazing but I sadly couldn't bring my Adobe PS CS3 with me.

This machine is very quiet, although, on the second day I started to notice the fan running. It is a unique sound in my opinion compared to all the other towers and laptops I've ever experience. The best way I can describe it is, it sounds like you are hearing through closed windows, your neighbor down the street running a generator. I hope this is normal and not a sign of bad things. It's quiet but noticeable when its on.

The sound... I am by no means a sound system snob (except when it comes to my vehicles). This computer's sound is lacking. It's OK for movies and background sounds, it just resembles an inexpensive bluetooth speaker. The enhanced setting is a bit murky and the normal is fuzzy/dull. I haven't discovered if you can customize anything yet. I don't particularly care, just the price of this device made me hope for better. The sound in my car (2006 Volvo S60R with factory dolby surround sound 11-speaker using just a grom AUX input to listen to mp3s on my phone) sounds WAY better, but I do realize this computer is trying to put out "surround" sound from a single plane of speakers.

Although it's still the honeymoon I'm really hoping I continue to enjoy this computer and stay satisfied with having chosen an AIO. With the power, speed, and storage I am hoping to get many many many years out of it (with the cost, many many many many many years). I can't imagine ever wanting anything with a bigger screen or "better" picture. This thing is massive and I wasn't coming from a shrimp, my laptop was 17.3". My extra wide full size keyboard looks normal to small beneath this monster.

I did not purchase a secondary warranty at this time due to universally terrible reviews and jaded mistrust.

If you like fully featured smart watches, it is hard to find anything this watch can't do! It runs Google's Wear OS, which is their watch variation of Android, so Google users should feel right at home with it. It's got a Play Store for apps, a really fluid interface, and of course it integrates really well with an Android Smartphone. I've been told it doesn't play as nicely with iPhones, but a lot of the core features are standardized and cross platform so it can still function as a really nice watch and allow notifications and call support regardless of device.
My wife had a Fossil Wear OS watch previously, and the feature set is very similar except for one huge plus this has: A SPEAKER! Many of the third party entry level Wear OS watches have a microphone for digital assistant commands and voice-to-text typing, but lack a speaker for it to talk back. So you have to read your responses on the screen and you can't exactly take phone calls. But THIS ONE DOES! Thanks to the speaker, you can full on take calls like a modern day Dick Tracy. That's really useful and cool, especially if you put your phone down or have it in a pocket you don't want to pull it out of all the time.
But here's the big con:
BATTERY LIFE. While this is better than other wear OS watches I've tried, it seems like Wear OS is so feature-filled, they generally need to be charged as often as smartphones do. Battery obviously depends on usage, but average use seems to last about a day or two at a time. Heavy usage and you'll need to top it off every night at least. This isn't the fault of this watch, but rather Wear OS in general. Other smart watches such as the Samsungs and FitBits can go for days to nearly a week on a charge, which means you not only won't have to worry about charging it more than once or twice a week, but you also can do sleep tracking and just leave it on at night. That's something I'm trying to do in order to have healthier sleeping habits. Some devices such as the Mi Band and Amazefit can go for around 20 days on a charge! I was using a Mi Band 3 before trying this watch, and while it doesn't run apps or have a full color screen or take phone calls, I think I prefer having a watch that only needs to be charged about once a month, and can show me my sleeping data as well as pedometer and activity charts, all while alerting me to notifications. I feel like Wear OS has a ways to go before I'm ready to switch over full time. The good news is that devices ARE getting better, as this shows. If you love Wear OS and the smartest features available, this is a good option. But personally I think I'm going back to my "smartwatch lite" that has less bells and whistles but actually fits better functionally into my life.

I ordered this bag and had the opportunity to compare it side by side with the Blackhawk Tactical Briefcase. It is clear from examining them that both are constructed from the same basic set of patterns, probably in the same Chinese factory. They are nearly identical. There are minor differences, most notably that the Blackhawk bag is completely lined with a thick waterproof material. The BBP bag is lined with a lightweight orange nylon fabric, making it lighter, and more flexible - the Blackhawk bag is more ridgid, owing to the waterproofing material and some additional stiff padding in the computer storage compartment. Both bags have comparable pockets, with a combination of zipper and velcro closures. The buckles on the Blackhawk bag are more heavy-duty, and I think they will last longer. The Blackhawk bag has two large velcro areas, on on the exterior flap and one inside, for attaching hook-and-loop patches, ID, insignia, etc. The BBP bag does not have these, instead opting for an extra pocket.

The most significant difference other than the water proofing is the strap - the BBP bag is convertible into a backpack (of sorts), but the versatility sacrifices excellence as either a shoulder bag or backpack. The strap is inadequately padded for one-shoulder carry, and the strap rigging is awkward. By contrast, the Blackhawk bag cannot be carried as a backpack, but it comes with a very robust and nicely padded, grippy shoulder strap. The Blackhawk bag also has a sturdy rubberized cover over the carry handle, which provides a more secure grip than the unsheathed nylon handle of the BBP bag.

Overall, both are versatile bags and would probably suit your needs, but the awkward strap configuration of the BBP bag led me to choose the Blackhawk instead.

There are many, many true wireless earbuds out there. What attracted me to these were the features that they boasted: Wireless Charging, Active Noise-Cancelling, and bluetooth 5.1. So how does these earbuds compare to some of the cheaper offerings and does it justify being twice as expensive as some of them?

In terms of price, these earbuds can be considered cheap. Comparable to the mid-tier brands out there such as Anker and MPow, and much, much cheaper than Bose and Jabra brands. Still, there are many that cost half the price.

With the pricing in mind, let's look at the good of these earbuds:
+ Long battery life -- I'm on my fourth hour of listening to an audiobook and the battery is still showing 50% on my phone.
+ Battery status reporting to phone -- I'm sure most of the recent bluetooth headphones and earbuds do this now, but it is still nice.
+ Type-C port for charging -- The move to type-c as the standard charging port for all devices is happening and I'm glad NANNIO didn't cheap out and use a micro-usb. One less cable to worry about.
+ No app necessary -- The passthrough and ANC features can be turned on by tapping the touch controls twice.
+ Google Assistant Support -- Tap three times and Google Assistant launches.
+ No ugly microphone stick -- The tear-drop shape of these buds look much better than the ugly sticks that Apple's products have, in my opinion.
+ Smooth transition between left-only, right-only, and stereo -- These earbuds allow one to choose to use only one earbud while keeping the other in the charger without having to pair the other piece separately. It's something that I take advantage of on long drives. I keep one bud in the ear to listen to my audiobook and switch out when the battery runs out.

The bad:
- Not low profile -- The Anker SoundCores is pretty inconspicuous in the ear, but these NANNIOs, being white and sticking out more are anything but low profile.
- ANC not very effective -- The ANC levels are adjusted to be pretty minimal on these buds so while it is possible to hear the difference between the feature being on and off, it is also noticeable that only the lowest hums are cancelled out. Earbuds simply aren't good for ANC. Buds simply don't fit perfectly in the ear canal and when the jaw moves, the fit shifts. By this fact, there is always sound leaking through, reducing the efficiency of any ANC system. In earbuds, ANC is really just a gimmick.
- Passthrough needs to have wind noise reduction -- The reason for passthrough, in my mind, is to be able to hear surrounding sounds if wearing earbuds while running. It uses the microphone on the earbuds to pass external sounds through, but when running, there will always be wind noise. Without wind noise reduction, it makes this feature useless. I don't know of any earbuds that have addressed this issue.

So why did I still give these buds 5-stars? Because it is priced perfectly for what it is and what it promises. It has more features and quality that makes it better than the lower $30 dollar earbuds, but isn't a brand that can demand over $100. When I selected the Philips AS140/Fidelio Docking System for the Android, I really did not have any expectations only the hope that it would be easy to set up and do what I wanted it to do....play music and maybe wake me up. I definitely did not want something too complicated or difficult to operate. And to be honest, the Philips has just the right amount of technology and features for me because there are times when I am technically challenged. Simply stated, the directions for electronics need to be easy to read and understand. And who could ask for more than easy to follow directions will illustrations (even in Spanish if you need them)? And while I probably have not untapped all of its possibilities, I think I have a decent understanding of its basic features.

Setting up the Philips was easy enough. You simply go to the Android Market and install Songbird on your phone and PC (this allows you to download music and access it). In general, I consider the Philips Docking Station to be a super tuner (I am sure that there is a better word for it...but again, I am a girl), which allows you to access local and internet radio stations as well as podcast). You even have an option for an alarm clock and timer. When you attach your android phone (I have the LG G2x and it fits perfectly with or without the case), you can use the blue tooth feature as sort of a remote control. The phone doesn't even have to be attached to the docking station for you to surf radio stations or podcast. I was even able to access "Pandora" (a station that I access on my telephone) and listen to my favorite music selections. And remember, you aren't limited to just the radio, or other programs, but you can download music (from Songbird) to your PC and access it from your phone.

The positive things about the product:
(1) Easy set up. Download program, and you are in business!
(2) Decent sound quality. The sound is clear. It seems a little heavy at times on the bass, but maybe that is simply because I need to play with the features a little more and learn how to address it.
(3) The time automatically syncs between your cell phone and the station so you don't have to really worry about it.
(4) Your phone charges while docked.
(5) The blue tooth technology allows you to use your phone as a remote...changing the stations easily.
(6) There is a timer and alarm feature/option.
(7) Downloading music is simple.
(8) It's cute and doesn't take up a whole lot of space on your nightstand or dresser. And if you don't want to necessarily use it as an alarm clock, you could even use it in your kitchen. It's probably better than one of those under the cabinet radios.

Overall, I like the Philips AS140/37, it has some pretty neat features that a girl who isn't necessarily technologically savvy can enjoy. It's easy to set up and use. I give this system a solid 4.

My favorite use for it, though, is turned so the longest part of the bottom lip is tucked up under my bed bolster and the edge of the tray is resting against the bolster. This provides a very stable, sturdy, little bed table that can hold a phone or tablet upright in the top slot (cables can go through the bottom if needed) and an Apple TV remote plus a drinking glass and a big bowl of popcorn.

NOTE: I am writing this review for the 1TB platter-based Passport drive.

I have a 250GB Passport I bought several years ago and it has served me well, though it has gotten close to full over time (I never imagined at the time that I would fill that thing up). I have had good fortune with it so I expected the same from this 1TB version, and so far I have been right. In addition to the larger capacity, it is very definitely a speed upgrade from my old Passport.

This is a small drive in terms of physical footprint, approximately 4”x3”x0.5” in dimension. That’s a double-edged sword. On one hand, it is small enough to stuff in a shirt pocket which makes it an excellent on-the-go storage solution that’s almost as convenient as a thumb drive. But, that also means it is easy to misplace or lose (or have stolen if left unattended).

It comes with software that allows you to password-protect the drive which is a nice deterrent in the event that the drive is taken. It’s certainly not foolproof, but it’s sufficient to keep the large majority of unauthorized access out. To be honest, since the drive does not leave my home I have not used the software at all.

When you plug in the drive to a Windows or Linux system, the OS immediately recognizes the drive and it is available immediately for use. In the case of Windows, you can immediately explore the drive and read from it and write to it. For Linux, it depends on how you have configured automount and which desktop management software you use, but the kernel does register the presence of the drive and you can display the partition table.

This is a USB 3.0 drive, making it a huge speed upgrade from my older 2.0-based Passport. This is a great solution for storing all of your pictures, movies, important documents, and as in my case large downloads and purchased software packages. With 1TB of space, I don’t think I am going to run out of space anytime soon.

As a bonus, this is a very quiet drive.

I put this drive on a USB power meter to see how much it draws from the USB port. At rest it pulls 0.17A. When actively reading, it peaks just under 0.6A which is surprisingly low. My concern was that this would add some strain on the USB port over a longer period of time but this seems to be an unjustified concern. That said, I am more likely to connect it to a USB hub instead of directly to a USB port.

So far I have no complaints with this drive. It’s a big step up for me from my older Passport, being larger, faster and more quiet. It’s not cost prohibitive either which is just a bonus. If you need a decent backup drive with large capacity and a small footprint, this one is worth consideration.

I have a Foscam WiFi security camera in a steel pole barn. Even with a high gain antenna on the camera and a fiberglass door, my connection was pretty bad. Choppy video and lost connections were common. I needed to get the antenna outside.

Although this antenna isn't outdoor rated, it is pretty easy to make watertight. Some tape over the mounting screw holes on the back and a little self vulcanizing rubber electrical tape around the antenna joint and no water is going to get in. You could use something like RTV silicone too. Keep the moisture out and you now made it outdoor capable. It was pretty close the way it comes and I'm sure it would probably be fine for a long time, but sealing it completely is pretty easy. The magnet mount works great on the steel siding. The camera I have, like most, comes with a standard SMA connector vs.the SMA-RP (reversed pin), but you can get an adapter here on Amazon. [[ASIN:B005H488Y4 SMA Male to SMA-RP Female Adapter]]

Added a 20 foot cable with standard SMA male and female connectors and now I have a great outdoor antenna for an indoor camera in a steel building that is great for blocking radio signals. It works very well and the results exceeded my expectations.

Just a head's up, for the less-tech savvy:

This is NOT a wifi signal amplifier, as such. You WILL be creating a NEW wireless access point (aka wifi log-on)...even if you install this in "repeater" mode--vs. the wired-to-wireless AP (access point) mode.

So, for example, instead of logging into whatever your network is called, when you need to use the wifi that this repeats for you, you'll be logging into a new connection. They call it, by default, "My Repeater" (I assume that is so you'll never forget who actually owns it), but you can rename it to anything you want (mine is henceforth known as Fluffy Gigglebuns). You'll still use the same password as you use for your main connection, though...and therein lies the genius of it. You can make your guests feel special (or, in my case, humiliated) by personalizing the repeater network name, but the password will be the same as it is for whatever network AP you are having it repeat.

Lastly, this does offer an extra feature I think is worth mentioning:

You can also use this as a wireless adapter to connect a multimedia or other tech device that requires or ONLY allows internet connectivity via an ethernet (aka wired) connection.

So if you have something like an older roku, or game console, etc. that can only connect to the internet via an ethernet cable, you can apparently use THIS device to quickly convert it to use your wifi connection.

To let you know where I am coming from on this review, I have two sons, 9 and 4. We do a lot of camping without mom, but want to share our adventures. So far, our trips have destroyed a Canon Powershot 450 (overly hydrated while canoeing) and a Powershot 980IS (smashed into ground during a fall.) So the idea of a waterproof, shockproof and hopefully kid-proof camera sounded perfect.

Purpose for camera: Rugged camera to take along canoeing, fishing, camping, and hiking for snapshots and quick, shareable movies.

I have never owned a camera in this class, and the one thing I am trying to keep in mind is the price point. This is not intended to be a high-end performance device, but more a rugged snapshot camera. I was a little suspect on 1080P on a hand held device under $175 (still am,) but the 5 MP camera is adequate for photos to email to grandparents and to show off our catches and camps to mom.

Design -

The camera is very nicely designed. It is physically attractive and comfortable in the hand. The winged doors lock into place well in their watertight positions and are, well kind of cool. The screen is adequate for playback and we spend a lot of time watching what we filmed over and over. The controls are spare, but easy to understand and operate. The four major flaws I found are; the embedded battery, lack of a flash, lack of lens cover, and no headphone jack for previewing sound.

Battery-

It is unfortunate that the design team decided to go with an internal non-removable battery. This seems to move the device into the "disposable" class since it is useless once the battery dies. I suspect that the battery can be replaced fairly easily, judging by the hex screws in the camera body, but there is a big difference between slipping a battery in and out and sending the camera out for replacement. Also, I can make a huge argument for being able to carry a back up battery. At least for now though, the battery seems to have a decent charge. We have filmed and played back films for at least two hours between recharges and have never seen the battery near empty.

Performance -

Image capture: 1080p is a lot to ask from such a small sensor. For that matter, so is 720p. So I am satisfied with the images I am getting, not great but what I would expect. I usually shoot Canon DSLR's (except when camping with kids) so I am at times frustrated by the lack of manual controls of any kind. Autofocus, autoexposure... with no way to change anything beyond file format and resolution. The images and video I am getting are a little noisy and especially so in low light. Blurring from camera or subject motion is common on stills. This is where the flash option would be nice. But in daylight, or decently lit interior shots the images are definitely passable. Again, judging this camera on its price point and function, it really is decent. If I want good stills, I'll go with a Canon 50D, if I want a snapshot of my kid pulling a bass into the canoe, this is perfect.

I am uploading a video with more details on picture and movie quality.

Sound: For a single source mike on the camera, it does pretty good. Definitely picks up footsteps or breathing, so don't film while walking up hill. Truly emphasizes if you are out of shape. Picks up ambient sound well and in tests in a light breeze, did fine.

Interface: I had the interface lock up on me once and I was unable to get it to power off or get out of a locked state. I had to use the small reset button to get it to reboot and clear the freeze. So I have thrown a very small paper clip in its case. Without being able to pull the battery, the reset button seems to have been the only option. Otherwise the device is very fast loading up, and the interface is intuitive and easy to use. Although occasionally when browsing I end up in fast forward or reverse when watching a movie and it takes a little to get it back to play or browse.

Summary:

All in all, I am really happy with this camera. It is full of limitations which you should understand before purchase. For the price, it is a decent camera and it fits our intended purpose to a Tee. My kids love the ability to take a movie, then watch it immediately. I like the feeling that it might survive the kids for a while. I feel like I'm being pretty critical of the camera, and I guess I am. But I'm giving it four stars because it does what I want it to, and after using it for a couple weeks, I really like it. Just don't expect the world from a inexpensive camera.

The TROND Flat Plug Power Strip Surge Protector is a great concept. Everything about it shows that some thought has been given to its design. Unfortunately, their choice of materials weren't as well thought out.

Some design concepts that attracted me to this surge protector is that it gives you 8 power plugs in a surface area that's just under 4 x 4 inches. The four plugs at the top are grounded while the 4 on the side are two-prongs. In addition, the wall plug is flat, giving you a lot of options as to where you can plug this product in. Finally, there are three USB-A ports and one USB-C port.

However, as I've mentioned, some design choices are questionable. As with many surge protectors, the USB ports are under-powered. The Type-A ports are not too bad at 5V/2.4A, but there is no quick charge capability. The Type-C is not PD, so your charging options are no better than the Type-A ports. You're stuck with 5V/3A with a total wattage shared between them at 14W or 3.4A.

My second gripe is with the build material. Compared to many power strips, the plastic covering this product feels quite cheap. It has a smooth texture and just feels... thin to the touch. The same plastic also covers the wall plug. In addition, the power wire is thinner than other power strips that you'll find. They feel more like the two-prong extension cords, except that it has three wires.

Now, I don't have proof that their choice of materials will be an issue at all, but it does give me pause.

[[VIDEOID:9c7f474d82697dfd8035b3c7cf95ccc5]] I am a longtime graphics tablet user, having started with a Bamboo small. Since then I have had several tablets including a Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch, am Intuos4 and finally an Intuos5 Medium. All of the tablets I have used have been Wacom tablets; this is my first experience with another brand, and it is the first time I have even heard of Huion as a brand. To me it makes sense to compare this tablet with my Intuos5, with which it actually compares quite well for about 20% of the cost.

My test system for testing this graphics tablet is a Dell laptop, with an Intel i7 processor and 16G RAM, running Windows 10 and Corel Painter X3.

Comparing this tablet to the Intuos5 it is approximately the same size (both are medium tablets). They both look very similar at a glance and there are some distinct similarities in the pen and pen holder as well. In operation they are both similar but there are some very distinct differences, and each one has advantages over the other.

One of the differences between these two tablets is that the Huion tablet has a numbered gauge across the top of the writing surface and includes a replacement surface in the box; the Wacom does not. The gauge is not a big deal but it does make a nice measure if you are looking for consistency in length of lines. The replacement surface is another matter – it is easy to damage the surface and over time it does get scuffed, so being able to apply a new surface is a huge plus to me.

The pens are different and there is give and take with them. The Wacom pen is sealed and does not need batteries or recharging. It is also reversible and both ends can be configured for drawing. Typically one end it set up as an eraser. The Huion pen is rechargeable and is not reversible. I prefer the Wacom pen, but I like the feel of the Huion pen and it works well.

The pens both come with a stand, extra nibs and a nib extractor. The Wacom stand is slightly heavier, but otherwise they are functionally equivalent.

The software is obviously different, and I have been experimenting with the Huion software to learn how to configure the buttons. The Wacom software is a little more intuitive, btu I have found the Huion software to be a bit more versatile and it provides better control. Speaking of buttons, the buttons are a little different between these two tablets with the Wacom providing fewer buttons but providing a scroll wheel.

Both tablets have 2048 pressure levels, and the only real way to test the pressure levels and drawing capabilities of each is to use a drawing application and start experimenting. The Targus VuScape Protective cover and stand is a pretty good, helpful aid for those who own an Apple Ipad2. It features a thin, lightweight design that is meant to hold the iPad2 snugly in place while you work.

Having a stand for your iPad is certainly a good idea and I like that this stand can be used to position your iPad in different ways. There are multiple grooves so that you can display your iPad at different angles. The cover can also be folded back completely, allowing the consumer to hold the iPad in the hands without the stand.

This protective cover/stand does have some nice features to offer, but after using it for a while, it is more than apparent that the stand is not perfect. Probably the greatest issue is that the stand isn't as sturdy as I would prefer. If you use the stand on a solid, flat surface, you shouldn't have too many problems, but place it on other surfaces and it tends to bend just a little bit. The slightest bend will cause the grooves to give way just a little, and the iPad will no longer be securely held in place.

I generally like the thin, lightweight design of this stand, but the thinness possibly goes a tad far. If the manufacturer had made this stand just a little bit thicker, it would be stronger and more likely to hold the iPad in place without any problems. I suppose this is the trade- off one must make when selecting a stand such as this. Lightweight is nice, especially for something like an iPad, but lightweight means the stand is lacking in strength.

All in all, this is a good stand and certainly worth considering, but not a deluxe stand like I expected. Again, as long as you are willing to sacrifice sturdiness for lightweight design, you should be fine. And try to use only on the flattest surfaces for the best results. Follow these guidelines and you should find yourself reasonably happy with this protective cover and stand from Targus.

Super thin, huge 17" touch screen with colors that just POP, large touchpad mouse, and silent chiclet keyboard. These are just the initial impressions one would see at first blush when approaching this high-quality laptop. Look a little deeper and one would find that this Dell XPS 17 sports a powerful 11th generation I7-11800H cpu with a dedicated RTX 3050 graphics card with Nvidia's real-time ray tracing and 16gb of ram. A 512GB ssd rounds out the entire package.

The Dell XPS 17 is simply elegant and high-quality. I was able to upgrade this laptop to Windows 11 painlessly and the new UI just looks great on this screen. It runs silently during normal web browsing and video watching. When playing games, the fan kicks in and the cooling seems adequate, but I still have an external laptop cooler helping it along.

Speaking of games, this laptop will run the latest games, but being at the bottom of the RTX line of graphics cards, the screen's 3840x2400 resolution simply is too much for the 3050 to run at the highest quality. It means that one would either run at a lower resolution or lower quality. The resolution issue can be alleviated if one turns on DLSS for resolution scaling.

So that is one of the first problems I would point out with the specs that I have in this laptop. The RTX3050 paired with the super high resolution means one must compromise in some way. In addition, performance in VR is somewhat poor. Half Life: Alyx runs well at low quality settings but any higher and the screen stutters and can cause nausea -- this was tested through wired and wireless configurations.

The second complaint that I have for this laptop is that the only included ports are 4 usb Type-C ports, headphone jack and an SD card reader. It is great that the ports support up to Thunderbolt 3, but the fact that no Type-A ports are available, dongles will be a part of life. It's nice that Dell includes a dongle that sports an HDMI and a Type-A port, there is no ethernet or display port support out of the box.

A good 9-in-1 dongle will cost you at least $60 and even then, the quality could be questionable. I happened to have a 9-in-1 dongle, but the ethernet port seems to lose connection constantly. This means that either you take a chance with a $60 no-name dongle or you spend over $100 for a proven one.

This then brings me to the last problem that I want to point out. A gaming PC has very high power requirements. Currently, there is no Type-C product that will provide (or pass through) the 130W that the Dell XPS 17 will require. It means that the nifty dock that you bought to get the additional ports that you need? It won't be able to power the laptop. You can connect a 100W charger to the laptop, but you will get a warning from the operating system. So perhaps on travel, one can get away with trickle charging the laptop, but at home, you will always be stuck with taking up two ports, one for power and one for your monitor.

Overall, this is a GREAT laptop with high quality build, but at the current specs, some things just cause awkward situations that one needs to work around.

I bought a ZuneHD 32GB as a replacement for my iPod Video. I still have the iPod but I don't particularly care for it (never really did) so I decided to search for a better MP3 player. After digging online for a while I decided on the ZuneHD which has proven to be far and away better. It is not a perfect device but it's excellent for my needs.

Looking a lot like a small smart phone, the ZuneHD is a sleek and attractive device with a nice touch screen and a brushed metal back. Having never before used one of these I was a little confused at first on how it worked but the learning curve is easy and it took little time to get used to it. It works a lot like a tablet, actually. The screen is very responsive and navigation is simple.

I confess that I never used the ear buds. Instead, I use a set of really nice noise-canceling head phones and the sound coming out of the Zune is excellent. My music of choice is usually techno-trance stuff so there is a lot of base and a lot of synthesizer, and by default the sound is well-balanced and clear.

So, my main use for an MP3 player is to connect it to my car. My car has voice-controlled everything and I wanted to be able to listen to my music collection in the car without fiddling with the player directly. When I used the iPod I found that the system frequently got confused and the player would often select the wrong song. If it got confused enough, it would hang the voice activation for controlling the MP3 player for weeks at a time, so I gave up and put my Zune in the car instead. So far, the Zune and the car work together nearly flawlessly. As a bonus, the car keeps the Zune charged up.

The only drawback I have found with the Zune is that there is no way to expand the storage capacity. It would be nice to have the ability to add a MicroSD card in to expand the capacity.

I am exceptionally satisfied with my Zune. I likely will never buy another iPod again, now that I know how much better an MP3 player can be.

I have a Dell laptop that has served me well and I also have an older Dell workstation that has been great. I had high hoped for this tower system, and unfortunately it doesn’t quite meet expectations. If you are looking for an affordable gaming system, this one will work on the lower end.

I’ll start with the positives.

It comes with a 7th-generation core i7 processor and it is definitely fast. It is not one of the low power consumption processors, so when you look at the CPU in the device manager you see 8 of them reported - this is a good thing.

Everything is integrated with this system and there are plenty of ports. You don’t need a separate graphics card (though you can add one - more on that in a minute), sound is built in, Bluetooth is built in too and it even has integrated wireless networking.

This is a very attractive system too, and it’s quiet. If you don’t like a noisy system\, this one has you covered.

It comes with 1TB storage. It’s disk-based so it’s slower than an SSD but with that amount of space you have more than enough space for most uses.

And, it’s affordable. It will not break the bank if you already have a monitor and keyboard/mouse combo.

And now for the bad news.

I am not the least bit impressed with the graphics card. With modern games the more graphics memory you have the better, and having only 2GB video RAM is not enough to get it done anymore. My son is an avid gamer and has demonstrated to me that his business-grade laptop gets better frame rates. So, we are shopping for a better and more generous graphics card.

Another area where we will be expanding is the system RAM. The RAM is DDR4 and it’s fast, but the system comes with only 8GB. Our present plan is to double it.

No documentation? I know that the trend is to not include install/recovery media, but come on - there should be more than just a quick start in the box.

This is a decent desktop system that would be find in a business environment, but it falls a little flat when it comes to gaming. It needs a better graphics card (well, at least more video RAM) and it needs more system RAM to be a respectable gaming system.

Really like this Chromebook so far. This is our 3rd Chromebook. My first Chromebook (now used by the kids) was an 11" Acer C720 from a couple of years ago. My second Chromebook was an 10" Asus Chromebook Flip from last year, which is very similar to this Acer R13, except that the screen on the Acer is much bigger. I still use the 10" Asus for air travel when something small and light is great for the suitcase, but the 10" size is really too cramped for everyday use.

The Acer R13 is better in almost every way than the Acer C720. The screen is sharper and more colorful. The keyboard and touchpad are much more responsive. The CPU is much faster, though not in the same league as the Intel Core CPUs that you find on the top-of-the-line Chromebooks. The metal case on the R13 is very professional looking compared to the plastic case on the C720. Battery life with the C720 was good, but great with the R13. Despite the bigger size and metal case, the R13 is only half a pound heavier than the C720. The R13 uses a standard USB-C charging cable, unlike the proprietary cable on the C720 that I am always worried about losing, but you do only get one USB-C port that is used for both charging and data transfer (2 ports would be nicer). The only thing I like better about the C720 is the full-sized SD card slot. For some reason, the R13 only has a micro-SD card slot, so you can't quickly pull the SD card out of your camera and view the photos on your laptop screen. Also, most people have a pile of old SD cards that they could use reuse, but micro-SD is less common. Why Acer???

The R13 has a touchscreen, which my Asus Flip also has. The Acer C720 does not have a touchscreen. For Chrome apps, the touchscreen isn't that useful. However, Android apps are available for the R13 (if you switch the Chrome beta channel) and also the Asus Flip. Android brings a whole new level of functionality to Chromebooks. A larger screen improves the user experience of many Android apps and just having these apps available makes your Chromebook much more useful since most Android apps have better user interfaces or better functionality than Chrome web apps. Android apps are especially interesting when you are using your Chromebook without a WiFi connection since Android apps are much more likely (than Chrome apps) to be functional without an internet connection. Many if not most Android apps are much easier to use with a touchscreen vs the touch pad. If you're going to use Android apps, definately buy a Chromebook with a touchscreen. The glossy touchscreen on the R13 does collect fingerprints pretty quickly, though.

Yes, $400 is a lot for a Chromebook, but Chromebooks are a lot more functional these days, especially now that they run Android apps. You can get a slow cheap Windows laptop for the same price, but a Chromebook starts up so much faster that you'll really only want to use Windows if you need to use particular apps that are not available for Chrome or Android.

In the days of COVID... this is how the story begins. Let's set it up. Combine the elements of Work from Home, quiet space at a premium, available enclosed semi-outdoor space, and awesome weather, and you have a situation where the enclosed patio becomes not just ideal for the day-to-day work schedule, but it becomes AWESOME! Only problem is the wifi is on the other end of the property with a solid home construction bulkhead in between along with a sheer wall and other means of interference. I was dropping Zoom meetings, getting late messages, I had a solid 4-5 seconds of speech delay, and my phone would not alert me to anything.

At that point I thought, maybe the router just isn't strong enough. It's only about 40 feet away but still. So I took a chance on a reasonably priced and well-featured (this one) version of a wifi-extender and I am now at full speed. No drops, no lagging, full speed even through a VPN connection. I wasn't sure this was going to be the answer to my speed issues since the base connection isn't terribly fast, but it absolutely worked.

I do need to bring up a quick caveat... the word "extender" may be misleading. The means of extension is by acting as a relay. Thus in order to connect to the home network via the extender, you actually need to connect to the extender instead. If you are prone to moving about the house/property/office, and you need the strongest available connection, you may find that you need to manually switch back and forth to whichever is strongest in the particular location you are at in relation to either the wireless router or the extender. For my purposes this was fine since my work computer stayed put... I just had to switch wifi networks on my phone when I worked in that location.

This is the first switch that I have owned that can be configured.  That's a big plus.  Once you determine the IP address of the switch, you simply enter it in your browser, enter the default password (which you can change) and you are into the setup program that is internal to the switch.  You can do individual settings for each of the 8 ports, if you know what the settings mean (I didn't.)  This is an optional thing; you can use the switch without any configuration; just plug it in and it is ready to go.  There are two reasons why I didn't give this a 5 star rating.  1) The indicator lights showing active ports are on the same side as the cables.  Since I want cables to go out the back, I can't see the lights with the switch facing me.  My prior switch had lights on one side and cables went out the other.  In all honesty, I can't say that the lights ever provided much benefit and could be distracting, so this might be an advantage to some people to have both lights and cables on the back.  What's the point of the lights if you can't see them, unless you want the cables facing you?  2) In order to register the switch and get a program to determine the IP address of the switch (so that you can configure it), you have to use a mobile device (a smart phone) and install the Netgear Insight application and set up a Netgear account.  Strange that you need to use a device other than a computer to do this and it is rather a nuisance.  Apparently there is no Windows version of Netgear Insight.  You have to use your IOS or Android device.  Another problem I had is that you supposedly can change your password on your device, which I tried, but apparently the password did not meet the requirements, but was never informed of that by the program.  I was able to change the password on the device after getting into it via the IP address.  Netgear makes good products and I have purchased other Netgear products in the past with good results.  This is another quality product, so if the placement of the lights doesn't bother you, I would recommend it, especially if you need individually configurable ports.

I received these phones as a review sample and wanted to test the claim that they are studio quality. In point of fact they are very close. What I mean by studio quality is they are neutral sounding - there is no bias towards any particular frequency band. These are fairly even on the highs, mids and lows.

Of course, if you are listening to modern music that emphasizes low frequency response with a lot of bass you may want to check out other phones that do a better job. I will say that while the frequencies are naturally divided, the separation is excellent so I am certain these phones have a crossover.

Since there are ample specs in the product description (and two video reviews at the time of this one) I will spare you a recitation of that information. I tested these using a few key albums, and also plugged the 1/4 inch connector directly into my Roland RD-300NX keyboard to hear that instrument's natural responses. Both tests confirmed that these are studio quality. However, audiophiles who want unbiased sound will also love them. I played some of my favorite test albums like Miles Davis' Kind of Blue, Ahmad Jamal's Live at the Pershing and some 20-bit mastered CDs. In all cases the frequency response in each band was perfect and the ability to hear nuances (including the natural reverb on Kind of Blue) was a treat. More importantly I heard the albums the way the engineers wanted me to hear them.

To be sure I do have other phones that are at this level of quality, but most are in a much higher price range. I did not expect to be impressed with I accepted a review sample, but not that I've had time to put these through their paces I am impressed. They are now in my practice room/music studio and there they will remain. Definitely recommended.

Wow! Talk about an effortless, totally-bubble-free installation of a screen protector on a large tablet! This crystal-clear MOSHI IVISOR XT NO-BUBBLE SCREEN PROTECTOR installed in less than a minute on my Kindle Fire HDX 8.9" tablet--or in about two minutes, if you include the time it took to wipe the screen with a microfiber cloth (included). There were absolutely no bubbles that needed to be coaxed out with a cardboard "squeegee" (definitely not included!).

The "secret" behind the easy Moshi iVisor installation is that only the black band around the edges of the protector sheet has adhesive. When there's no adhesive in the middle of the protector sheet, you can't catch dust motes or air bubbles between the sheet and the tablet's backlit viewing area.

Also, the protector sheet is made of stiff plastic that makes it easy to handle. You just place the sheet gently on the tablet, using the camera and light sensor cutouts as a guide, and then apply light pressure to the black edges to secure the adhesive. If you get the placement wrong, you can try again, because the screen protector is removable. It can even be removed, stored away, and reapplied at a later time.

Once the screen protector is installed, it's virtually invisible. There is no loss of touchscreen sensitivity, and the protector itself is crystal clear. I've installed a lot of screen protector film--on cameras, cellphones, and 7" and 9" tablets--and until now I thought it would be impossible for anyone to make a screen protector for a large tablet that would go on bubble-free and also be invisible after the installation. This Moshi iVisor XT screen protector has proved me wrong.

When I first set up a home network, I selected a Cisco "Linkys" G router (EA1300) because I recognized the brand name. Later I upgraded to a Cisco dual-band N router ([[ASIN:B007IL7AKM Linksys EA4500]]), which was--and still is--a superb router. My latest upgrade, to this LINKSYS AC1900 (EA6900) DUAL BAND SMART WI-FI ROUTER, represents another leap forward in the performance of my home network.

The wireless signal is stronger in every corner of my two-story condo. All of my devices (some 25 computers, tablets, music players, Kindles, cellphones, Roku, etc.) connect very quickly. Best of all, I'm getting Comcast's promised high-speed Internet speeds of more than 50 Mbps with the Comcast-supplied new telephony modem. (An online speed test site just now clocked the download speed at 57 Mbps). In fact, my present home network is capable of even faster speeds--the home network is limited by the speed of the slower external Comcast network.

This router is extremely easy to set up. You just connect it, and follow the prompts from the built-in software. Whenever you access the router to adjust the settings, and click on some part of the Menu, you find excellent "contextual" help screens that fully explain the meaning of each of the settings. The Menu is set up differently from the menus for the EA4500 and EA1300, but the basic methodology for the settings is the same--the settings are just presented in a way that's easier for a non-techie user to understand.

I read a newspaper review that recommended NOT buying this excellent EA6900 router, because of testers' problems with the second band and with nonfunctioning USB ports. I think that the testers probably received a defective router--and should have requested a replacement. Even a reliable brand like Cisco may sometimes ship an occasional bad electronics device.

Because I only need a single-band router, I haven't tested the second band on my EA6900 router. (The second band did work fine on my EA4500 router, but using the second band didn't improve the signal strength, so I didn't continue using it.) However, I did test the USB ports on the EA6900, and both work really well. In fact, the router recognized and easily accessed a couple of external wireless storage drives--connected with a 100-foot (!) USB cable--when my PC was flakey about recognizing those same drives when they were connected directly to the PC with the long cable.

I absolutely love this EA6900 router, which I've been using for more than a month now. Because of my home wiring, the router is located a long way from any of my wireless devices, and I have a lot of nearby neighbors with competing wireless Internet connections. But with the EA6900, there have been virtually no dropped connections, and the strong signal is something that I've long been wishing for!

WARNING- This is going to be an in depth review. I will be adding to this as time goes on and we are able to use more features of this intricate router. We have had quite a few challenges which prevented us from setting this up quickly like we expected. I am reviewing this in depth as we continue to use it because we finally got it to work correctly and I want to let you know a few things that are important for now.
---------------------------------------------------------------

Wow. Have you ever gotten something you expect to be a quick set up and off you go using it without a hitch? As you install your item onto your network, suddenly, that fast and easy prospect turns out to be ridiculously complex and frustrating. That was our experience with this router. Let's see what happened.

WHAT IS THIS ROUTER LIKE?
WARNING! THIS WILL NOT HANG ON THE WALL
First things first- we like to hang our routers on the wall. This router can not be hung on the wall. That was obstacle 1 for us. We had to try to figure out something that would work in our room. We have a network, but it is not near our desktop. The things from around the house that need to reach the router- and the modem, well it has to be hung on the wall.

The trick was to find a way to hang it on the wall that would allow us to work with it, connect and disconnect cables when needed, and still be able to see it. Then we had to put the modem near it too. This is a rather large router. I have enclosed a photo of what we finally found that made this work out. We used a mail holder which also allowed us to attach the modem to the front of it making it a nice centralized tech center near the location where it had to be.

WHAT WILL THIS DO?
There are a lot of antennae on this router, so things can get a better signal. There are also quite a few capabilities of this router which are really nice.
-There are a variety of ways you can get this up and running, one of which is the internet wizard.
-You can set up a Geo-filter
-You can use an anti-bufferbloat feature (devices which are hogging too much can have certain amounts allocated )
-You can allocate bandwidth to each device
-You can manage traffic allocation
-You can add keyword blocks to prevent certain sites from accessing your information
-You can set up a guest wi-fi network so that if you have visitors they can use your service w/o password
-Share USB storage on router devices
-You can set up a VPN connection
There is more, but that gives an overview of many of the things you can do with this router.

HOW DID THIS SET UP FOR US?
We had no end of internet problems for a while so again we were unable to get this set up. Finally once the internet stabilized again in our area, we were able to try to set this up. Once we set it up, it would look like all was well, but it would not recognize the internet. Because the internet has to be disabled to set up the router, it makes it hard to work on the router when you can not consult the internet to see what to do.

We finally discovered that there is an update that needed to be installed with this router. The update is XR500-V2.3.2.32. We downloaded it to the desktop and then installed it as per instructions. FINALLY THE ROUTER WORKED!

HOW HAS THE PERFORMANCE BEEN?
We have avid gamers in our home, and although they have not been playing as much as usual, they are definitely noticing a much smoother experience in the gameplay. As for other devices, they have been doing a wonderful job. With the wi-fi on our modem, we were constantly having buffering, dropped signals, etc on our devices. Since installing the router, we have had far less issue and the performance is much better.

We have had two people in the house playing games online, someone watching roku and another using the internet for surfing, and all good performance and smoother experiences than before.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a power packed router with lots of fabulous features. It took much longer for us to install than we expected, but much of it was due to finding a way to mount it first, and then trying to overcome the glitch that would not let it recognize the internet. We have seen great improvement in performance from daily tasks to gaming.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. The performance made it worth it to go through the frustration to find a way to mount it, and to also overcome the glitch. I still think they should have made a way to wall mount this. I was tempted to remove a star for that, but it is not really enough to remove a whole star.

Here is where this bag falls short. In an effort to make the backpack compact there is little storage space and it’s just not comfortable to carry on the back. The laptops padded location is directly resting on the users back - this is not unusual in backpacks of this style but with this particular bag it feels stiff and awkward. Regardless of how I’ve tried to shift and arrange items within the bag this backpack is just not comfortable in use. Had additional padding been used between the laptop and the surface that rests against the users back it would have helped as would allow for the bag to shape more to how backpacks are carried.

Once a laptop and power adapter are packed inside this backpack there is little room left for anything more than a few flat folders. This lack of capacity makes it impractical for students who must carry all they need for a day of classes.

I had been looking at these types of drawing tablets and wanted to give this one a try. I'm not a professional, and I know that things like "lag" are sometimes a concern, but I personally didnt find excessive lag (not that I could notice, anyway). Installation was a breeze, simply download the apps and away you go. (I'm using a windows 10 system). I was able to immediately use the Penwalker thing on my main screen with nothing open (scribbling notes right across my screen, etc). Then I pulled open photos hoping and tried some simple scribbling- that's when I noticed that the touch sensitive nature of this system is really effective - pressure effects line weight, etc. The pens are lightweight, yet the pressure sensitivity gives them a certain "feel". I think I could get used to this.

Then I opened Clip Studio Paint Pro and just doodled for a moment. Alternating between brushes, fades, erasers, etc. Again, the "feel" is what impressed me most (in spite of the lightweight pens). There's function buttons identified right on the tablet, (everything appears to work as it should), and when you bring the pens tip within an inch or so of the tablets screen, you can use to pen like a mouse to position the cursor- then touch the screen to do your work. Same with the eraser end - turn the pen around and point the eraser end to the screen and position your cursor with it - then touch down to erase.

As an amateur, I've barely scratched the surface of this tablets capabilities, but I can already tell that it's going to be fun learning some new skills as I spend more time with this. For me, this one's a winner!

I use earbuds a lot since I typically prefer the lightness and ease of use compared with traditional headphones. Right out of the box these were a bit puzzling as to how to position them for use. But, after a bit of fiddling with the over-the-ear loop, it becomes clear.

The in-ear comfort is good. It comes with a variety of ear tips including two types I’ve not used before: a double flange silicon tip and a triple flange silicon tip. The flanges allow the ear bud to make a much better seal in your ear canal. That not only helps cut out ambient noise intruding, it also improves the bass response. I found the double flange works best for me, but the variety of tips included appears sufficient to fit pretty much any ear.

It also comes with an excellent case for storage, and adapters for airplane use and for 1/4 inch plugs. I especially like the case since it’s small enough to make it easy to carry along (roughly 3.5 inches by 3 by 1.5 inches thick) and is reinforced to avoid being crushed. It has mesh pockets to keep everything stowed, and looks nice to boot (black with red contrast in the middle). All-in-all, it’s a great kit in terms of useful accessories.

I’m not as pleased with the cord. While I like how sturdy it is, it has a “Y” link that always seems to be in the way when I’m working out. I got used to it eventually, but a more streamlined cord system would have been a better design approach. Another negative is the 3.5mm plug. It needs to be seated just so or you get sound cut-outs or static. I tried it with several devices to be sure the issue is with the plug and not the device. A more robust plug is needed for this – you shouldn’t have to fiddle with it to get it to seat properly.

The over-the-ear loops are also a bit annoying at first. Granted, that’s certainly due to the fact that I usually use standard in-ear buds without the loop, so any type of loop feels weird to me at first. The material is soft and bendy, so you can position it in any variety of ways. It could benefit from some additional padding. On the plus side, they do hold the buds in very well. Quick head movements that would have loosened an in-ear bud didn’t jar these loose at all.

Now for the really important feature: how they sound. In a word, excellent. My benchmark for moderately-priced earbuds has been units made by RHA out of the UK. These sound nearly as good. Very clean sound but still ample bass provided that you select the right tip. For me, the standard tip (the one installed as delivered) gave me very little in terms of bass. Selecting a different tip to provide a better ear fit did wonders for bass response.

They are a bit more airy than the RHA sound. That could be a plus or a minus depending on your preferred type of music. Very heavy bass music is not a good match for these. Pretty much everything else is, and I appreciated the enhanced clarity. It’s the type of sound that, when you hear it, the first word that would come to mind is “clean.”

They look odd, make take you a moment to figure out how to position them, but provide a very open, natural sound. It comes with a well-designed kit of useful extras. However, the plug issues, the cord, and the ear loops collectively knock it down a star. Still well worth considering, however, and I would certainly recommend them.

You may know about the announcement from Lenovo a few weeks ago that going forward the company will be certifying all their ThinkPad and Thinkstation workstations for Linux. First things first: If you're looking for a gaming computer or something to handle graphics-intensive programs, this isn't it. It doesn't have a screaming fast processor, although it is a capable one. The onboard AMD Raven graphics module is pretty capable (I tried it out on a big display), but this model has no expansion slot for a video or audio card or any other such upgrades.

It does have a bay for a big 3.5 inch HDD with SATA connectors. And it comes with a 256GB SSD already installed on the motherboard. It also comes with 4GB RAM (and a second slot to add more), and a wired keyboard and mouse and the power supply. It has four USB 2.0 ports in the back, and two 2.0 and two 3.0 (gen 1) USB ports in the front. Also on the front are a card reader slot, the optical drive, mic and headset connection ports, and the power button. The back also has an HDMI port, VGA-out port, and and ethernet port.

It's about the size of an ITX mini tower form factor box, which is a little larger than a big dictionary. It stands upright, so the footprint is pretty small. And it's lightweight compared to a big desktop box.

I didn't even complete the first boot into Windows before attempting a Linux install. Tapping F2 on boot will get you into a graphical menu for picking your boot device, and F12 will get you into a deeper menu for selecting boot order and into the BIOS.

I have worked with several K&F Concept lenses and filters in the past and I have had excellent results with them. I am still very much a beginning photographer and I am still learning as I go but I have learned a lot in the process. One of the things I have especially come to appreciate is the fisheye effect. Up to this point I have only had the ability to work this out via software, so I was pleased to have the opportunity to work with this fisheye lens. So far I have had a lot of fun with it and I love how it works, though I have again learned a few things along the way.

A fisheye lens is somewhat similar to a magnifying glass with a great deal of distortion. The center comes out clear and the edges are distorted and warped, giving the effect of looking through a lens that is very thick in the middle and thins out towards the edges. Straight edge objects like sidewalks become warped and bent.

This particular lens is a chunky and hefty fellow, actually comprised of two lenses instead of just one. There is a large macro lens that can work independently of the fisheye lens and it is very good for taking very close-up shots. The fisheye lens attaches to this macro lens and relies on it.

I took several shots with the fisheye lens and I discovered something I did not realize though it is fairly obvious now. When using the minimum amount of zoom, the distortion is maximized and you get the most effect. The more you zoom in the more dampened the effect though it is still noticeable. I used the lens to take two pictures of the case in which the fisheye lens packs, one zoomed in all the way and one zoomed out all the way. For the one zoomed out, you can see the warping effect on the blinds over the windows and you even can see the entire image framed in a black circle. The image zoomed in has minimal distortion.

I should state that this particular lens is designed for 58mm threads. Make sure your camera can use it before you buy it. If you have a different thread size for your lens, buy the right sized fisheye for that lens.

This is one of the most fun lenses I have. It works great and it does a good job of giving the distortion you want with a fisheye lens, and it is not particularly expensive. I am very pleased with it and am looking forward to working with it for many years.

Software: The card comes with its own recording program which I have not used since I found Windows Media Center to be much more to my liking. You will, however, have to install the software to get the remote working, after which you can uninstall it. Usability:
This card has worked flawlessly for me since the day I installed it. I have only used it to record TV from a basic cable feed, though it can also record from an antenna or FM radio. One thing I will note (because I don't believe the description states this) is that with only one cable feed plugged in, the card is capable of recording on two channels at once. I was pleasantly surprised by this.

These have been my experiences. Yours will probably vary.
